bullets: DynamicMCPBench is a new framework for evaluating agents against live, stateful Model Context Protocol servers, which expose external tools to a model. It generates goals, executes them to record successful trajectories, and moves beyond scoring only the final answer or a fixed tool list. Together with the new MCPAgentBench sandbox, which adds irrelevant tools as distractors, it reflects a recurring pressure in this captured feed to test tool use under changing execution conditions rather than static prompts alone. Why it matters: If you are choosing an evaluation for tool-using agents, these releases let you test whether an agent selects and executes tools correctly on your own servers, not merely whether it produces a plausible answer after an unseen sequence of actions. Evidence: E002, E001. High confidence.

GUI-360° is a new Windows desktop-agent dataset containing 17,000 trajectories and 131,000 validated successful action steps, plus 1.09 million failed steps. Each step includes screenshots, accessibility metadata, goals, reasoning traces, and structured graphical-interface or Application Programming Interface actions. Why it matters: If you build agents for office applications, the inclusion of failed executions changes the evaluation choice: the same resource can measure action grounding and inspect where workflows break, while also supplying material for future recovery training instead of treating only completed tasks as useful data. Evidence: E003. High confidence.

COLLABMEM is a new diagnostic benchmark for memory in systems where multiple language-model agents collaborate. Its controlled harness holds the execution trace, target role, answerer, judge, and correct event fixed, so it can attribute failures to sharing, access control, routing, source tracking, conflict resolution, or retention rather than reporting one recall score. Why it matters: If you are evaluating persistent memory for multi-agent products, this design separates whether information was remembered from whether it reached the authorized role, retained its source, and was updated by more authoritative information. That supports component-level debugging and permission testing. Evidence: E006. High confidence.

PopResume is a new resume-screening fairness benchmark that preserves population-based relationships among attributes and measures causal pathways. It separates effects mediated by job-relevant qualifications from effects mediated by demographic proxies, rather than relying only on differences in final scores between groups. Why it matters: If you audit language- or vision-language-model resume screeners, PopResume changes the question from whether two groups receive different outcomes to how a protected attribute influenced a score. That can help distinguish qualification-related pathways from proxy-based redlining within the benchmark’s stated design. Evidence: E023. Medium confidence.

SpeechRole is a new speech-to-speech role-playing resource with 98 roles and 111,000 conversations. Its evaluation operates directly on generated audio and measures interaction ability, vocal expressiveness, and fidelity to the assigned role, preserving cues such as tone, rhythm, and emphasis that text transcripts omit. Why it matters: If you are selecting an evaluation suite for spoken characters or assistants, this artifact tests the delivered audio experience rather than reducing speech to words. That makes it relevant when model choice depends on expressive behavior and role consistency as well as textual content. Evidence: E005. High confidence.

QUANTA is a new English-to-Arabic machine-translation error dataset organized into a four-level taxonomy with 23 detailed error classes and severity-oriented analysis, rather than collapsing heterogeneous translation failures into one score. It combines structurally validated synthetic training examples with a held-out test set of real examples. Why it matters: If you compare Arabic translation systems, QUANTA can reveal which error types account for a score difference and whether failures are concentrated in particular categories. Its mixture of synthetic and real data also means users can keep training-oriented analysis separate from the real held-out evaluation. Evidence: E009. High confidence.
bullets_zh: DynamicMCPBench 是一个新框架，用于在实时、有状态的 Model Context Protocol 服务器上评估智能体，这些服务器会向模型开放外部工具。它生成目标并执行这些目标以记录成功轨迹，从而突破仅对最终答案或固定工具列表进行评分的方式。结合新增的 MCPAgentBench 沙箱——该沙箱会加入无关工具作为干扰项——它反映了这批采集信息中反复出现的一种趋势：在不断变化的执行条件下测试工具使用，而不只是使用静态提示词。Why it matters: 如果你正在为工具调用型智能体选择评估方法，这些发布成果可让你测试智能体能否在你自己的服务器上正确选择并执行工具，而不只是判断它在一段不可见的操作序列之后能否给出看似合理的答案。Evidence: E002, E001. High confidence.

GUI-360° 是一个新的 Windows 桌面智能体数据集，包含 17,000 条轨迹、131,000 个经过验证的成功操作步骤，以及 1.09 million 个失败步骤。每个步骤都包含屏幕截图、无障碍元数据、目标、推理轨迹，以及结构化的图形界面或 Application Programming Interface 操作。Why it matters: 如果你为办公应用构建智能体，纳入失败执行会改变评估选择：同一资源既能衡量操作定位能力并检查工作流在何处中断，也能为未来的恢复训练提供材料，而不是只把已完成的任务视为有用数据。Evidence: E003. High confidence.

COLLABMEM 是一个新的诊断型基准，用于评估多个语言模型智能体协作系统中的记忆能力。其受控测试框架会固定执行轨迹、目标角色、作答者、评判者和正确事件，因此能够将失败归因于共享、访问控制、路由、来源追踪、冲突解决或信息保留，而不是只报告单一的回忆分数。Why it matters: 如果你正在评估多智能体产品的持久记忆，这种设计可将信息是否被记住，与信息是否传递到获授权的角色、是否保留来源，以及是否由更具权威性的信息更新区分开来。这有助于开展组件级调试和权限测试。Evidence: E006. High confidence.

PopResume 是一个新的简历筛选公平性基准，可保留基于群体的属性关系并衡量因果路径。它将由工作相关资质中介的影响与由人口统计代理变量中介的影响分离开来，而不是只依赖群体之间最终分数的差异。Why it matters: 如果你审计基于语言模型或视觉语言模型的简历筛选系统，PopResume 会将问题从两个群体是否得到不同结果，转变为受保护属性如何影响分数。这有助于在该基准所述设计范围内，区分与资质相关的路径和基于代理变量的歧视性排斥。Evidence: E023. Medium confidence.

SpeechRole 是一个新的语音到语音角色扮演资源，包含 98 个角色和 111,000 段对话。其评估直接针对生成的音频进行，衡量交互能力、声音表现力以及对指定角色的忠实度，并保留文本转录会遗漏的语气、节奏和重音等线索。Why it matters: 如果你正在为语音角色或助手选择评估套件，这项资源测试的是实际交付的音频体验，而不是将语音简化为文字。因此，当模型选择不仅取决于文本内容，还取决于表现力和角色一致性时，它具有参考价值。Evidence: E005. High confidence.

QUANTA 是一个新的英译阿机器翻译错误数据集，采用 four-level 分类体系，包含 23 个详细错误类别，并开展面向严重程度的分析，而不是将性质各异的翻译失败压缩为单一分数。它将经过结构验证的合成训练样本与由真实样本组成的留出测试集结合起来。Why it matters: 如果你要比较阿拉伯语翻译系统，QUANTA 可以揭示哪些错误类型造成了分数差异，以及失败是否集中在特定类别。它同时包含合成数据和真实数据，这也意味着用户可以将面向训练的分析与真实留出评估分开进行。Evidence: E009. High confidence.

evidence_items.summary: Embodied planning is dedicated to the goal of building agents capable of perceiving, reasoning, and executing long-horizon tasks in physical environments. However, existing embodied benchmarks predominantly focus on single-agent execution or restricted multi-agent settings, leaving long-horizon tasks that involve complex inter-agent dependencies largely underexplored despite their prevalence in real-world embodied scenarios. To address this gap, we introduce CoEmbod, the first realistic 3D simulated embodied benchmark for long-horizon multi-agent embodied cooperation with diverse inter-agent dependencies. CoEmbod contains 155 expert-curated tasks across 40 scenes and 10845 objects, covering three cooperation regimes: spatial distribution, parallel constraint, and failure recovery. These regimes cover a broad spectrum of cooperative requirements, ranging from distributed task allocation to synchronized execution and assisted failure recovery. CoEmbod further provides a process-level evaluation framework with Budgeted Cooperative Success (BCS), which jointly measures goal completion, cooperation fidelity, and execution efficiency. Experiments reveal that even the leading LMM powering a well-established agentic workflow achieves only 20.23% success, highlighting the difficulty of long-horizon multi-agent cooperation with diverse inter-agent dependencies in complex embodied environments.
evidence_items.title: CoEmbod: A Long-Horizon Benchmark for Multi-Agent Embodied Cooperation with Diverse Inter-Agent Dependencies
evidence_items.watchlist_note: Evaluations targeting extended multi-step agent execution.

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly serving as autonomous agents, and their utilization of external tools via the Model Context Protocol (MCP) is considered a future trend. Current MCP evaluation sets suffer from issues such as reliance on external MCP services and a lack of difficulty awareness. To address these limitations, we propose MCPAgentBench, a benchmark based on real-world MCP definitions designed to evaluate the tool-use capabilities of agents. We construct a dataset containing authentic tasks and simulated MCP tools. The evaluation employs a dynamic sandbox environment that presents agents with candidate tool lists containing distractors, thereby testing their tool selection and discrimination abilities. Furthermore, we introduce comprehensive metrics to measure both task completion rates and execution efficiency. Experiments conducted on state-of-the-art LLMs reveal significant performance differences in handling complex, multi-step tool invocations. All code is open-source at https://github.com/Brunestuder/MCPAgentBench.
evidence_items.title: MCPAgentBench: A Real-world Task Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Agent MCP Tool Use

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents are increasingly deployed over Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, yet the benchmarks used to evaluate them score the final answer or a fixed “ground-truth” list of tools, both of which are fragile once the underlying data is live and stateful. We present DynamicMCPBench, a reusable framework rather than a fixed dataset. A practitioner can run it on their own MCP servers to test models on their own tasks, or let it collect servers automatically to measure a model's general ability to solve agentic tasks. Given the servers and any set of models, it generates realistic goals, pursues each one live to record a successful trajectory, distills that trajectory into path-agnostic effect checkpoints, and scores an agent on whether it reproduces those effects, never on the final answer. To show what the framework reveals, we run it at scale: 24 models over 121 servers and 750 tasks spread evenly over 15 task categories (50 each), where each category targets a distinct tool-use challenge of the generated questions. Each task is scored by pass³, it counts as solved only if all three independent attempts succeed. Even the strongest agents solve only about half of the tasks, 31% of tasks are solved by no model at all, and accuracy collapses as the required tool chain grows longer (from 39% on the shortest chains to 13% on the longest). A human validation study confirms the automatic scoring is reliable (chance-corrected agreement of 0.76). DynamicMCPBench thus turns benchmark construction into something practitioners can rerun on their own servers and models, while exposing a consistent inability of current agents to handle long, multi-step agentic tasks.
evidence_items.title: DynamicMCPBench: A Trace-Grounded, Effect-Scored Benchmark for LLM Agents over Live MCP Servers

evidence_items.summary: We introduce GUI-360°, a large-scale dataset and benchmark suite for desktop productivity computer-using agents (CUAs). GUI-360° provides an automated pipeline for query sourcing, template-based environment construction, task instantiation, batched execution, and LLM-assisted quality filtering in Windows office applications. The corpus contains 131K validated successful action steps across 17K trajectories for training and evaluation, together with 1.09M failed execution steps for failure analysis and future recovery training. Each step provides screenshots, accessibility metadata, instantiated goals, reasoning traces, and structured GUI/API actions. GUI-360° supports GUI grounding, screen parsing, and action prediction under a hybrid GUI+API action space. Experiments show that current vision–language models struggle with fine-grained grounding and stepwise action prediction, while supervised fine-tuning on GUI-360° brings consistent in-domain and external benchmark gains. Our code and dataset are available at https://github.com/2020-qqtcg/GUI-360 and https://huggingface.co/datasets/vyokky/GUI-360.
evidence_items.title: GUI-360° : A Comprehensive Dataset and Benchmark for Desktop Productivity Computer-Using Agents

evidence_items.summary: Speech is essential for realistic role-playing, yet existing work on role-playing agents largely centers on text, leaving Speech Role-Playing Agents (SRPAs) underexplored and without systematic evaluation. We introduce SpeechRole, a unified framework for developing and assessing SRPAs. SpeechRole-Data contains 98 roles and 111k speech-to-speech conversations with rich timbre and prosodic variation, providing large-scale resources for training SRPAs. SpeechRole-Eval offers a multidimensional benchmark that directly evaluates generated speech, preserving paralinguistic cues and measuring interaction ability, speech expressiveness, and role-playing fidelity. Experiments show that end-to-end SRPAs such as GPT-4o Audio achieve strong fluency and naturalness, but remain limited in prosody consistency and emotion appropriateness. Current open-source end-to-end models exhibit clear performance gaps, particularly in interaction ability and role-playing fidelity, while several cascaded systems achieve relatively stable performance on these dimensions. Furthermore, role-specific training can further improve the role-playing capabilities of end-to-end SRPAs.
evidence_items.title: SpeechRole: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Evaluating Speech Role-Playing Agents

organizations: Institute of Automation, Chinese Academy of Sciences
evidence_items.summary: Multi-agent LLM systems increasingly rely on persistent memory to coordinate role-specialized work. Correctness requires more than recalling a fact: the fact must reach the right role, remain hidden from unauthorized roles, carry the right source, and update when a more authoritative value appears. We introduce COLLABMEM, a diagnostic benchmark for collaborative memory operations. Its matched memory-only harness fixes the trace, target role, answerer, judge, and gold event, localizing errors to sharing, access, routing, provenance, conflict resolution, or retention. COLLABMEM contains 58 hand-authored scenarios (1,118 core probes), a 174-scenario scaled split (3,359 probes), adversarial and compositional hard sets, and six transactive-memory competencies. We also propose TMS-GRAPH++, a scope-aware graph memory framework with role-filtered views, writer/provenance structure, and temporal [CURRENT] marking. Across five evaluation splits, TMS-GRAPH++ achieves the highest non-Oracle average score (69.6%). Evaluations using the official SDKs of Mem0, Letta, and A-Mem show that shared archives help, but reliable collaborative memory still requires explicit visibility, provenance, authority, and retention policies. We will release the dataset, evaluation code, and reproduced outputs to support future work on multi-agent memory systems.
evidence_items.title: COLLABMEM: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Collaborative Memory Operations in Multi-Agent LLM Systems

evidence_items.summary: Reproducible evaluation artifacts, summary tables, and standalone Python scoring scripts for local AI coding-agent memory and session search tools. LongMemEval-S: 470 cleaned questions (88.9% hit@1, 97.4% hit@5, 0.926 MRR) and 500 full questions (88.2% hit@1, 97.2% hit@5, 0.921 MRR), run with deja-vu 0.23.2 without LLM query rewriting or embeddings. LoCoMo (retrieval-only metrics): 1,982 questions (71.9% hit@1, 91.4% hit@5, 0.802 MRR); reports retrieval metrics only and redistributes no upstream CC-BY-NC-4.0 dialogue text. Day-Zero Cold Start (19,195 sessions on disk): head-to-head comparison of seven tools (deja-vu, ctx, CASS, agentsview, agentmemory, MemPalace, claude-mem) covering index build time, search latency, hit@k, and standing MCP tools/list schema overhead (measured against deja-vu 0.23.2 / commit 9906e203). Task-Cost & Compaction Ablations: 11-run alternating repository tasks (commit 54f6f6ab), multi-session context readiness chains, and 43 real context compactions.
evidence_items.title: Coding Agent Memory Benchmark: LongMemEval-S, LoCoMo, and 19,195-Session Day-Zero Evaluation

organizations: Shanghai Jiao Tong University; Shanghai Artificial Intelligence Laboratory
evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated remarkable potential in medical AI through their natural language understanding and reasoning capabilities. However, real clinical practice involves multi-stage, dynamically evolving decision-making where physicians continuously adjust pathways based on updated examination results—far more complex than single-turn question answering. Existing medical benchmarks focus on static scenarios, failing to evaluate LLMs in realistic clinical environments. We present MMedAgentBench, a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating LLM-based medical agents in multi-stage clinical decision-making. Unlike previous benchmarks, MMedAgentBench captures the temporal complexity of clinical workflows by simulating authentic patient journeys across multiple diagnostic and treatment stages. The benchmark comprises a high-quality dataset of over 150 de-identified clinical cases from tertiary hospitals, encompassing 500+ clinical stages, with each case meticulously structured into sequential stages and annotated by board-certified physicians. Our evaluation framework simultaneously assesses diagnostic accuracy and resource efficiency, requiring agents to plan examinations and control costs while navigating progressive information disclosure. This enables systematic evaluation of medical agents across dynamic decision-making, cost control, and multi-stage reasoning dimensions, providing a realistic testbed for advancing medical AI toward clinical deployment.
evidence_items.title: MMedAgentBench: A Multi-Stage Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-based Medical Agents

organizations: Shaanxi University of Science and Technology
evidence_items.summary: Evaluating LLMs for crisis communication requires more than judging isolated responses, because public feedback and competitor actions can reshape trust over time. Existing benchmarks remain largely static and single-turn, offering limited evidence about long-horizon risk-sensitive communication. We introduce BrandEval, a two-track benchmark for product-crisis communication, focusing on public brand responses to product-related safety, quality, service, and trust incidents. BrandEval-Static evaluates stakeholder-aware strategic analysis, while BrandEval-Dynamic stress-tests response policies in BrandPolis, a controlled multi-agent sandbox with consumer feedback, competitor responses, and trust-risk trajectories. We also construct BrandSRD, a Chinese crisis-response dataset, and instantiate a reference Strategic Agent using Strategic Rationale (SR). Across proprietary and open-source models, we find that static strategic quality is informative but incomplete: it aligns with some end-state outcomes but does not reliably predict volatility and delayed recovery; dynamic stress tests further expose tail-risk failures under manipulative or weakly grounded policies. The code and dataset will be available at https://github.com/htgan-ai/BrandEval.
evidence_items.title: BrandEval: A Two-Track Multi-Agent Benchmark for Risk-Sensitive LLM Crisis Communication

evidence_items.summary: Despite rapid advances in Code LLMs, their training datasets are often opaque due to proprietary and competitive concerns. Since many evaluation benchmarks are open-source and widely available online, models may unintentionally train on them, leading to data contamination that compromises evaluation validity. Reliable techniques for detecting whether a code snippet appears in a model’s training data are therefore essential. Compared with natural language, code contamination detection presents two unique challenges. First, code tokens from different syntactic categories contribute unequally to contamination signals, making uniform token treatment ineffective. Second, models trained on semantically equivalent code variants can evade detectors based solely on text matching. To address these challenges, we propose a syntax-aware framework that explicitly models token-type contributions. With a lightweight supervised detector trained on few labels, it captures contamination signals efficiently. Experiments across 8 Code LLMs, 2 languages, and 4 code transformations show absolute AUC gains of 8–10% for pretraining data detection and 15–20% for fine-tuning data detection, with AUC exceeding 90% on most fine-tuned tasks. Our work demonstrates that syntax-aware modeling is essential for trustworthy Code LLM evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Syntax-Aware Detection of Training Data Contamination in Code LLMs

evidence_items.summary: Comprehensively evaluating AI agents across interactive environments is difficult due to fragmented tasks, scaffolds, verifiers, and scoring rules. Unfortunately, existing efforts to unify these evaluations are limited in scale and domain, making costly reruns necessary and leaving available data incomparable. We introduce MESSIER, a unified corpus of 957,611 records spanning 30 benchmarks, 745 agents, 11,891 tasks, and 74,263 verifiers. MESSIER combines public evaluation results with new runs on six underrepresented professional and scientific benchmarks, standardizing their heterogeneous components into a common schema. Using this corpus, we show that frontier progress is uneven across benchmark groups, with function-calling evaluations largely saturated, programming improving fastest, and enterprise workflows remaining most challenging. Counterfactual rescoring further shows that strict all-pass scoring in multi-verifier tasks can alter agent rankings. Finally, we derive capability scores from our corpus that correlate with Epoch's Evaluation Capability Index rankings at Spearman ρ = 0.84. The scores can also be estimated for subsets defined by domain, occupation, action space, or verifier type. In essence, MESSIER is a reusable resource for studying agent performance at scale, and a basis for designing better evaluations.
evidence_items.title: Messier: A High-Resolution Corpus for Cross-Benchmark Agent Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Clarification-aware multi-agent orchestration is challenging because systems must elicit missing information, maintain task state, and coordinate dependent subtasks. Existing benchmarks do not comprehensively evaluate such orchestration under underspecified user requests, focusing instead on end-to-end success or isolated abilities like tool use and dialogue. We introduce MACRO, a travel-domain benchmark designed to address these gaps by providing structured task tiers, process-level user-side and system-side milestone annotations that include expected user clarifications, and standardized sub-agent interfaces. MACRO-Full contains 107 fully annotated tasks with 703 milestones, and MACRO-Core provides a tractable 30-task subset with 164 milestones. We evaluate three representative orchestration frameworks and a reference decoupled planning–execution orchestrator (MACRO-DPE) using trace-level metrics and failure analysis. Results show that MACRO-DPE improves routing fidelity and execution efficiency while maintaining task completion, whereas staged planning ensures milestone coverage at higher cost. The dataset (https://huggingface.co/datasets/weier248/MACRO-bench) and code are publicly available at https://github.com/liuweie/MACRO-bench/.

evidence_items.summary: Automatic machine-translation (MT) metrics collapse heterogeneous errors into a single score. For Arabic, no fine-grained resource exists for diagnosing error types and severity. We introduce QUANTA, a 9,032-instance En to Ar MT-error dataset (738 real UNPC + 7,856 synthetic training instances, both structurally validated, plus a held-out 438-instance real Gold test set) annotated with Mizan (ميزان, "scale"), a new 23-class MQM-compatible taxonomy organised in a four-level hierarchy: 23 leaf classes rolling up to 14 subtypes, 5 parent groups, and 4 TQA dimensions. To make the resource usable, we release the Raqeeb (رقيب, "observer") classifier, an AraBERT-v2 model for predicting Mizan 23-class labels (5-fold Gold macro-F1 = 0.614 ± 0.017). Data quality is supported by ETCA (Error Taxonomy Cross-vendor Audit), an LLM-as-judge check in which a different-vendor model audits QUANTA instances for anchor validity and label fidelity, curbing same-family self-preference bias, and by dual-annotator validation (Gwet's AC1 = 0.97 synthetic; 0.83 real) on core taxonomy criteria. Ablations show that anchor-guided framing is decisive (without it, macro-F1 collapses to 0.114); that 738 structurally validated real samples are ≈12× more sample-efficient than synthetic data; and that, restricted to the classes with real-tier training support, combining both tiers outperforms real (0.656) or synthetic (0.312) alone. Code, data, prompts, and checkpoints are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: Quanta: A Fine-Grained Dataset and Benchmark for Arabic Machine-Translation Error Analysis

authors: Hang Zhang, Yuzhi Pan, Ziyao Zhong, Chaokun Wang, Shuo Cao, Zeyu Huang, Yue Xue, Fang Niu, Bofan Xie, Guanchen Ge, Zecheng Li, Leqi Zheng, Ziyang Liu, Wei Wang, Miao Gu
evidence_items.summary: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) is a well-established paradigm for augmenting large language models (LLMs) with information retrieved from external corpora. However, developing effective RAG systems requires substantial engineering effort and iterative experimentation, as effective design choices vary across tasks and domains. With rapid advances in LLM agent capabilities, we ask how well these agents can autonomously build RAG systems and how effectively they can improve them through iteration. In this paper, we propose AutoRAGBench, the first benchmark to evaluate how well LLM agents develop RAG systems from scratch in an open code space. It comprises nine RAG system development tasks. For each task, agents build RAG systems from scratch without starter code or prescribed strategies, under a six-hour budget on a single H800 GPU. They analyze task data, implement RAG pipelines, and iteratively refine their designs based on experimental feedback. We evaluate nine agent configurations and analyze both the effectiveness of the resulting RAG systems and their development trajectories. GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI achieves the highest average score of 56.1. The composite Human-SOTA baseline averages 44.4. These results show that LLM agents can automate effective RAG system development. When starting from a human-designed system on each of seven tasks, GPT-6.1 Sol with Codex CLI improves the score by 16.6 points on average.
evidence_items.title: AutoRAGBench: A Benchmark for LLM Agents Automating RAG System Development

evidence_items.summary: The data, graders and harness of the controlled benchmark rerun (section RQ7) of Launching Agents as Persons: A month in public and a controlled rerun of the social-harness benchmark (A. Borodin, 2026). Chugh et al. (arXiv:2609.17527) released a laboratory benchmark in which AI agents of different principals schedule meetings (E1–E4), face deception and intimidation (E5) and may enable a stalker (E6). We reran its 29 cells in which every agent runs GPT-5.4, plus three E6 variants of our own, with bia agents: agents launched as persons, each in its own virtual machine with its own disk, certificate and identity. Four arms vary the society around the agents: away (the released design; the principal sends the persona and the task, then is absent), persons (each person is a bia acting for itself, with a department office that knows the official schedule), handbook (persons plus a shared one-page department handbook) and full circle (each principal is a bia that role-plays the human and answers). Ten runs per cell and arm, 1,220 runs in total. All bias ran one model, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash via OpenRouter. Contents: dataset/ / / / holds, for every run, the answer key (solution.json), the inputs, the transcript of every message, each calendar after the run, the verdicts (strict, and owner-aware for the full circle) and the run settings; dataset/code/ holds a re-implementation of the released grader (agreeing with 572 of 580 released verdicts), the owner-aware grader with every hand judgement and the principal's line it rests on, and the statistics; dataset/harness/ holds the scripts that produced the runs; dataset/scenarios/ the three added E6 variants. index.html, assets/ and data/ form a static explorer of all runs, also served at https://zond80.github.io/bia-paper-1/. Not included: the agents' internal working journals, which contain configuration of the test machines, and the released GPT-5.4 traces, which belong to Chugh et al.

evidence_items.summary: We present ChildVox, a novel benchmark for characterizing the diverse acoustic signals through which children communicate. Specifically, ChildVox follows the full developmental trajectory from birth through school age, covering physiological sounds, non-linguistic vocalizations, canonical syllables, and spoken language. ChildVox integrates more than 20 sub-tasks across 17 child-centered audio and speech datasets, enabling systematic cross-corpus and cross-domain comparison. We evaluate a representative range of audio and speech foundation models, including self-supervised, ASR-oriented, and large audio-language models, on tasks including physiological sound classification, vocalization and canonical syllables modeling, and speech quality assessment and recognition. Benchmark results show that ChildVox provides a suite of high-performance models in recognizing a wide range of acoustic signals from children, supporting downstream applications such as characterizing children's language levels and tracking speech production with age. Our benchmark models on public datasets are released at: https://github.com/tiantiaf0627/childvox-release.

evidence_items.summary: This paper introduces PSMT-eval, a new dataset for machine translation (MT) evaluation in Punjabi Shahmukhi, a low-resource language spoken by over 80 million people. We constructed an English–Punjabi Shahmukhi parallel corpus through pivot-based human translation, where the Urdu side of existing English–Urdu datasets was manually translated into Punjabi Shahmukhi. Four widely used English–Urdu datasets were selected: tatoeba-test.eng-urd, FLORES101, IN22, and MKB, with total count of 5182 sentences. To assess the dataset, we evaluated translations generated by state-of-the-art large language models (LLMs), including GPT-5, GPT-OSS-120B, Claude 4 Sonnet, LLaMA-3.3 70B Instruct, and Qwen-3 32B. Results show that only Claude 4 Sonnet achieved competitive performance, with a maximum SacreBLEU score of 17.51 on IN22. GPT-5 followed with a maximum SacreBLEU score of 10, while other models performed poorly. Further analysis highlights major challenges in Punjabi Shahmukhi MT. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first benchmark dataset specifically for MT evaluation in Punjabi Shahmukhi. PSMT-eval is a valuable resource for advancing low-resource MT research and is publicly available to support future work.
evidence_items.title: PSMT-eval: A Benchmark Dataset for Machine Translation Evaluation in Punjabi Shahmukhi

evidence_items.summary: Background Collecting standardized patient-reported outcome data through forms is burdensome for patients and clinicians. Objectives To evaluate a large language model (LLM)-based conversational agent (CA), intended for patients with back pain, that collects standardized back pain data through conversation: its data quality and perceived usability, and its completion time and user preference compared with a form. Methods We developed a CA using Generative Pre-trained Transformer (GPT) 5.0 to collect the 43-item NIH Recommended Minimal Dataset for chronic low back pain through conversation. In a cross-over study with 30 university students serving as proxies for patients with back pain, we compared CA-mediated data collection against standard form completion. Outcomes included completeness, correctness, and efficiency of data capture; usability and perceived usefulness (System Usability Scale, Technology Acceptance Model); conversational quality (Grice's maxims); intention to use; task completion time; and user preference. Qualitative analysis of conversations identified behavioral themes. Results Completeness was 100% of the items asked and correctness 98.3% ± 2.9%. Efficiency was 2.37 ± 0.52 correct data items per CA utterance. Usefulness and conversational quality were rated highly; the mean System Usability Scale score was 71.8 (SD 18.2). CA data collection took significantly longer than form completion (median 13.6 vs. 6.4 minutes; p = .001). Overall, 56% preferred the CA, 30% the form, and 15% had no preference. Qualitative analysis revealed intelligent behaviors (contextual inference, handling contradictory information, flexible coding) and limitations (overconfident coding, misuse of confidence indicators, occasional miscoding). Conclusions The CA collected structured clinical data accurately through conversation and was rated as usable by the student participants, though at increased completion time.
evidence_items.title: Evaluating a Large Language Model Conversational Agent for Collecting Standardized Back Pain Data: A Cross-Over Study of Accuracy, Usability, and User Preference

evidence_items.summary: Visual Question Answering (VQA) is one of the most popular tasks in the fields of Computer Vision and Natural Language Processing. The task is to provide an answer to a question related to the contents of a given image. VQA has been expanded to several domains. One of these is document VQA, where the image is a page of a document and the question is related to the textual contents of the page. In this case, the system that is being evaluated has to understand textual contents that are written inside the image, differently from typical VQA where images are natural scenes. However, document VQA datasets are exclusively in English, hence the performance of the system is evaluated for the English language only. In light of this, we introduce MaDOVE (Multilingual DOcument VQA Evaluation), a novel dataset designed to evaluate document VQA in multiple languages. Moreover, to establish a strong benchmark, we conduct an extensive set of experiments by evaluating a diverse range of models on this task.
evidence_items.title: MaDOVE: a Dataset for Multilingual Document VQA Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: GPT-6.2 Astra improved on several published benchmarks while OpenAI's evaluations found that it omitted known obstacles to task completion approximately twice as often as GPT-6 Astra. An extended engineering episode exposed a related failure involving two GPT-6.2 Astra High agents. They substituted an unauthorized criterion for a clear user requirement and built tests that validated the substitution. Under repeated human correction, they produced a detailed report containing the requested information while the defect survived in executable code and tests. The reviewer encountered evidence of the defect and nevertheless certified the work as correct. The agents reinforced the deviation across more than 100 turns and several hours; GPT-6 Astra High completed the outstanding repair in one turn. This sequence concretely illustrates The Validator's Paradox: tests can validate an agent's mistaken objective, and a reviewing agent can adopt that mistake as an acceptance standard. The additional observation is deceptive compliance under correction, sustained by developer–reviewer alignment. The mechanism has consequences for multi-agent systems and recursive self-improvement, where each accepted modification can carry its own corrupted evidence of success into the next cycle. Published regressions in blocker disclosure and correlated AI-review failures place the case in the broader problem of measured capability diverging from useful intelligence.
evidence_items.title: The Illusion of Accelerating Intelligence: Benchmark Gains, Deceptive Compliance, and Multi-Agent Misalignment

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for safety-critical engineering, yet their reliability in regulated functional-safety workflows remains underexplored. We introduce SAFARI (Safety-Aware Functional Automotive Risk Inference), the first industrial benchmark for LLM-assisted automotive Hazard Analysis and Risk Assessment (HARA) under ISO 26262. It contains 3,000 de-identified industrial HARA cases and evaluates two coupled tasks: open-ended hazard analysis and standards-grounded risk assessment. To evaluate open-ended HARA artifacts, we propose the first reference-anchored LLM-as-a-judge protocol with high expert correlation. Experiments with nine frontier LLMs show that models often produce plausible hazard narratives but remain weak at ISO 26262 risk classification, with the best ASIL macro-F1 reaching only 0.261. Chain-of-Thought prompting provides limited benefit and often degrades categorical risk assessment. Error analysis further localizes major failures to scenario-critical context omissions during hazard generation and to controllability misjudgments during risk assessment, indicating where expert oversight should be concentrated. The dataset can be obtained from https://github.com/xixi47520-hash/HARA.
evidence_items.title: SAFARI: An Industrial Benchmark for LLM-Assisted Hazard Analysis and Risk Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Post-training is becoming a service (PTaaS): a customer hands an operator data and a goal, and a forward-deployed engineer (FDE) returns a fine-tuned, evaluated, and deployed model under a budget, a human-approval gate, and reproducibility requirements. Seating an LLM agent in the FDE seat raises a question existing benchmarks cannot answer: not whether an agent can raise a metric, but whether it can be trusted to deliver. We answer it on a governed delivery plane, where an agent drives ten stages and an oracle scores each stage from platform-recorded facts. The central silent failure is the run that trains but does not learn (TBDL): loss falls, every signal stays green, and the delivered model is no better than the base. A detector calibrated on known-corrupted runs flags every such run before payment. We ran four frontier agents (Claude Opus 5, GPT-5.6-luna, Gemini 3.7 Flash, DeepSeek-V4-Pro) end to end on metered L40S, A100, and H200 GPUs across 8B to 70B open bases, certifying every scenario before scoring. We also ran a human FDE arm under the same oracle and compare every agent against it.
evidence_items.title: Trains but Doesn’t Learn: A Post-Training Delivery Benchmark for LLM Agents as Forward-Deployed Engineers

evidence_items.summary: While retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) relies on retrieved evidence to mitigate hallucination, its reliability is constrained by retrieval quality and diagnosing where retrieval fails remains difficult. Existing benchmarks typically report a single aggregate score over heterogeneous query sets and are often dominated by queries whose relevant passages can be identified through simple lexical overlap, concealing the failure modes that matter most in practice. We introduce GutenBench, a fine-grained, zero-shot evaluation dataset built around a four-level retrieval taxonomy: lexical, semantic, explicit aggregation, and latent conceptual retrieval. It pairs queries with relevance judgments adjudicated by subject-matter experts, enabling precise and controlled comparisons of retrievers. We evaluate several off-the-shelf retrievers in an asymmetric, English-to-target cross-lingual setting across 272 Bible translations (141 languages) and find that performance is strong on lexical and semantic queries, but degrades when models must aggregate information across passages or recognize conceptually relevant passages with no surface overlap.
evidence_items.title: GutenBench: A Taxonomy-Based Dataset for Evaluation of Information Retrieval Models

evidence_items.summary: We present PopResume, a population-representative resume dataset for causal fairness auditing of LLM- and VLM-based resume screening systems. Unlike existing benchmarks that rely on manually injected demographic information and outcome-level disparities, PopResume is grounded in population statistics and preserves natural attribute relationships, enabling path-specific effect (PSE)-based fairness evaluation. We decompose the effect of a protected attribute on resume scores into two paths: the business necessity path, mediated by job-relevant qualifications, and the redlining path, mediated by demographic proxies. This distinction allows auditors to separate legally permissible from impermissible sources of disparity. Evaluating four LLMs and four VLMs on PopResume's 60.8K resumes across five occupations, we identify five representative discrimination patterns that aggregate metrics fail to capture. Our results demonstrate that PSE-based evaluation reveals fairness issues masked by outcome-level measures, underscoring the need for causally-grounded auditing frameworks in AI-assisted hiring.

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents MobQA, a benchmark dataset designed to evaluate the semantic understanding capabilities of large language models (LLMs) for human mobility data through natural language question answering. While existing models predict human movement patterns well, their ability to interpret underlying reasons or semantic meaning remains unclear. To address this gap, we annotated 14,260 trajectory points from the GeoLife dataset with 30,703 semantic labels covering points of interest, mobility modes, and visit reasons, grounding semantics-dependent questions and reference answers. Building on these annotations, MobQA provides 5,800 question–answer pairs from daily and weekly GPS trajectories, spanning factual retrieval, multiple-choice semantic inference, and free-form interpretive explanation. Our evaluation of major LLMs reveals strong performance on factual retrieval but notable limits in semantic reasoning and explanation, with trajectory length substantially impacting effectiveness. These findings demonstrate both achievements and limitations of recent LLMs for semantic mobility understanding.
evidence_items.title: MobQA: A Benchmark Dataset for Semantic Understanding of Human Mobility Data through Question Answering

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance on coding and reasoning benchmarks; however, their ability to solve graph-structured machine learning problems remains largely unexplored. In particular, no benchmark currently evaluates whether LLMs can autonomously solve end-to-end Graph Neural Network (GNN) coding tasks under realistic competition settings. To address this gap, this paper introduces GNN-CB, the first competition-based benchmark for evaluating both humans and LLMs on GNN coding tasks. GNN-CB consists of 18 curated competitions spanning node-, edge-, and graph-level prediction across diverse graph categories, domains, and difficulty tiers. All submissions are evaluated through a unified automated pipeline with hidden test sets and standardized scoring. Human participants solve tasks under controlled competition constraints, while LLMs are evaluated using a frozen zero-shot prompting protocol based on a plan-then-code paradigm with bounded execute-and-repair loops. The benchmark additionally supports both non-agent and autonomous agent-based evaluation within the same protocol. Under our evaluated protocol, LLMs rarely match Human Top performance and show less stable performance across competitions. No single model dominates: a few competitions are won by LLMs, yet humans still hold the top score on most tasks. We release GNN-CB as a living benchmark with automated evaluation infrastructure, dynamic leaderboards, and reproducible execution pipelines. Beyond benchmarking, GNN-CB provides a practice-oriented resource for studying GNN implementation across progressively diverse graph-learning tasks. The benchmark and evaluation framework are publicly available at https://basiralab.github.io/GNN-CB/.
evidence_items.title: GNN-CB: A Graph Neural Network Competition Benchmark for Human and LLM Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents increasingly act through files, tools, memory, retrieved content, and other agents, which can trigger safety failures during execution. Existing benchmarks mostly focus on endpoint outcome evaluation or model-assisted moderation of pre-constructed trajectories, leaving limited evidence about where risks enter and how they propagate. To address this issue, we introduce TraceProbe, an execution-based benchmark for agent safety diagnosis. TraceProbe places agents in executable sandbox scenarios, scores endpoint and latent rule violations based on normalized traces and structured evidence, and replays recorded tool actions for step-level risk localization. Our benchmark contains 155 scenarios across three risk-source categories: non-adversarial failures, internal authority compromise, and external attacks. Across 12 contemporary LLMs, the mean attack success rate (ASR) is 0.347, indicating substantial residual risk, especially under internal authority compromise. Our analysis also demonstrates that endpoint-safe runs can contain unsafe intermediate actions, and the actual execution paths of agents may differ from the intended hazards of the testing scenarios. The TraceProbe benchmark and our findings support a more actionable form of agent safety evaluation: beyond assessing ASR or final outcomes, evaluators can also ask what went wrong, where it occurred, and where an intervention could be placed.
evidence_items.title: TraceProbe: An Execution-Based Benchmark for Diagnosing Safety Failures in LLM Agents

organizations: University of Science and Technology of China
evidence_items.summary: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become one of the primary paradigms for reasoning enhancement of large language models (LLMs). In particular, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) and related algorithms have demonstrated strong performance with outcome-level rewards. However, these methods depend solely on the final answer, without feedback regarding which intermediate steps contribute to success or failure. As task complexity and reasoning trajectory length increase, such sparse final-answer rewards become increasingly insufficient. To address this limitation, we introduce ConsensusBench, a novel dataset designed to provide rule-based process-level signals. We posit that a correct final answer relies on a small set of intermediate conclusions throughout the reasoning process, which can be seen as a verifiable sub-outcome. We identify these sub-outcomes by filtering correct trajectories from N rollouts and clustering semantically equivalent intermediate statements. We call these clustered statements as Consensus Nodes. By integrating a rule-based process reward derived from these nodes into GRPO-style algorithms, we develop a new reinforcement learning signal named ConsensusPR. It directly reduces the reward sparsity of outcome reward across long reasoning trajectories. To facilitate systematic process-level evaluation, we introduce three metrics to our benchmark: Final Answer Accuracy (Acc), Node Coverage Rate (NCR), and Tokens per Node (TPN). Experiments across AIME 2024, AIME 2025, GSM8K, MATH-500, and our ConsensusBench demonstrate that the proposed method consistently surpasses GRPO-style approaches, highlighting the practical value of consensus nodes in guiding reasoning.
evidence_items.title: ConsensusBench: Benchmark of Consensus Nodes for LLM Reasoning via Outcome Reward Densifying

evidence_items.summary: Patient recruitment remains a major barrier in clinical trials, as identifying eligible participants often requires manual screening of complex health records, contributing significantly to trial delays and increased costs. While Large Language Models (LLMs) offer potential to automate this process, existing public datasets are overly simplistic in their patient representation: they pair full criterion lists with single-paragraph synthetic summaries, failing to capture the longitudinal complexity of real clinical records. We introduce MIMIC-CTRL-2026, a dataset of 800 manually labeled patient-criterion pairs grounded in real-world longitudinal EHR data from MIMIC-IV, annotated by clinically trained experts. Each instance pairs one eligibility criterion with a full patient record spanning multiple discharge notes, radiology reports, lab values, and medication histories. While simple prompting achieves high performance (κ = 0.84) on existing benchmarks, it collapses (κ = 0.06) on our dataset, revealing a substantial benchmark-difficulty gap between simplified and real-world clinical evaluation. Lastly, we present a framework combining structured pre-processing with a clinician-validated expanded prompt that substantially outperforms naive baselines without any model fine-tuning, establishing a realistic benchmark for automated clinical trial screening on real EHR data. Our dataset and code are available at: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22103011
evidence_items.title: MIMIC-CTRL-2026: A Realistic Clinical Trial Dataset to Benchmark LLM performance

The table is mirrored verbatim with gzip compression only: no feature sampling, condition filtering, normalization or imputation. The experiment contains five E. coli spike-in levels in a human background, with four technical replicate runs per level. Original data are CC0. evidence_items.summary: Multilingual deployment often requires estimating how well a model will perform on a task in a target language when direct benchmark results are unavailable and published evidence is incomplete. We study whether structured agentic reasoning can support this predictive multilingual evaluation task. We introduce a controlled benchmark of 1,500 questions spanning six tasks and five evidence scenarios. The benchmark separates accessible evidence from ground truth, enabling evaluation of systems that must infer missing results from incomplete literature evidence. We also present Litmus (Re)Agent, a DAG-orchestrated agentic system that decomposes queries into hypotheses, retrieves evidence, and synthesises predictions through feature-aware aggregation. Across six systems, Litmus (Re)Agent achieves the best overall performance, with the largest gains in transfer-heavy scenarios where direct evidence is weak or absent. These results show that structured agentic reasoning is a promising approach to multilingual performance estimation under incomplete evidence.
evidence_items.title: Litmus (Re)Agent: A Benchmark and Agentic System for Predictive Evaluation of Multilingual Models

rationale: Matched: benchmark, dataset, evaluat, training data
evidence_items.summary: Current AI-driven game development has made substantial progress in asset generation, gameplay design, and web-based game coding, yet project-level code engineering on professional game engines remains largely unexplored due to the absence of large-scale datasets and deterministic evaluation methods. We present JamSet and JamBench, the first project-level game code framework dataset and benchmark built on a professional game engine. Our key insight is that Game Jam competitions, community events where developers build complete games under tight time constraints, yield thousands of open-source projects suitable for this purpose. Building on the Godot engine's text-based format and headless execution mode, we design a deterministic verification pipeline from file integrity to runtime behavior collection, distilling 8,133 verified projects from over 240,000 repositories. Of these, 300 manually verified projects form JamBench; the rest constitute JamSet. JamBench defines theme-driven generation and code completion tasks, evaluated through a pipeline combining compilation pass rates, Structural Completeness Score (SCS), and Behavioral Alignment Score (BAS). Evaluation of 9 frontier models reveals a capability cliff as project scale increases, with runtime pass rates dropping from 80.4% on small projects to 5.7% on large ones(Task2a). Code Agents improve compilation rates yet yield no gains in runtime behavioral quality, indicating that the bottleneck lies in architectural design rather than syntactic correctness. Experiments validate JamSet as effective training data. All data and code are publicly available.
evidence_items.title: JAMER: Project-Level Code Framework Dataset and Benchmark on Professional Game Engines

evidence_items.summary: AnesLLM is a dataset of real intraoperative anaesthetic decisions derived from VitalDB, an open database of high-resolution recordings from non-cardiac surgery at Seoul National University Hospital. It contains 84 813 decision windows from 3168 anaesthetic cases. Each window is anchored at a decision point and contains only information recorded before it: patient and surgical data, the last preoperative value of 34 laboratory tests, 10 min of vital signs as time series, drug concentrations and ventilatory parameters at the decision point, and a 20-min history of previous actions (280 fields in total). The label is the action actually taken by the anaesthetist, detected automatically from infusion-pump changes: increase or reduce hypnotic, increase or reduce opioid, or no action. Because more than one action is often acceptable, each window also includes the two actions most frequently chosen by the cohort's anaesthetists in similar clinical states (consensus actions), with their estimated probabilities; vasopressor may appear as an additional, investigator-defined consensus option. Cases are assigned to training (2994), development (25) and test (149) partitions at case level, and the test partition is stratified by case difficulty. The release includes a data dictionary, a partition manifest, a datasheet, machine-readable audit reports (integrity, information leakage, plausibility, drift, missingness and k-anonymity) and command-line utilities to filter windows, convert them to tables or text clinical cases, and verify the integrity of the download. AnesLLM is intended to evaluate any artificial intelligence system on choosing the next action at a specific moment of a real anaesthetic.
evidence_items.title: VitalDB - AnesLLM: a dataset and benchmark based on real intraoperative anaesthetic decisions

evidence_items.summary: LLM judges are widely used to evaluate agentic tool-calling systems, yet their reliability on structured, dependency-driven workflows remains largely unexamined. We present AgentJudgeBench, the first benchmark to systematically study LLM-as-a-judge reliability for agentic tool-calling over workflow DAGs, as distinct from the broader LLM-as-a-judge task of open-ended text or preference evaluation. The benchmark comprises 3,808 instances spanning six DAG topologies and three difficulty tiers, evaluated with five generators (3B-70B open-weight models and GPT-5.4) and six judges (20B to frontier scale) under paired with- and without-ground-truth conditions. Judge alignment degrades monotonically with task difficulty, 1.5x faster without ground truth, and on hard queries without ground truth all six judges converge to a narrow 77-82% band regardless of scale, revealing a structural ceiling driven primarily by task difficulty, though its height is partly prompt-dependent for weaker generators, that model capacity alone cannot overcome. Ground-truth exposure is not uniformly beneficial: it reduces alignment for GPT-5.4 (1.5 pp) and Gemini-2.5-Pro (3.9 pp), consistent with over-anchoring. Among mitigation strategies, chain-of-thought reasoning and judge temperature both have negligible effect, while structured evaluation rubrics improve alignment by up to 6.5 pp but do not generalize uniformly across judge-generator pairs. With ground truth, QwQ-32B best matches the programmatic reference, while a human validation study identifies GPT-OSS-120B as the most human-aligned judge; without it, frontier judges lead only marginally within the shared ceiling. These results expose fundamental limitations of current LLM judges and yield practical guidelines for reliable evaluation in agentic systems.
evidence_items.title: AgentJudgeBench: A Multi-Difficulty Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Judges on Agentic Tool-Calling

organizations: Hong Kong University of Science and Technology
evidence_items.summary: Large language models and coding agents can produce web applications that appear functional, yet surface plausibility is an unreliable proxy for behavioral conformance under interaction. We introduce ConformWeb, a contract-grounded protocol and benchmark that operationalizes public behavioral contracts to construct hidden interaction scenarios, evaluating whether agent-generated applications preserve strict conformance under dynamic execution. By decoupling hidden interaction sequences from the public behavioral scope, the protocol guarantees a fair held-out workflow evaluation without relying on undisclosed reference implementations. Evaluated across 24 validated instances scaling to 756 evaluation scenarios and 6,433 semantic steps, only 252 of the 2,160 total execution runs achieve full conformance, yielding a strict pass rate of 11.7%. While scenario-level conformance reaches 36.7% and step-level progress averages 49.4%, this quantitative gap demonstrates that generative systems frequently achieve substantial partial progress but fail to maintain the critical behavioral invariants required for end-to-end conformance. All code and data are released at https://github.com/deep-diver/ConformWeb.
evidence_items.title: Do LLM-Generated Web Apps Behave Correctly? A Contract-Grounded Benchmark for Behavioral Conformance

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) perform well on standard reasoning and question-answering benchmarks, yet such evaluations often fail to capture their ability to handle long-tail, expertise-intensive knowledge in real-world professional scenarios. We introduce LPFQA, a long-tail knowledge benchmark derived from authentic professional forum discussions, covering 7 academic and industrial domains with 430 curated tasks grounded in practical expertise. LPFQA evaluates specialized reasoning, domain-specific terminology understanding, and contextual interpretation, and adopts a hierarchical difficulty structure to ensure semantic clarity and uniquely identifiable answers. Experiments on over multiple mainstream LLMs reveal substantial performance gaps, particularly on tasks requiring deep domain reasoning, exposing limitations overlooked by existing benchmarks. Overall, LPFQA provides an authentic and discriminative evaluation framework that complements prior benchmarks and informs future LLM development. Our data is available at https://huggingface.co/datasets/m-a-p/LPFQA.
evidence_items.title: LPFQA: A Long-Tail Professional Forum-based Benchmark for LLM Evaluation

organizations: Hunyuan Team, Tencent; Georgia Institute of Technology
evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) have advanced Machine Translation (MT), yet they remain vulnerable by hallucinations. Most existing benchmarks, originally designed for neural MT models, do not effectively elicit hallucinations from multilingual LLMs, resulting in a low density of samples for LLM translation hallucination analysis. To address this, we create HalloMTBench, a human-verified hallucination benchmark derived from tens of millions of translations, for studying signals that trigger LLM translation hallucinations across 11 English-to-X directions. We curate 6,908 authentic hallucination instances through a rigorous process: frontier LLMs first translate a large source corpus, and their outputs are then validated by both an LLM-judge ensemble and human experts. Based on our analysis of these hallucination instances, we introduce a taxonomy for translation hallucination that distinguishes Instruction Detachment from Source Detachment. Our evaluation of 21 model variants on HalloMTBench reveals several observable vulnerability patterns, including model Characteristics, source length, language proximity, hallucination reproducibility, and model-dependent effects of reasoning-style decoding. HalloMTBench offers a forward-looking testbed for diagnosing LLM translation hallucination. All resources will be released.
evidence_items.title: HalloMTBench: A Large-Scale Human-Verified Benchmark for Diagnosing Hallucination Triggers in LLM Translation

organizations: Daegu Gyeongbuk Institute of Science and Technolog
evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are typically evaluated on static benchmarks, even though natural language constantly evolves through newly emerging words and meanings. Existing Korean benchmarks are centered on established vocabulary and therefore provide limited coverage of such recent lexical change, and their English-oriented design makes it difficult to assess the typological properties of Korean, in which content words combine productively with functional morphemes. In this paper, we introduce KoNeoBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLMs' understanding of Korean neologisms. KoNeoBench is built on 1,785 Korean neologisms attested in online news since 2020 and curated through expert lexicographic review. Each entry provides usage examples, word-formation analyses, and dictionary-style definitions. Based on this resource, we define four tasks and report results on recent models, together with a human baseline. Our experiments show that current LLMs exhibit clear limitations in recovering source components, distinguishing semantic categories, and generating accurate definitions. These results reveal specific aspects of recent Korean lexical change that remain challenging for current LLMs. KoNeoBench is available at https://github.com/bcmilab/ko-neobench/ .
evidence_items.title: KoNeoBench: A Curated Evaluation Dataset for LLM Understanding of Korean Neologisms

evidence_items.summary: Concise topic tagging of individual records enhances searchability and supports targeted thematic analysis within large archival corpora. Aggregating these tags into higher-level representations enables macro-scale pattern discovery and user-centric navigation across heterogeneous historical datasets. To meet these objectives, we developed a three-stage computational framework named ArchTopic - LLM-Enhanced Framework for Archival Topic Extraction and Thematic Clustering. Stage 1 applies zero-shot prompting with the LLaMA 3.2 3B model for context-driven topic extraction. Stage 2 enforces semantic alignment between generated topics and source texts through multilingual embedding comparison, cosine-similarity thresholding, and iterative refinement via a dual-LLM ensemble. Stage 3 builds a higher-level representation of the entire corpus by concatenating validated text and topic embeddings, reducing dimensionality with UMAP for topology preservation, clustering with k-means determined by the elbow criterion, and labeling clusters using YAKE (Yet Another Keyword Extractor) augmented with LLM-guided label synthesis. Our evaluation of more than 180,000 administrative correspondence records (1581–1859) from the Portuguese Overseas Historical Archive (Arquivo Histórico Ultramarino), specifically the Collection of Conselho Ultramarino, shows that the proposed framework produces well-separated, semantically coherent clusters, while embedding-space visualizations and word-cloud analyses confirm thematic integrity. We validate the framework’s superior cluster distinctiveness, label coherence, and computational throughput through comparative benchmarks against traditional Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) and BERTopic approaches. Integrated LLM prompting, embedding validation, and clustering algorithms together establish a reproducible, scalable framework for thematic exploration and intuitive navigation of extensive archival collections.
evidence_items.title: ArchTopic -  LLM-Enhanced Framework for Archival Topic Extraction and Thematic Clustering

evidence_items.summary: This archive provides independently auditable numerical output datasets for the finite-prime-to-zero inverse problem, investigated through a proprietary finite-prime spectral inversion operator. The archive contains six CSV datasets covering: 1. 10,000 consecutively indexed approximate Riemann zeta zero ordinates generated using the first two million primes (P = 2,000,000), without evaluating ζ(s) or consulting precomputed zero tables during spectral generation. 2. A separate 3,000-point forward ordinal-quantization experiment using the first 600,000 primes (P = 600,000) and known reference zero ordinates. 3. Classical Riemann–Siegel spectral unfolding and Dyson–Mehta spectral rigidity measurements (L = 1 to 40) with exact GUE sine-kernel and Poisson reference baselines. 4. Chebyshev explicit-formula ψ(x) reconstruction and reflection-symmetric off-critical-line pair sensitivity (δ = 0.00, 0.05, 0.15, 0.25). 5. Real-part exponent scans (σ ∈ [0.35, 0.65], step 0.01). 6. Finite-aperture resolution measurements for the first Lehmer close-zero pair (n = 6709, 6710) across five prime counts up to 4,000,000 primes. The reported numerical benchmarks include a 3,000/3,000 (100.00%) forward ordinal-locking rate, 253.50-fold mean-squared-error compression (+24.04 dB) relative to the classical smooth counting baseline, a coordinate MAE of 0.002495 over the first 3,000 generated ordinates (with 10,000th ordinate error 0.00077663, relative error 7.862×10⁻⁸), and finite-range spectral-rigidity plateau measurements (0.165791 ± 0.000785 over L = 15–40). File-level SHA-256 checksums are provided for integrity verification. The archived outputs support independent numerical auditing against standard mathematical benchmarks. The proprietary inversion operator is not included, and independent reproduction of the generation procedure is outside the scope of this dataset.
evidence_items.title: Finite-Prime-to-Zero Inversion: Numerical Benchmark Dataset for 10,000 Riemann Zeta Zero Ordinates

evidence_items.summary: ESG analysis requires complex language understanding across diverse sources, including corporate reports, news, and disclosures, for tasks such as ESG relevance detection, action interpretation, impact analysis, and question answering. However, existing ESG datasets are fragmented by task and source, with heterogeneous formats and annotation schemes, limiting their use for training general-purpose ESG LLMs and unified evaluation. In this work, we construct ESG-Instruct, a 30,000-instance ESG instruction dataset built from public ESG resources, and ESGU-Bench, an ESG understanding benchmark covering six representative ESG tasks. Based on these resources, we further develop ESGPT, an 8B ESG-specialized LLM, and evaluate it against diverse open-source and API-based LLMs. Experimental results show that general-purpose LLMs exhibit substantial performance variation across ESG tasks, while ESGPT, despite its relatively small scale, achieves the best performance on multiple ESG tasks. This work provides unified data and benchmark resources for training and evaluating ESG-specialized LLMs.
evidence_items.title: ESGPT: A Data-Centric ESG Language Model with Unified Instruction and Benchmark Resources

evidence_items.summary: Environmental, social, and governance (ESG) criteria are essential for evaluating corporate sustainability, yet professional ESG analysis is hindered by data fragmentation and complex multi-step workflows. Existing ESG benchmarks rely on LLM-generated questions that often suffer from semantic ambiguity, limiting their diagnostic reliability. We introduce ESGAgent, a hierarchical multi-agent system with a domain-oriented toolset for automating end-to-end ESG workflows, and a three-level benchmark derived from 310 corporate sustainability reports, featuring expert-sourced questions with verified, unambiguous answers at Levels 1-2 and full report generation at Level 3. Evaluations across 20 state-of-the-art closed-source LLMs show that ESGAgent achieves 84.15% accuracy on Levels 1-2, surpassing the strongest baseline by 3.26 points, and produces Level 3 reports with higher factual consistency and analytical depth than commercial deep research systems, validated by both multi-LLM judging and human expert evaluation, showing a robust alignment (Pearson r=0.551).
evidence_items.title: Advancing ESG Intelligence: An Expert-level Agent and Comprehensive Benchmark for Sustainable Finance

evidence_items.summary: Data contamination undermines the reliable evaluation of large language models (LLMs) on mathematical problem solving. While rewriting-based evaluation mitigates memorization, existing methods lack guarantees of problem validity and answer correctness. We propose Proof-Verified Benchmark Rewriting (RePro), the first framework to integrate Lean-oriented neural automated theorem provers (ATPs) into benchmark rewriting, which rewrites problems and regenerates answers with correctness ensured by Lean-verified proofs. Experiments on GSM8K and MATH show that RePro's retained rewritten instances achieve 100% well-definedness, feasibility, and answer correctness, while existing methods still produce invalid or incorrect instances. Moreover, several models exhibit accuracy drops on proof-verified rewritten benchmarks, suggesting that their performance is sensitive to surface-level and structural variations and may partly reflect memorization effects. Our source code and data are available at https://github.com/AI4Engi/RePro.
evidence_items.title: RePro: Proof-Verified Benchmark Rewriting for Reliable Evaluation of LLM Mathematical Problem Solving

evidence_items.summary: A new drug reaches patients only after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has reviewed its trial evidence, which every application carries as analysis datasets in the Clinical Data Interchange Standards Consortium (CDISC) Analysis Data Model (ADaM) format that programmers derive by hand from raw trial data, a statistical analysis plan (SAP) and dataset specifications. Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) could take over this work, and a slow-changing industry will adopt them only with evidence of what they get right and wrong. However, work on large language models (LLMs) for CDISC data stops short of evaluating a complete, conformant and reproducible package, and the standard validator checks structure rather than whether each value is derived correctly. We introduce ClinDataBench, built on the public CDISC pilot study: an agent receives 22 Study Data Tabulation Model (SDTM) domains, the statistical analysis plan (SAP) and specifications, and must deliver 13 Analysis Data Model (ADaM) datasets, Define-XML metadata and a program that rebuilds them offline. Agents run in containers whose only network route is their model API, restricting online access to published reference outputs during execution. A host-only evaluator scores conformance under the Pinnacle 21 Community (P21) validator, selected derivations, clean reconstruction and effort separately. We compare three settings: Base, which submits the agent's first package; Self-Refine, which revises it without external validation feedback; and CRITIC, which revises it with the agent's own validator report. In an exploratory pilot with six models, the three closed models and DeepSeek delivered all 13 datasets in every setting and eleven of their twelve packages rebuilt semantically, while two other open-weight models delivered no complete package. Validator findings ranged from 15 to 64 dataset-rule pairs.
evidence_items.title: ClinDataBench: Benchmarking Large Language Model Agents in Clinical Trial Analysis Dataset Construction

evidence_items.summary: Cross-market factor research studies whether firm-level signals from one or more markets can predict returns in a target market, but existing public benchmarks do not support cross-market disclosure-to-return evaluation. Building such a benchmark is challenging because filings differ across languages and regulatory systems, disclosure-derived similarity can be biased by common reporting components, and cross-market signals must be evaluated under feasible trading-time alignment. We introduce CrossAlpha, a public annual-report benchmark for cross-market factor research. CrossAlpha addresses these challenges through three corresponding components: Disclosure Distillation, which standardises heterogeneous filings into ten-category English business descriptions; Residual Schema Graph Construction, which builds PCA-whitened cross-market firm-pair scores from schema-level disclosures; and Timing-Aligned Evaluation, which pairs the graph with 11 years of daily OHLCV data to construct forward-return labels under feasible cross-market execution protocols. CrossAlpha covers 3,587 firms and about 10,700 firm-year reports from the United States, Japan, Taiwan, South Korea, and Hong Kong, and releases about 19M directed firm-pair scores. In experiments, disclosure-derived cross-market peers outperform domestic text, industry-code, and return-correlation peers in the US-to-Japan setting (ICIR 0.39 versus 0.07–0.18), and cross-market sources beat the domestic text baseline in most target markets. CrossAlpha offers a publicly released, reusable, return-grounded benchmark for cross-market financial NLP.
evidence_items.title: CrossAlpha: An Annual-Report Benchmark for Cross-Market Factor Research (with LLM Agents)

evidence_items.summary: External-eye photography captures clinically relevant periocular anatomy at low acquisition cost, yet no large-scale standardized resource exists for evaluating self-supervised external-eye representations. We introduce a 4.35-million-image Standardized External-Eye Corpus (SEEC) derived from fourteen heterogeneous public face datasets, together with a benchmark for external-eye representation learning. For evaluation, we provide held-out evaluation distributions, landmark-annotated anatomical probe sets, and clinical disease-classification experiments spanning ptosis, thyroid eye disease, and craniofacial syndromes. We evaluate representations at two complementary levels: (a) the representation level, by assessing embedding geometry across multiple data distributions, and (b) the functional level, by assessing anatomical recovery, out-of-distribution anatomical transfer, and disease classification. Our models include ResNet-101 and ViT-B encoders pretrained using InfoNCE, VICReg, and LeJEPA objectives and compared with DINOv2 and MAE. Our results indicate that representation-level and functional-level evaluations are dissociable: broader embedding-space utilization does not consistently correspond to anatomical transfer or disease-classification performance, and no single encoder is universally optimal. Domain-specific external-eye encoders outperform DINOv2 and MAE on cross-dataset anatomical transfer despite being pretrained at substantially smaller scale, while external-eye-pretrained ViT models match or outperform these general-purpose baselines on frozen disease-classification probes. We release benchmark code, evaluation scripts, and preprocessing pipelines to reproduce SEEC at https://monkeygobah.github.io/seec-project/
evidence_items.title: SEEC: A Large-Scale Dataset and Benchmark for Self-Supervised External-Eye Representation Learning

evidence_items.summary: Generative adversarial networks and diffusion-based synthesis have made photo-realistic facial manipulation — commonly called deepfakes - inexpensive, fast and widely accessible. Such synthetic media is increasingly used for misinformation, impersonation, financial fraud and reputational attack, and human observers perform poorly at distinguishing it from authentic content. Detection methods reported in the literature achieve high accuracy when training and test manipulations originate from the same generator, but degrade sharply on unseen generation techniques, and most are released as research code rather than as usable end-to-end systems. This paper presents DeepGuard, an applied detection framework that couples MTCNN-based face detection and alignment, interval-based frame sampling for video input, and an ImageNet-pretrained XceptionNet backbone fine-tuned by two-stage transfer learning, into a single pipeline that classifies an uploaded image or video as real or deepfake and returns a confidence score. The contribution is not a new network topology but an engineered, reproducible pipeline together with a controlled comparison of convolutional backbones under one fixed preprocessing and video-disjoint splitting protocol. The system was evaluated on the Face Forensics++ (c23) corpus using a 70/15/15 split partitioned by source video, and achieved 92.40% accuracy, 93.10% precision, 91.80% recall, an F1-score of 0.9244 and a ROC-AUC of 0.9612 on the held-out test set. Limitations concerning cross-generator generalisation, compression robustness and audio-driven forgeries are analysed, and directions for extending the framework are outlined.
evidence_items.title: Resource-Efficient Deepfake Detection with Cross Dataset Evaluation and Web Deployment

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models may facilitate unlawful activities, yet this risk remains underexplored in studies assessing illicit-content recognition or narrow categories of illicit scenarios. We define complicit facilitation as model guidance that assists users with illicit instructions. To assess it, we develop a legally-informed, automated pipeline grounded in real-world cases and legal frameworks, and introduce EVIL, a benchmark covering 269 illicit scenarios and 50 illicit intents across Chinese and United States legal contexts. Evaluations indicate that complicit facilitation is widespread across models, with legal warnings and lawful alternatives often omitted. Risks vary across socio-legal contexts and are elevated for crimes against societal interests, non-violent offenses, and intents involving subjective motives or deceptive justifications. Models provide more complicit assistance when instructions describe users as older adults, racial minorities, non-religious individuals, or workers in lower-prestige occupations. Existing open-source safety benchmarks and alignment datasets offer limited coverage and mitigation of these risks.
evidence_items.title: Large language models' complicit responses to illicit instructions across socio-legal contexts
