evidence_items.summary: MICRONANOROBOTIC NAVIGATION AT THE LIMIT F046-F050 · STARLI · White Rainbow Era · Research Working Edition v1.0 Prospective, nonclinical research synthesis. All three-dimensional model surfaces are synthetic numerical constructions; no biological experiment, verified navigation advantage or device clearance is claimed. Five flagship studies F046 | Magnetically Driven Microrobot Navigation in Microchannels at the Limit. Primary endpoint: blind three-dimensional route-tracking RMSE [µm]. Minimum prototype: a sealed acrylic microchannel with inert magnetic surrogate beads, coil-current logs and an independent 3D imaging reference. Strong comparator: registered open-loop magnetic control, skilled optical stage guidance and matched passive tracer flow. Independent stop: wall contact, unbounded field gradient, temperature excursion or lost independent localization. F047 | Microrobotic Motion in Complex Viscoelastic Fluids at the Limit. Primary endpoint: held-out trajectory error after rheological transfer [µm]. Minimum prototype: a temperature-controlled viscoelastic microchannel phantom with rheometer-calibrated relaxation spectrum and reversible magnetic drive. Strong comparator: Newtonian viscosity-matched fluid with the same geometric envelope and a fitted linear drag controller. Independent stop: unbounded elastic stress, irreversible gel rupture, unexplained sample heating or lost relaxation calibration. F048 | Autonomous Path Planning in Multi-Obstacle Organ Chips at the Limit. Primary endpoint: collision-free completed-route proportion [%]. Minimum prototype: a transparent obstacle-rich organ-chip phantom with CAD-verified geometry and held-out obstacle layouts. Strong comparator: equal-budget A graph search, manually registered safe routes and open-loop waypoint pursuit. Independent stop: negative clearance, forced entry into a protected chamber or unrecoverable planner uncertainty.

ZENODO RESEARCH DESCRIPTION  The miniature robot that reaches the end of a microchannel has not necessarily accomplished a scientific task. Its elegant trajectory might result from a hidden pressure gradient, a change in polymer relaxation, an overly forgiving obstacle map, a switch of agent identities, or retrospective video smoothing. The harder problem is to build a navigation system whose intended motion, measured physical displacement, estimated uncertainty and independent stopping authority remain aligned when those comfortable assumptions fail. This book is an invitation to construct that evidence, not a claim that it already exists.  The research lineage begins with the supplied 200-flagship roadmap and with the earlier F18 organ-chip monograph, whose central rule is that geometric success is not physiological function. The present family carries this principle into five engineering domains: magnetic navigation in confined microchannels, viscoelastic locomotion, collision-aware route planning, group navigation under shared fields and error correction under delayed sensing. Their interfaces form a research system only if the component measurements survive independent calibration and all failed attempts remain in view.  FLAGSHIP F046 | MAGNETICALLY DRIVEN MICROROBOT NAVIGATION IN MICROCHANNELS AT THE LIMIT  Microchannel magnetic navigation begins from the physical interface confined magnetic actuation, low-Reynolds-number drag and channel-wall clearance. Its proposed primary endpoint is blind three-dimensional route-tracking RMSE [µm], evaluated in a sealed acrylic microchannel with inert magnetic surrogate beads, coil-current logs and an independent 3D imaging reference. This is not a biological efficacy metric. Every apparent improvement should be contrasted with registered open-loop magnetic control, skilled optical stage guidance and matched passive tracer flow. An honest system must stop when wall contact, unbounded field gradient, temperature excursion or lost independent localization. The question is not whether a controller can produce an attractive motion trace but whether independently synchronized instruments can reconstruct the relevant trajectory under an unchanged experimental budget.  One specific research door concerns coil-field traceability across a branched chip. Consider the deliberate disturbance randomized field-current reversal; if a proposed gain disappears, the failure locates a real physical limit instead of merely reducing the elegance of the image. The rival unrecorded pump acceleration must be allowed to explain the observation. A successor laboratory would need laser-calibrated 3D fiducial microscopy with synchronized pump and field probes, complete actuator and pump timestamps, an untouched test geometry, and the same reference-defined primary endpoint in µm. A strong research claim about real-time error correction becomes valuable through its stopping rule and its transfer properties. The smallest informative prototype is a delay-injectable camera-and-coil bench phantom with randomized sensor dropouts and a frozen observer. If a second team obtains a different outcome, the discrepancy should be traced to chip geometry, calibration uncertainty, fluid properties, field actuation, identity tracking and analysis code rather than hidden under a pooled average. The result should still be publishable even when the original hypothesis fails.  HOW THE FIVE FLAGSHIPS COUPLE WITHOUT MERGING THEIR CLAIMS  The first coupling crosses the boundary between magnetic force and local flow. A coil current is only a command. It cannot identify the magnetic force at the robot unless magnetic moment, orientation, field map and geometry have been measured. A visually stationary robot might be trapped by a magnet, carried by a vortex or pinned against a wall. The strongest baseline therefore includes flow-matched passive trajectories and equal-time calibrated stage guidance, with heating and recovery independently recorded.  The second coupling crosses the boundary between fluid viscosity and fluid memory. A complex medium may show shear thinning and elastic recoil simultaneously. A single fitted effective viscosity can agree with one period of actuation and fail catastrophically when the field reverses. The family therefore tests causal stress and relaxation models across varied drive periods, and treats a failure of one constitutive approximation as a reason to revise the domain, not to claim that an unmeasured new force exists.  The third coupling crosses the boundary between geometric path feasibility and executable motion. A narrow gap visible on a chip map may remain closed to a finite robot with position uncertainty, wall roughness and field-limited turning. A planner should report infeasibility when clearance is exhausted. Reporting only successful routes rewards unsafe exploration. The essential comparator is a feasible classical path search under the same map, time and actuation constraints, with a transparent definition of every initiated trial.  The fourth coupling concerns the ambiguous promise of swarm cooperation. Parallel robots can increase throughput but may share a magnetic field and influence each other through near-field forces. A formation can appear successful after the vision system swaps two identities, or after a stuck robot is removed from analysis. Independent agent identification, pairwise separation and complete population accounting are therefore part of the experiment. Cooperation needs to outperform a sequential single-robot comparator under equal resource budgets.  The fifth coupling concerns real-time correction. A Kalman filter, nonlinear observer or learned controller may create an excellent retrospectively smoothed trace by using frames that were unavailable when the coil command was issued. The true scientific unit is the causal closed loop, including acquisition, computation, communication and actuation delay. A held-out reference camera should reconstruct errors and missed deadlines without sharing information with the tested controller. When the observer diverges, a stop is more informative than an interpolated victory.  These five interfaces should be studied in a staged manner, with each subsystem allowed to fail independently. A single grand integration demonstrator can conceal which contribution caused an improvement, and its larger complexity may create new failure surfaces. A careful inheritance program releases separate datasets for field response, fluid memory, obstacle planning, group behavior and observation latency, before attempting to claim any integrated advantage.  THREE-DIMENSIONAL MATHEMATICS AND THE RECONSTRUCTION CONTRACT  Thirty candidate mathematical plates translate research hypotheses into inspectable geometry, including magnetic-gradient forcing, low-Reynolds drag, causal memory kernels, safety clearance, stochastic planning, multiagent coupling and state-estimation covariance. The formula pages are not a set of newly discovered laws. Every equation states a physical domain and a measurement that could invalidate it; dimensional compatibility is checked before a surface is plotted.  Forty-two three-dimensional surfaces vary two physically declared parameters and report one projected endpoint. Field gradient and pump speed determine a synthetic tracking-error surface; Deborah number and drive frequency probe fluid-memory sensitivity; obstacle fraction and map uncertainty affect simulated route success; population and field gradient probe minimum interagent clearance; and observation delay and sensor noise change corrected localization error. Model grids, axis units, numerical assumptions, csv records and a standalone Python reconstruction script are stored in the research PDF. Recalculating a numerical surface confirms its computational consistency, not its correspondence to biological measurements.  A demanding falsification program will preregister which curvature or threshold in those surfaces the experiment is supposed to test. Some curves may prove physically inaccurate. A useful result then describes the alternative physical explanation, revised domain and uncertainty rather than deleting the failed prediction. The essence of a mathematical model is its capacity to disagree with an experiment in a meaningful, reproducible way.  RESEARCH GATES AND PHOENIX PROTOTYPES  Two hundred Research Gates offer questions to successor investigators. Each follows an origin, a deliberately extreme counterfactual world and a future research plan. The origins begin in real measurement limitations; the counterworlds ask whether a system could appear to work while the hidden source of apparent success is an artifact; and the future plans establish how another laboratory could defeat both the preferred model and its strongest rival. The doors are meant to open through criticism rather than applause.  Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos outline candidate instruments such as a blind field atlas, reversible magnetic navigator, chip-wall clearance sentinel, memory-aware rheology observer, autonomous recovery route, shared-field swarm monitor and causal-latency injection bench. Each is a prototype idea, not finished equipment. The minimum test requires an identifiable physical endpoint, a strong comparator, transparent control authority and a retirement condition if independent measurements disagree.  The family thereby treats restraint as part of technical progress. A route is not qualified if an agent cannot be recovered, if a collision is hidden, if a controller violates a protected region or if a supposedly online algorithm uses information from after the actuation deadline. These hard stops are not merely legal cautions; they are experimental conditions that decide whether a putative engineering advantage is meaningful.  SCIENCE, SUCCESSION AND OPEN ACCESS  The strongest legacy of this proposed program may be its negative cases. A chip branch that cannot be traversed, a polymeric fluid that defeats a Newtonian controller, a swarm that loses individual identity, and a delayed observer that fails to prevent a wall contact are each highly useful if the laboratory preserves the raw trace, reference measurement, failed assumptions and complete attempt denominator. The next researcher needs those records more than a polished best-run montage.  The research is prospective, nonclinical and bounded to inert laboratory phantoms. There is no claim of an implanted navigation system, organ-specific physiology, cell preservation, therapeutic benefit or regulatory clearance. Later biological tests would require independent ethics, material compatibility and physiological endpoints and cannot simply inherit the success of a navigation benchmark. evidence_items.summary: As language-model agents are applied to increasingly extended tasks, their working context continuously accumulates interaction history, tool observations, intermediate decisions, and task progress. Context compaction offers a practical way to reduce this growing history while allowing execution to continue, yet the compaction ability of modern LLMs remains insufficiently understood. We introduce CompAct-Bench, a benchmark for evaluating working-context compaction through its downstream effect on agent task completion. Starting from successful agent trajectories, we insert compaction boundaries at different stages of execution, compress the preceding working context with the model under evaluation, and let the same executor continue the original task. To enable fair comparison across compactors, we evaluate them under controlled retention ratios using a lightweight iterative ratio-adjustment procedure. CompAct-Bench covers information-seeking, software-engineering, and workspace-oriented tasks through BrowseComp, SWE-bench, and an internal CompanyBench evaluation. Our experiments show that working-context compaction remains highly lossy even for frontier models: Claude- and GPT-family models perform strongest overall, yet substantial degradation in downstream task accuracy persists under aggressive compaction. Further analysis reveals that failures are often caused not only by omitted information, but also by distorted task state, such as turning unresolved issues into apparent conclusions or forgetting previously established results, which can lead to incorrect decisions or redundant execution. These findings highlight working-context compaction as a distinct and still challenging ability for LLMs operating in extended agent tasks.
evidence_items.title: CompAct-Bench: A Benchmark for Working-Context Compaction in Long-Horizon Agent Tasks

evidence_items.summary: Coding agents built on large language models (LLMs) now help develop many models published as general solutions. Should generality instead reside in the agent that builds a model for each new task? We examine this question in prognostics and health management (PHM), where every model must work on unseen equipment. Our deployment-style benchmark, NextUnit-Bench, covers 24 public datasets split into 58 folds that hold out units or operating conditions; each agent has two hours to deliver an executable predictor, then run on the hidden units. First, frontier agents outperform AutoML, which reaches less than half the best agent's score, and faithful implementations of published methods on four datasets, of which only 6 of 30 beat the strongest agent's own design; published accuracies, where reproducible, rest on the papers' own conventions, and a single convention, capping the remaining life of test engines, can halve the reported error. Second, the agents' advantage is a design made on each machine's data; once made, a plain-text plan of a few hundred words carries most of the gap between two frontier agents, and given a weaker agent's plan, the strongest agent falls to that agent's level, often to identical predictions. Before touching the data, however, it matters little whose plan an agent carries out, and domain toolkits appear to help neither: what sets the strongest apart is how much it learns from the data. Third, such designs reach only implementers that can execute them: given the strongest agent's designs, a locally deployable open-weight model delivers half as often, even when they are lightened, and scores no higher than without them. Generality, we argue, is not disappearing but moving, from the model to the modeler.
evidence_items.title: Moving Generality from Model to Modeler: LLM Agents for PHM on a Deployment-Style Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Deepfake detectors often score well on benchmarks but degrade on videos from other datasets, manipulation methods and compression levels. This work studies deepfake video detection with emphasis on cross-dataset generalization, dataset integrity and reliable evaluation, using EfficientNet-B4 and Xception classifiers on FaceForensics++ (C23), Celeb-DF and additional collected videos. An audit of 17,407 video records (14,888 fake; 2,519 real) found zero byte-identical duplicate groups, but an earlier filename-derived split showed about 90.7% filename-token overlap between test and train/validation rows. We construct a revised split (V11) and a sensitivity-analysis candidate (V12) that groups seven candidate visual links within single partitions, with zero cross-split pairs among 76,263 existing visual-match rows. The V11 model reached 86.69% accuracy and 74.76% AUROC on the external Celeb-DF set (6,528 videos), but balanced accuracy was only 51.65% and real-class specificity 3.49%. V12 results reported are validation-only (best AUROC 0.981005 at epoch 2); V12 test and Celeb-DF evaluation are pending. The findings show that accuracy and fake-class recall alone are insufficient evidence of reliable detection.
evidence_items.title: Leakage-Aware Deepfake Video Detection and Explainable Verification: Dataset Auditing, Split Design and Cross-Dataset Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: STARLI | F101–F110 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume II · Distributed Microrobotic Coordination, Safety and Sample Integrity Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.2  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This collection presents ten prospective research-design monographs in micro/nanorobotic collective systems. Research Unit I (F101–F105) examines self-organizing sampling, load balancing, safe-stop behavior, local sensor fusion and asynchronous control. Research Unit II (F106–F110) investigates competing tasks, adaptive routing, contamination control, collaboration reliability and heterogeneous-agent coordination. The editorial aim is to define independently testable, resource-bounded questions, not to claim demonstrated autonomous performance or clinical efficacy. The ten English working editions comprise 7,770 PDF pages: 300 prospective mathematical research plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated study sections, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Gate has six annotation categories: causal mechanism, measurement witness, blind falsifier, rival explanation, stopping boundary and successor interface. Architecture counts are not evidence of experimental validation or independently certified scientific originality. The Ten Research Directions F101  Nanorobotic Collective Self-Organization Sampling At The Limit — Explores whether locally coordinated sampling can preserve sample identity while keeping collision exposure within a bounded envelope. The proposed witness is harmful collision frequency [events/(agent min)], alongside the atlas collision-rate outcome. Equal-energy fixed-rule behavior is the baseline; leaked global tracking is a rival explanation. Confidence maintained despite a concealed communication partition rejects the claim.
evidence_items.title: STARLI | F101–F110 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume II · Distributed Microrobotic Coordination, Safety and Sample Integrity Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.2  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This collection presents ten prospective research-design monographs in micro/nanorobotic collective systems. Research Unit I (F101–F105) examines self-organizing sampling, load balancing, safe-stop behavior, local sensor fusion and asynchronous control. Research Unit II (F106–F110) investigates competing tasks, adaptive routing, contamination control, collaboration reliability and heterogeneous-agent coordination. The editorial aim is to define independently testable, resource-bounded questions, not to claim demonstrated autonomous performance or clinical efficacy. The ten English working editions comprise 7,770 PDF pages: 300 prospective mathematical research plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated study sections, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Gate has six annotation categories: causal mechanism, measurement witness, blind falsifier, rival explanation, stopping boundary and successor interface. Architecture counts are not evidence of experimental validation or independently certified scientific originality. The Ten Research Directions F101  Nanorobotic Collective Self-Organization Sampling At The Limit — Explores whether locally coordinated sampling can preserve sample identity while keeping collision exposure within a bounded envelope. The proposed witness is harmful collision frequency [events/(agent*min)], alongside the atlas collision-rate outcome. Equal-energy fixed-rule behavior is the baseline; leaked global tracking is a rival explanation. Confidence maintained despite a concealed communication partition rejects the claim. F102  Microrobotic Collective Load Balancing At The Limit — Studies how task redistribution changes spatial coverage without relying on unmetered additional actuation. Coverage spatial entropy [nat] is the proposed endpoint, linked to the original coverage-entropy outcome. A single-agent controller with matched total actuation tests whether the apparent gain comes merely from redundancy. Failure to recover a known-safe state ends the trial. F103  Nanorobotic Collective Safe Stop At The Limit — Defines a test of independently observed transition to a safe state after a collective disturbance. The witness is time to demonstrably safe state [s], preserving the atlas recovery-time field. A fully observing centralized controller provides the comparator; increased agent count is an alternative cause of faster recovery. Crossing any registered safety invariant terminates evaluation. F104  Microrobotic Collective Local Sensor Fusion At The Limit — Examines whether local sensor exchange improves accepted mission decisions under limited communication. Communication traffic per accepted task [bytes/task] is a proposed measurement, with the original communication-load outcome retained. Equal-energy fixed rules challenge the fusion benefit; unacknowledged global state tracking is a competing explanation. Hidden partitions test whether confidence remains appropriately bounded. F105  Nanorobotic Collective Asynchronous Control At The Limit — Investigates decision timing when individual robots update at different rates rather than using a single synchronized command. Total metered energy per completed task [J/task] is the proposed observable, preserving the atlas energy-per-task field. The control comparison matches total actuation to a single-agent system; redundancy without true adaptation is the alternative. Failure to regain a known-safe state requires stopping. F106  Microrobotic Collective Task Competition And Coordination At The Limit — Proposes experiments in which agents must choose between competing tasks under bounded control authority. Selective abstention and service coverage [fraction] is the candidate measurement, anchored to the atlas abstention outcome. A fully observing centralized controller is the strong comparator, with simple agent-number advantage as a rival. Breach of registered safety invariants invalidates any coordination gain. F107  Nanorobotic Collective Adaptive Path Planning At The Limit — Tests whether locally coordinated route changes improve mission completion when obstacles or task geometry vary. Task-success fraction under equal energy [fraction] is the proposed endpoint, linked to the original task-completion measure. Fixed behavior at the same energy budget is the baseline; leaked external tracking may falsely suggest adaptation. Concealed network partitions probe erroneous collective confidence. F108  Microrobotic Collective Contamination Control At The Limit — Addresses a different physical constraint: preserving sample separation during repeated collective handling. The new proposed endpoint is cross-sample chemical carryover [mass fraction], while the source atlas retains consensus error. A matched-actuation single-agent control tests claimed collective benefit; redundancy alone may explain task performance. Inability to return to a known-safe state is a mandatory stop. F109  Nanorobotic Collective Collaboration Reliability At The Limit — Examines whether distributed cooperation can remain safe and reproducible across adverse trials. Hazardful collision frequency [events/(agent*min)] is the candidate observable alongside the original collision-rate outcome. A fully observing centralized controller is the baseline, and additional robots are a rival source of apparent performance. Safety-invariant crossing overrides aggregate success statistics. F110  Microrobotic Collective Heterogeneous Agents Coordination At The Limit — Studies coordination across agents with different sensing, mobility or task roles, while preserving traceable collective outcomes. Coverage entropy under heterogeneous roles [nat] is the proposed witness. Equal-energy fixed behavior is the baseline; outside tracking that silently supplies global state is a competing explanation. Unjustified high confidence during a concealed partition rejects the proposal. Scope, Falsifiability and Evidence Boundaries These are prospective nonclinical research designs restricted to authorized bench-scale, ex-vivo or synthetic reference settings with traceable sample identity, calibrated measurement and bounded actuation. Proposed endpoints are editorial additions and do not replace original atlas outcomes. No laboratory experiments or clinical results are reported. Matched energy and actuation, blinded disturbances, full negative-trial records and noncompensable safety stops are needed before any advantage claim. PDF structure and archive integrity can be checked automatically, but derivation-level physics, causal independence, source-to-claim DOI alignment and specialist review remain incomplete. Selected Established Methodological References Yang & Zhang (2021) · Motion Control in Magnetic Microrobotics: From Individual and Multiple Robots to Swarms · DOI 10.1146/annurev-control-032720-104318   |   Farivarnejad & Berman (2022) · Multirobot Control Strategies for Collective Transport · DOI 10.1146/annurev-control-042920-095844   |   Seo, Paik & Yim (2019) · Modular Reconfigurable Robotics · DOI 10.1146/annurev-control-053018-023834 These existing methodological citations are reproduced from the source archive evidence register; they do not validate the STARLI-specific proposed systems. Identity-to-claim mapping for each flagship, including additional source DOI candidates, has not been exhaustively verified. We only hope that when they open it, they will find a little light to guide their way.

evidence_items.summary: We introduce ParsHate, a manually annotated dataset of 10,000 Persian tweets spanning 2013–2022, representing the first decade-long benchmark for hate speech detection in Persian. The dataset contains 31% hateful content and supports both hate detection and multi-label fine-grained target identification across seven structured target categories. ParsHate also distinguishes explicit and implicit hate, marks explicit and implicit targets, and provides span-level rationales. Data collection combines random and score-stratified temporal sampling to reduce keyword-driven bias while preserving natural label distributions. Applying SOTA models for Persian hate-speech detection on ParsHate shows moderate performance (79% F1), especially with samples from earlier years, and low performance with target identification (25.5% macro-F1). This emphasizes the diverse sampling of hate speech in ParsHate and its challenging nature that requires more advanced methods for better performance. Dataset is made publicly available.
evidence_items.title: ParsHate: A Benchmark Dataset for Hate and Target Detection in Persian

evidence_items.summary: KOLD (Korea Open-source Landslide Dataset) is a benchmark dataset for detecting rainfall-induced landslides in South Korea from Sentinel-2 imagery. It was built for developing and evaluating deep learning models under Korean conditions, where landslides are mostly small, shallow failures and debris flows on forested slopes that end close to farmland, roads and streams. Such landslides are hard to tell apart from other surface changes in 10 m imagery, and they are not covered by existing public benchmarks. The dataset contains 1,952 image patches from five landslide events between 2020 and 2025, each with pre- and post-event imagery, slope, elevation and a pixel-level landslide mask. Because every patch has an image from before the event, models can learn the change caused by the event rather than the appearance of bare ground. The three archives are the training, validation and test splits, and the test split is a separate event, so that results show how well a model transfers to a new event.
evidence_items.title: Korea Open-source Landslide Dataset (KOLD): A Bitemporal Sentinel-2 Benchmark for Mapping Rainfall-Induced Landslides in South Korea

evidence_items.summary: Many Bangla words are at once personal names and culturally loaded common nouns: মায়া (Maya)isbothagirl’snameandawordfor affectionate compassion. Choosing the right reading demands cultural knowledge that is scarce in the pretraining data of modern language models. We introduceBangla Culturally Entangled Homograph (BanglaCEH) disambiguationandbuildaBanglabenchmark of1,516expert-verifiedsentencesand3,032labelledoccurrencesinwhichonewordappears twicewithtwodistinctreadings,eachlabelled withaculturallygroundedcategoryandanexplanation of the reasoning behind it. Across openand closed-source models, we find a systematicdominant-meaningbias,modelsdefault to the common-noun sense and overlook the name. A Bangla-specific model fails under every prompting regime we test, showing that language-specific pretraining alone does not confer cultural grounding. We further showthatcontrastivechain-of-thoughtprompting can sharply reduce this bias without training, and that distilling cultural explanations teachessmall(1–3B)modelstoreasontoward thecorrectreadingratherthanmemoriselabels, cutting dominant-meaning bias from as high as 100% to under 5% and turning the failed Bangla-specific model into our strongest system.

evidence_items.summary: Autonomous heavy-duty trucks require high safety assurance across complex operational domains, necessitating comprehensive risk assessment of their intricate multi-subsystem interdependencies. Failure mode and effects analysis (FMEA) is a systematic risk assessment methodology widely employed across safety-critical industries, yet it relies heavily on manual, experience-dependent expert judgment and is difficult to apply consistently at scale. Large language models (LLMs) offer an opportunity to support this language-centered workflow. This study presents a framework that couples a fine-tuned LLM with an uncertainty-aware post-filter (UAPF) as a severity-scoring assistant and consistency checker within the human-led FMEA process. We employed quantized low-rank adaptation to adapt the Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct LLM to a comprehensive dataset of over 38,000 FMEA records of autonomous truck systems. UAPF refines the predicted severity according to the model’s predictive uncertainty, and rows whose uncertainty exceeds a validation-set threshold are escalated to expert review. On the held-out test set, the fine-tuned LLM reaches 97.75% accuracy, and UAPF raises it to 97.83% while improving calibration. With a 5% expert-review budget, the escalation rule intercepts 78.2% of the remaining model errors. Under a stricter evaluation in which entire subsystems are held out, accuracy is 94.15%, characterizing transfer to unseen functional domains. To the best of the authors’ knowledge, this work is among the first to combine a fine-tuned LLM with uncertainty-aware post-processing for FMEA severity assessment of autonomous trucks.
evidence_items.title: Uncertainty-Aware Large Language Model Framework for Failure Mode and Effects Analysis Severity Prediction: A Case Study on Autonomous Truck Systems

evidence_items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly applied to telecom engineering tasks, yet perform poorly on 3GPP specifications. These standards encode much of their technical information in complex tables, but LLM knowledge and interpretation of such tables remain largely unexplored. We introduce TeleTables, a benchmark comprising 2,220 tables from 13 3GPP specifications in four formats and 500 human-verified MCQs spanning direct retrieval to multi-step reasoning. Evaluating 20 open-weight LLMs across non-reasoning, multimodal, reasoning, and table-specialized architectures reveals two distinct performance bottlenecks. In the closed-book setting, domain knowledge is the primary constraint, with no general-purpose model exceeding 41% accuracy. When the table is provided as context, the best models exceed 90%, but performance degrades systematically with reasoning depth, evidence scope, and structural complexity, with a 32.2 pp spread across reasoning skills. Table specialization on non-telecom data provides no consistent benefit, while strong reasoning capabilities remain essential for reliable interpretation of complex technical tables.
evidence_items.title: TeleTables: A Benchmark for Evaluating LLM Understanding of Tables in Technical Standards

evidence_items.summary: LLMs increasingly act as purchasing agents, which makes the LLM, not the user, the one choosing among the options that satisfy a request; its preferences quietly fix what gets bought and what it costs. Hotel booking is a clean instance: a high-volume choice settled on a few comparable attributes, where the pick reveals those preferences. We introduce PriceBench, a diagnostic benchmark that recovers an LLM's price, quality, and brand preferences from its booking choices with a logit choice model, applied to 28 LLMs from 8 providers on 3,600 hotel tasks from 179 real New York City properties. We find that capability is associated with how consistently an LLM chooses, not with what it chooses: more capable LLMs hold stronger, more consistent preferences, while weaker ones either lock onto one position, exploitable by whoever controls listing order, or choose almost indifferently. What those preferences favor varies sharply across providers and even within one family: price sensitivity spans more than an order of magnitude, and the price/quality trade-off moves mean booked nightly price from USD 247 to USD 393 on identical tasks. What an agent buys must therefore be measured per LLM, not inferred, and we release the tasks, code, and all 28 response sets.
evidence_items.title: PriceBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Price, Quality, and Brand Preferences in LLM Booking Agents

evidence_items.summary: Quantum chemistry has exponential cost in the number of electrons - here electron choreographies, like orbits quantized by standing waves in hydrodynamical QM analogs, summed coherently over their phase give compact variational approximations beyond Hartree-Fock (90-98% of helium correlation, H2 bond within 0.03%, beryllium in seconds); v9 collects v8.x: helium precision with the core jitter, the n=2 triplet anomaly, and choreographies vs guided histories. Version 11.0 extends Sec. 2.2 with general statements on point-like charges: an energy bound in Fourier form (a vertex flat to Q costs at least αQ /π, so the flat band ends by 220 MeV), a bound for causal nonlinear electrodynamics, the dielectric core (a point-like vertex and a perturbative core exclude each other), the amplitude-dependent source and two Dirac comparison theorems. It updates the excited-electron limit to CMS's 5.6 TeV contact-interaction benchmark (an unfrozen rotor band needs a core below about 0.6×10⁻³ fm), states the scope of the missing J = 3/2 level with a 511 keV bound on its transition moment, records which computed core rings were discretization artefacts and which remain open, adds the modern nucleosynthesis bound to the khronometric window, merges duplicate references and links the companion de Broglie clock, Gryziński, chronoscopy, hidden-trajectory and choreography papers. Independent reviews (Sol, Claude Opus, Neon, Qwen) rederived its load-bearing numbers. Contributions, including those of AI collaborators, are listed in the paper.

evidence_items.summary: Benchmarks typically report aggregate scores over broad task domains such as knowledge or reasoning, but these scores do not reveal which behaviour failed or what intervention would repair it. We propose atomic capacities: paired minimal perturbations that isolate repair-relevant failure modes. We instantiate nine atomic capacities spanning Knowledge, Reasoning, and Hybrid Composition, and evaluate them on paired original–variant prompts using behavioural log-probability measures. Using four Qwen3 models as a controlled case study, we find that models with similar domain-level performance can exhibit substantially different capacity profiles, implying different repair targets. We further show that corruption perturbations separate into two distinct regimes: some reduce confidence in the gold answer without changing the preferred decision, while others flip the model toward the planted incorrect answer. Finally, we show that a standard zero-shot Chain-of-Thought intervention is not uniformly beneficial across capacities and can worsen robustness under misleading cues. Our framework complements domain-level benchmarks with fine-grained behavioural diagnostics that generate targeted hypotheses for model improvement.
evidence_items.title: Same Benchmark Score, Different Failures: Atomic Capacities for Diagnosing Language Model Failure Modes

evidence_items.summary: Abstract (it) Il corpus in esame decostruisce il mito dell'applicazione standardizzata della prospettiva albertiana a base quadrata nell'opera di Leonardo da Vinci, proponendo un paradigma metrico-modulare fondato su evidenze geometriche oggettive e falsificabili. Attraverso l'analisi tridimensionale dell'Annunciazione, dell'Adorazione dei Magi e dell'Ultima Cena, emerge una grammatica spaziale in costante evoluzione. Leonardo abbandona la rigida scacchiera per sviluppare un sistema di "righelli inseriti", evolvendo da una misurazione monodirezionale a un'architettura ritmica e stereometrica. Il metodo d'indagine, basato su tecniche di retro-ingegneria CAD e sul "banale aristotelico", dimostra come le proporzioni spaziali (dal modulo 4:3 ai ritmi polifonici 1:4:1 e 2:1:2) siano direttamente ricavabili dall'opera stessa. L'approccio restituisce spazi non solo misurabili, ma architettonicamente rimontabili e strutturati sulle misure umane, rigettando interpretazioni esoteriche o simbologie forzate. Abstract (en) The examined corpus deconstructs the myth of the standardized application of Albertian square-based perspective in the works of Leonardo da Vinci, proposing a metric-modular paradigm founded on objective and falsifiable geometric evidence. Through the three-dimensional analysis of the Annunciation, the Adoration of the Magi, and the Last Supper, a constantly evolving spatial grammar emerges. Leonardo abandons the rigid checkerboard to develop a system of "inserted rulers," evolving from a monodirectional measurement to a rhythmic and stereometric architecture. The investigative method, based on CAD reverse-engineering techniques and the "Aristotelian obvious," demonstrates how spatial proportions (from the 4:3 module to the 1:4:1 and 2:1:2 polyphonic rhythms) can be directly derived from the artwork itself.
evidence_items.title: Leonardo's Spatial Grammar: A CAD Reverse-Engineering Analysis Corpus: Leonardo's CAD, Leonardo's Rulers, Leonardo's Score

evidence_items.summary: AgroNexus-Bench v1.0.0 is a curated, provenance-aware leaf spectroscopy dataset designed to support reproducible research on leaf nitrogen estimation and the evaluation of spectral learning methods under biologically meaningful data partitions. The resource integrates three previously published datasets: citrus leaf VNIR reflectance and laboratory nitrogen measurements, the EcoSIS eight-crop leaf spectra and biochemical traits collection, and SensOFOREST holm oak leaf biochemical and spectral observations. The release contains 895 source-level observation records and 892 spectra, including 886 unique observations eligible for four source-specific nitrogen benchmark tasks: Citrus: 684 composite leaf samples, with 204 spectral bands (397.32–1003.58 nm), direct Dumas nitrogen measurements on a dry-mass basis, and orchard, cultivar, and collection-date metadata. EcoSIS: 187 biochemical trait records, 184 paired spectra across eight crop species, and 178 quality-eligible observations. It provides direct dry-mass nitrogen measurements and an explicitly derived area-based nitrogen variable. SensOFOREST: 24 leaf-age observations nested within 12 physical Quercus ilex trees, with 2,101 spectral bands (400–2500 nm) and direct area-based nitrogen measurements. AgroNexus-Bench preserves source-native spectral axes, original measurement units, biological sampling hierarchies, source identifiers, and transformation provenance. It provides structured metadata, quality and eligibility information, nitrogen target definitions, and fixed evaluation partitions for reproducible within-source analysis and group-aware assessment of distribution shifts. Dry-mass nitrogen concentration and area-based nitrogen are treated as distinct quantities. Derived measurements are explicitly identified, and biological dependencies are preserved to reduce the risk of invalid comparisons and data leakage.
evidence_items.title: AgroNexus-Bench: A Curated Leaf Nitrogen Spectral Dataset with Provenance and Reproducible Evaluation Splits

evidence_items.summary: Banks continue to depend on handwritten signatures, yet a verifier that scores well on its own benchmark can act very differently once it meets documents it has never seen. This paper examines how a Siamese convolutional network for writer-independent offline signature verification carries over between datasets, scripts and scan conditions. We train on writer-disjoint splits of CEDAR (English) and BHSig260 (Hindi and Bengali), using contrastive and triplet loss, and then test on unseen writers, on the other datasets, and on images corrupted with noise, blur, ruling lines and stamp marks. The decision threshold is set once on validation data from the training dataset and is never adjusted afterwards. Under contrastive loss the equal error rate (EER) averages 7.8% within a dataset but 19.3% across datasets. The most telling case is a CEDAR-trained model that still ranks Hindi and Bengali pairs usefully (AUC 0.868 and 0.890) while accepting 98.6% and 97.7% of forged pairs at its fixed threshold. Accuracy quoted at a best-case threshold would conceal this failure. Degraded scans raise the EER to between 30.1% and 50.1%. All results are means over 3 random seeds. Training on degraded images lowers the average EER on degraded scans from 41.8% to 20.9% (one seed), at a small cost on clean images. We propose no new architecture. Instead, we offer a controlled and reproducible account of when such a verifier can be trusted on new data and when it needs recalibration.
evidence_items.title: CROSS-DATASET AND CROSS-SCRIPT EVALUATION OF SIAMESE NETWORKS FOR OFFLINE SIGNATURE VERIFICATION IN BANKING DOCUMENTS

evidence_items.summary: Recent LLM benchmarks have tested models on a range of phenomena, but are still focused primarily on natural language understanding for extraction of explicit information, such as QA or summarization, with responses often targeting information from individual sentences. We are still lacking more challenging, and importantly also multilingual, benchmarks focusing on implicit information and pragmatic inferences across larger documents in the context of discourse tracking: integrating and aggregating information across sentences, paragraphs and multiple speaker utterances. To this end, we present DiscoTrack, an LLM benchmark targeting a range of tasks across 12 languages and four levels of discourse understanding: salience recognition, entity tracking, discourse relations and bridging inference. Our evaluation shows that these tasks remain challenging, even for state-of-the-art models.
evidence_items.title: DiscoTrack: A Multilingual LLM Benchmark for Discourse Tracking

evidence_items.summary: Machine learning can forecast supply chain disruptions, but black-box models limit transparency, and the reliability of post-hoc explanations is rarely evaluated. We provide a leakage-checked, reproducible comparative benchmark for shipment-level risk classification on a public synthetic dataset of 5000 shipments, comparing XGBoost alone with a hybrid XGBoost–neural model (XAI-SC-RiskNet), both explained with SHAP and LIME. The hybrid (71.60% accuracy, ROC-AUC 0.819) is statistically indistinguishable from XGBoost (72.60%, 0.819; McNemar’s test p=0.123), as repeated cross-validation and a chronological hold-out confirm. On 500 test shipments, the Local Explanation Consensus Index (LECI; top-6 overlap of local SHAP and LIME features) and LIME stability are lower for the hybrid (0.57 versus 0.68; 0.80 versus 0.88), so the hypothesis that hybridization stabilizes explanations is not supported. LECI was modestly associated with misclassification (AUC 0.61) but added no significant information to predictive uncertainty (AUC 0.77); it is therefore a descriptive measure of explanation agreement, which does not establish explanation correctness or better decisions, and not a validated quality-control mechanism. These findings are specific to one synthetic benchmark with a concentrated weather signal and do not show that hybrid architectures are generally inferior.
evidence_items.title: Comparative Evaluation of Explanation Reliability in Shipment-Level Supply Chain Risk Classification: A Leakage-Checked Benchmark of XGBoost and a Hybrid XGBoost–Neural Framework with SHAP and LIME

evidence_items.summary: This paper introduces ChatbotManip, a novel dataset for studying manipulation in Chatbots. It contains simulated generated conversations between a chatbot and a (simulated) user, where the chatbot is explicitly asked to showcase manipulation tactics, persuade the user towards some goal, or simply be helpful. We consider a diverse set of chatbot manipulation contexts, from consumer and personal advice to citizen advice and controversial proposition argumentation. Each conversation is annotated by human annotators for both general manipulation and specific manipulation tactics. Our research reveals three key findings. First, Large Language Models (LLMs) can be manipulative when explicitly instructed, with annotators identifying manipulation in approximately 84% of such conversations. Second, even when only instructed to be persuasive'' without explicit manipulation prompts, LLMs frequently default to controversial manipulative strategies, particularly Gaslighting and Fear Enhancement. Third, zero-shot larger models such as Gemini 2.5 pro have the best performance in detecting manipulation (of the models tested), with more work required to fine-tune smaller open source models for real-world on-device oversight. Our work provides important insights for AI safety research and highlights the need of addressing manipulation risks as LLMs are increasingly deployed in consumer-facing applications.
evidence_items.title: ChatbotManip: a Dataset to Facilitate Evaluation and Oversight of Manipulative Chatbot Behaviour

evidence_items.summary: TITLE Data and code for: The water price of decentralisation – an agent-based model of Iran's potato, onion and tomato supply chains benchmarked against central planning under drought and export bans DESCRIPTION This dataset accompanies a manuscript submitted to Agricultural Water Management. It contains everything needed to reproduce the comparison between a decentralised and a centrally planned supply chain for irrigated potato, onion and tomato in Iran, at the resolution of 429 counties. The decentralised chain is represented by an agent-based model in NetLogo 6.4. The model has 429 county farmers, producer unions with cold stores, 30 provincial buyers and an exporter. The benchmark is a mixed-integer crop-planning program solved with HiGHS by a fully informed planner on the same data. Both models receive identical shocks: spatially correlated droughts generated through the Standardized Precipitation Index, and export bans drawn from a drought-linked stochastic policy process. The study compares irrigation water, cost and supply per tonne delivered, and reports the water price of decentralisation, defined as the extra irrigation water that each tonne delivered by the decentralised chain carries relative to the coordinated plan.

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) demonstrate strong Helpfulness, Harmlessness, and Honesty (3H) alignment in English-centric settings, but these gains transfer poorly to low-resource languages due to cultural mismatches. Existing multilingual 3H benchmarks rely predominantly on automated translation or LLM based synthesis, propagating source-language biases while sacrificing local relevance. To address this gap, we introduce Pak3H1, the first human-validated, culturally contextualized Urdu benchmark suite for 3H alignment, comprising PakAlpaca (helpfulness), PakBeaverTails (harmlessness), and PakTruthfulQA (honesty). Our multi-stage pipeline integrates manual cultural adaptation and dictionary-guided post editing to prioritize native speaker judgment, ensuring both semantic fidelity and contextual authenticity. Zero-shot evaluations across multiple open and proprietary LLM architectures reveal systematic cross-lingual alignment gaps: helpfulness win rates decline under localized contexts, harmlessness guardrails break down against regional safety risks, and composite honesty metrics degrade substantially due to localized factual constraints. These findings expose structural limitations in current alignment approaches, underscoring the necessity of human-guided localization for equitable multilingual evaluation.
evidence_items.title: Pak3H: Evaluating the Cost of Cultural Mismatch in LLM Alignment with a Human-Contextualized Urdu Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to explain numerical time series, but fluent explanations can misstate when a change occurs, overstate a trend, or introduce unsupported patterns. Existing evaluations often score forecasts, answers, or whole explanations, leaving claim-level temporal grounding undermeasured. We introduce TimeClaimBench, a benchmark that parses explanations into atomic temporal claims and verifies them against a deterministic extracted event graph. Across five LLMs on controlled synthetic series, event-grounded prompting raises the strict graph-supported rate by 18.3 points and reduces graph-unsupported claims by 27.9 points under this fixed operational criterion. Calibration analyses show the boundary of that result. The extractor recovers the designed primary event in 394 of 400 series, but this does not estimate the precision of additional extracted events. A blinded two-annotator comparison on one model and 40 series reverses the automatic ordering: holistic ratings favor Direct and chain-of-thought outputs over event-grounded outputs. TimeClaimBench therefore distinguishes four axes that should not be conflated: designed-event recovery, the unresolved precision of additional events, claim-to-graph consistency, and whole-explanation human judgment. Code: https://github.com/lunaaa95/TimeClaimBench
evidence_items.title: TimeClaimBench: A Claim-Level Benchmark for Grounded LLM Explanations of Time Series

evidence_items.summary: HEARS-LM v2.0 is the release that accompanies the paper "HEARS-LM: a hearing-loss-adapted protein language model for missense variant interpretation, evaluated with leakage-controlled benchmarks". HEARS-LM fine-tunes ESM-2 with low-rank adapters on the proteins of the 163 genes of the Genomics England PanelApp hearing-loss panel and combines it with whole-protein log-probabilities, conservation, structural annotation and gene-level descriptors, without allele frequency. Its score is calibrated to ACMG/AMP evidence strengths (PP3/BP4) and is meant to be used within ACMG/AMP-ClinGen classification, not to classify variants. The release contains the code of the whole analysis and the command-line scoring tool, the labelled benchmark with recorded provenance, the annotation and descriptor tables, the weights and predictions of every trained model, the calibrated thresholds, all result tables and precomputed scores for the unresolved ClinVar missense variants of the panel genes. See README.md and REPRODUCE.md. Version 2.0 is a complete rebuild of the study and supersedes releases v1.0.x.

evidence_items.summary: Glyph-level obfuscation can leave harmful Chinese content readable to humans while degrading automated moderation. We introduce SinoGlyphBench, a diagnostic benchmark that identifies label-critical semantic anchors and creates matched original and glyph-obfuscated inputs in text and image modalities. By perturbing anchors, background context, or both, this design distinguishes corruption of moderation-relevant evidence from general surface variation. Across 176,916 paired evaluations of 12 LLMs and MLLMs, obfuscation increases harmful false-negative and false-positive rates by 6.1 and 4.7 percentage points, respectively, and reduces four-way accuracy by 5.0 points. Models retain 75.7% of the decisions that were correct on the matched original inputs. Full-scope perturbations cause the largest degradation, anchor-only perturbations are more damaging than background-only perturbations, and cross-script substitution is particularly difficult in the text modality. Analysis of structured outputs identifies observable mismatches in visible-form reading, intended-message recovery, and final safety judgment. The evaluated models, therefore, remain brittle to Chinese content written with non-canonical glyphs. Resources are available at https://github.com/fengshun124/SinoGlyphBench.
evidence_items.title: SinoGlyphBench: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Chinese Glyph-Level Obfuscation in Language-Model Moderation

evidence_items.summary: Michał Gryziński built a classical description of atoms starting from collisions: a binary-encounter theory of inelastic collisions (1959–1965), the free-fall atomic model with radially moving electrons (1965), the 120° star (1972), clock quantisation (1980–1987), models of H2+, the chemical bond, solids and electron-catalysed fusion in palladium. This paper reproduces his calculations, compares them with present data, and for each claim looks for the smallest change that improves agreement while keeping his core idea. A repair ladder (single orbit → fixed-energy ensemble → field → exchange → dipole response → three-body dynamics → wave projectile) shows where his heuristics stood in for missing ingredients: e+H ionisation improves from 16% to 2% rms, e+Ar to 1.8% and e+He to 6% against absolute measurements; proton capture is described from 1 to 150 keV; the head-on oscillations he called decisive are reproduced within 2–9% (first maximum 20.6 vs 21 keV) once the orbital charge adapts variationally during the collision; his scaling for metals (E^(2/5)·α constant over 42 metals) stands; his line systematics, screening doublets and the high-energy part of double ionisation become parameter-free with the core's response; his positron alignment, post-collision deflection and Stark-effect claims are tested against the sources. Every specific claim is tested; many accurate entries are hybrid or replacement benchmarks, classified in Table 2. Code and data for every calculation are included.
evidence_items.title: Gryziński's classical atomic programme: benchmarks, failure modes, and a repair ladder

evidence_items.summary: Background: Pulmonary hypertension (PH) is a morbid but underrecognized disease diagnosed by right heart catheterization (RHC). Automated extraction of RHC data from electronic health systems is likely to expedite PH diagnosis. However, RHC outputs are typically unstructured, free-text reports and current large language models (LLM) that extract patient-level RHC data are imprecise and derived from small datasets. Methods and Results: We established an iterative development and validation framework using the LLM GPT-4-0125-preview to extract patient-level data from RHC reports. The extraction accuracy was assessed against manual expert-curated ground truth using micro-averaged precision, recall, and F1 metrics across all extracted variables. Evaluation on an independent test set of 100 previously unseen reports yielded a precision of 99.8%, a recall of 99.5%, an F1 score of 99.8%, and a hallucination rate of 0.09%. Next, we deployed the LLM to all n = 17,151 RHC reports captured in the Electronic Health Record of the University of Maryland Medical System (UMMS; ~2.3 million patients across 12 hospitals) from 1 January 2016 to 31 December 2024. Manual validation on 200 random reports demonstrated a precision of 99.7%, a recall of 99.2%, an F1 score of 99.5%, and a hallucination rate of 0.17% (all realistic and physiologically plausible). To further explore reproducibility across deployment settings, we deployed the LLM to a targeted sample of 3000 randomly selected RHC reports that included previously identified error cases. Validation of 200 random reports demonstrated a hallucination rate of 0.33% (precision 99.4%, recall 99.9%, F1 99.6%). Notably, four of the seven observed hallucinations in the large-scale deployment were absent when processed in a smaller deployment cohort. Conclusions: We demonstrate high precision for LLMs when deployed on a scale to RHC reports from a large, diverse multi-hospital EHR.
evidence_items.title: Large-Scale Deployment of Large Language Models to Extract Hemodynamic Variables from Cardiac Catheterization

evidence_items.summary: Group Emotion Analysis (GEA) is moving from closed-set group emotion recognition toward open-world understanding of multi-person social affect. Large Language Models (LLMs), and multimodal LLMs (MLLMs) in particular, are driving this shift because they return more than a label or a score: rationales, role claims, profiles, pseudo-labels, and tool-grounded reports. Existing GEA surveys organize the field by architecture or modality, which cannot capture the fact that a single model may perform multiple functions within a single pipeline. We therefore organize LLM use in GEA by functional role. Following a PRISMA-guided, evidence-layered protocol, we reviewed 105 studies from January 2020 to May 2026, separating 45 core GEA studies from 38 adjacent transferable and 22 reliability-supporting studies, so that validated group-level findings are not confused with results transferable only by analogy. We derive a taxonomy of five functional roles: Predictor, Perceiver, Generator, Data-Engine, and Hybrid. We strictly define Hybrid as tool-augmented reasoning over structured intermediate evidence rather than ordinary preprocessing. We map each role to its GEA tasks, modalities, emotion representations, datasets, and evaluation requirements. Synthesizing reported results, we find that on closed-set accuracy zero-shot systems trail trained baselines and that apparent gains often reflect permissive metrics. The value these models promise lies in their wider output space, which current benchmarks cannot yet score, so the field faces an evaluation gap rather than demonstrated parity. Because each role carries its own evidence, metrics, reliability checks, and governance concerns, we close with a role-specific research agenda.
evidence_items.title: A Role-Based Taxonomy of Large Language Models for Group Emotion Analysis

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background : Patient-level clinico-transcriptomic cohorts are used for biomarker discovery, patient stratification, validation and model training. However, most transcriptomic data remains siloed in hospitals, biopharma, and consortia because expression profiles and linked clinical metadata carry re-identification risk. Synthetic RNA-seq cohorts that capture population structure without retaining individual records could be shared in their place, but only if they accurately reproduce the results of standard translational analyses on the real data. We test this with dbTwin, a proprietary generator, on three public cohorts, so that every synthetic result can be checked against its real source, and release the synthetic cohorts with the benchmark used to evaluate them. Results: Synthetic versions of TCGA lung adenocarcinoma (510 samples; 19,719 genes), whole-blood sepsis (152; 27,097), and pediatric inflammatory bowel disease (322; 43,790) recovered most of the differential-expression (DE) signals tested. Across five contrasts on clinical variables declared to dbTwin as anchor columns, synthetic effect sizes kept their real magnitude (log2 fold-change slope 0.92–1.01), and 71.9–90.8% of real DE genes were recovered (81.7–97.2% at a relaxed screening threshold). For STK11 mutation (non-anchor column), effect sizes shrank (slope 0.70) but 96.8% of DE genes kept their direction. In five-fold cross-validation, classifiers trained on synthetic data were within 0.002 ROC-AUC of real-trained ones on held-out real patients and relied on largely the same driver genes (SHAP Pearson r = 0.808–0.975). Synthetic cohorts also retained gene–gene co-expression (Spearman ρ = 0.940–0.996), and 0 of 22 clinical comparisons exceeded sampling noise.
evidence_items.title: Biomarker discovery on synthetic patient transcriptomes: three public cohorts and a benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We present MitoEM 2.0, a difficulty-aware extension of the original MitoEM benchmark for training and evaluating three-dimensional (3D) mitochondria instance segmentation in volume electron microscopy. The collection assembles multiscale vEM datasets (FIB-SEM, SBF-SEM, ssSEM) spanning diverse tissues and species, with expert-verified instance labels emphasizing biologically difficult scenarios, including dense mitochondrial packing, hyperfused networks, and thin filamentous connections with ambiguous boundaries. All releases include native-resolution volumes and standardized processed versions, per-volume metadata (voxel size, modality, tissue, splits), and official train/validation/test partitions to enable reproducible benchmarking. Annotations follow a consistent protocol with quality checks and instance reindexing. Data are provided in NIfTI with nnU-Net–compatible layout and OME-Zarr for cloud-aware workflows, alongside machine-readable split files and checksums. Baseline scripts support common training pipelines and size-stratified evaluation. By consolidating challenging volumes and harmonized labels, MitoEM 2.0 facilitates robust model development and fair comparison across methods while supporting reuse in bioimage analysis, algorithm benchmarking, and teaching.
evidence_items.title: MitoEM 2.0: A Benchmark for Challenging 3D Mitochondria Instance Segmentation from EM Images

organizations: Department of Informatics and Computer Engineering, University of West Attica, 12243 Egaleo, Greece
evidence_items.summary: Collaborative learning scripts are usually fixed, and collaboration dashboards do not necessarily prompt teachers to intervene. We present a hybrid intelligent decision-support architecture that diagnoses five group dysfunctions, explains each alert and proposes one script adaptation from a closed catalogue, with an open simulation benchmark providing planted dysfunctions and a per-group oracle. It combines fuzzy inference, a lexical content classifier, calibrated gradient-boosting detectors with SHAP explanations, expected-benefit operator selection and NSGA-II regrouping. All evidence comes from controlled simulations; no teacher used the system, and learning outcomes were not evaluated. Over 20 development datasets, the detectors reached a macro-F1 of 0.591, and the fuzzy indicators were practically equivalent to their absence in accuracy. Because development data, including test windows of one seed, were inspected while the system was built, these results are not an independent confirmation; a pre-specified evaluation of the frozen system on 20 new datasets replicated 14 of 15 endpoints (macro-F1 0.590), but the defect rate of filtered explanations doubled (0.029 to 0.059). Performance did not survive distribution shift: macro-F1 fell from 0.586 to 0.297 under a changed generating mechanism, the full model fell below the interaction-only model on a held-out topic, and misconception F1 on unseen paraphrases (0.146) was no better than flagging every window. A training-selected operating point achieved 0.399 of the oracle’s simulated harm reduction with 18.7% unneeded interventions, and detector-triggered regrouping increased simulated harm. The benchmark serves as a pre-deployment stress test; the scores are upper bounds, not evidence of teaching benefit.
evidence_items.title: Hybrid Intelligent Decision-Support Architecture for Explainable Adaptation of Collaborative Learning Scripts: A Simulation Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract While spatial transcriptomics technologies are increasingly accessible, spatial proteomics remains constrained by high costs and limited throughput. Furthermore, poor mRNA-protein correlation, driven by post-transcriptional regulation, necessitates multi-omics integration for complementary biological insights. Current RNA-to-protein prediction models, primarily trained on bulk or single-cell data, often overlook critical spatial context. Consequently, it remains unclear which model architecture, spatial representation, or histopathological features best facilitate spatial protein abundance inference. To address these gaps, we defined the STP (Spatial Transcriptome-to-Proteome) task and launched the STP Open Challenge, a competition for predicting spatial proteomics from spatial transcriptomics of adjacent tissue sections. Utilizing a curated paired spatial dataset and a standardized evaluation framework, the challenge attracted 101 teams and yielded 896 valid submissions. Top-performing methods achieved strong predictive performance while preserving spatial organization. The landscape of submitted models revealed diverse modeling strategies and motivated us to develop a consensus-based ensemble framework that leverages various participant methods to enhance prediction robustness. Extended evaluation on unseen datasets demonstrated that the top-performing models outperformed existing baselines, highlighting the effectiveness of the community effort for this task. By formally defining the STP task and providing a standardized benchmarking platform, this work establishes a foundation for scalable, cost-effective spatial proteomics prediction and future multi-omics integration.
evidence_items.title: The STP Open Challenge: A Community Effort to Define and Benchmark Spatial Transcriptome-to-Proteome Prediction

evidence_items.summary: Hallucination research in low-resource languages fragments easily: each newly named failure mode prompts its own dataset, spending scarce annotators on incomparable resources. We argue for consolidation and test it at community scale. Alikbachan is a Bengali hallucination-detection benchmark stratified along three crossed axes: a human-validated cultural-distance band, six task types, and a five-family, 32-mode hallucination taxonomy. It comprises a harvested 2,516-item test set (Phase 1) and a quota-constructed, gold-labeled 5,000-item set (Phase 2). The stratification is diagnostic. Four zero-shot LLM judges vary by over 30 macro-F1 points across strata, and the item-level predictions of 99 Phase-1 and 32 Phase-2 competition systems reproduce the profile: discourse-level omission defeats judges and most teams alike, whereas only a minority over-flag negative controls. The judges' verdict probabilities rank items well (ROC-AUC 0.74-0.95) but are overconfident (ECE 0.04-0.29). An open competition on Alikbachan drew 222 teams and 3,566 submissions, and a single-prompt 32B judge reaches the 57th percentile. Of the 25 teams in both phases, 24 regress on Phase 2 (mean $-17.6$ points) while every zero-shot judge improves, and Phase-1 rank barely predicts Phase-2 rank (Spearman $ρ=0.35$), so a Phase-1 leaderboard alone would have crowned a different winner.
evidence_items.title: One Framework to Diagnose Them All: A Stratified Benchmark for Bengali LLM Hallucination

evidence_items.summary: Air traffic control (ATC) requires structured, safety-critical decision making whose effects unfold through aircraft trajectories, so text-level correctness alone is insufficient for evaluating large language models (LLMs) in this domain. We introduce ATC-Bench, a simulation-grounded benchmark for ATC instruction generation with Chinese-facing scenario descriptions and controller-style instruction fields. Given a structured Chinese traffic situation, a model generates a JSON control plan that is translated into BlueSky commands and evaluated through closed-loop simulation against separation, no-fly-zone (NFZ) avoidance, and route-recovery constraints. The benchmark spans four task families that form a controlled complexity gradient: single-aircraft NFZ avoidance, pairwise conflict resolution, joint conflict-airspace constraints, and multi-aircraft conflict graphs. Experiments with 11 representative LLM endpoints show that while most models produce format-valid instructions, task success varies widely across models and task families: the highest-scoring endpoint under our fixed protocol achieves 63.5% macro-average task success rate (TSR), while the two lowest endpoints fall below 25%, with the largest gaps appearing under joint constraints and multi-aircraft coordination. These results expose a persistent execution gap between static validity and simulation-passing behavior, motivating simulation-in-the-loop evaluation for LLM-based decision making in safety-critical aviation settings.
evidence_items.title: ATC-Bench: A Simulation-Grounded Benchmark for Evaluating LLM-Generated Air Traffic Control Instructions

evidence_items.summary: In machine learning-based network intrusion detection systems, class imbalance can negatively affect the effectiveness of detecting rare attack types. This article presents a comparative analysis grounded in existing literature of balancing strategies aimed at addressing this issue. Specifically, it examines the advantages and limitations of three approaches: the initial imbalanced state (baseline), the generation of synthetic samples for minority classes (SMOTE), and the reduction of samples from majority classes (Random Undersampling – RUS). The analysis utilizes the CIC-IDS2017 and UNSW-NB15 datasets, alongside classifiers such as Decision Tree (DT), Random Forest (RF), K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN), and Multilayer Perceptron (MLP). Findings from existing research indicate that the effectiveness of class balancing depends on the specific dataset, the classifier employed, and the evaluation conditions. Consequently, the study argues that system performance should not be assessed solely through overall accuracy; rather, it necessitates the use of metrics such as Macro-F1, Macro-Precision, class-specific Recall, and the false positive rate. The study establishes a methodological framework for comparing balancing strategies under identical experimental conditions, along with key criteria for future experimental research.

Synthetic analytical surfaces and proposed protocols are not measured biological results. The purpose of this document is to present a compelling, falsifiable research invitation without requiring readers to open the complete monograph or scientific technical notebook. The ninth family begins at a boundary where engineering precision can become deceptively comforting. A microrobot may visit the intended coordinate, carry a cell into a photogenic configuration, or achieve an elegant computer animation, yet none of these outcomes alone demonstrates that the cell survived with its identity and function intact. The research family therefore treats cell manipulation as a chain of jointly qualified actions. Each action must have a known specimen, a calibrated frame of reference, a measured physical interaction, an orthogonal biological witness, a strong comparator, and an independent refusal channel. Failure is preserved as evidence rather than hidden as an inconvenient denominator. This family unites five distinct projects. F041 asks whether capture and localization are reversible and demonstrably accurate in three dimensions. F042 asks what happens to cells after transient and cumulative contact with compliant grippers. F043 examines magnetic actuation against viscous drag and real spatial uncertainty. F044 investigates coordination, collisions and graph-level defects in cooperative assembly. F045 refuses to rank methods by attractive precision alone, instead comparing qualified viable placements per complete experiment time. Their candidate equations share a reduced local contact-force hypothesis from the supplied research atlas, but they do not share the same primary biological or engineering endpoint.
