The strongest existing methods already reveal why careful benchmarking matters. Skilled manual placement, optical tweezers, microfluidic traps, and contemporary soft microrobot systems have different strengths, calibration costs and exposure histories. Some are better at target selectivity, others at gentle contact or throughput. No single alternative should be deliberately left underoptimized to flatter a new microrobotic proposal. Every comparison must freeze the cell lot, assay time, recovery steps, sensor budget and criteria for a successful attempt. An unobserved contact, failed retrieval or delayed injury is part of the result even when it arrives after the camera stops recording.  F041 — MICROROBOTIC SINGLE-CELL CAPTURE AND LOCALIZATION  A cell that appears centered under a microscope may occupy the wrong depth, belong to a doublet or be attached to the device rather than captured by a reversible mechanism. For single-cell capture, the first quantitative promise is a three-dimensional localization error in micrometres. The argument begins with calibration rather than motor performance: reference beads, axial point-spread measurements, the effect of medium refractive index and a timestamped chain from image to actuator. The system must distinguish the moment of actual contact from a merely nearby trajectory.  One research door opens at target identity under mixed populations. Change target marker specificity while recording identity-confirmed capture fraction with an external reference. The competing explanation is cell identity confusion. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  Another sharp boundary appears in refractive-index mismatch in 3d tracking. Change optical index gradient while recording axial reconstruction error with an external reference. The competing explanation is biased axial localization. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  A useful negative case arises from localization covariance near channel walls. Change wall proximity while recording calibration covariance with an external reference. The competing explanation is anisotropic image point spread. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  There is a less obvious question about contact onset before stable capture. Change approach velocity while recording onset force peak with an external reference. The competing explanation is unobserved transient force. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  An independent laboratory should examine cell adhesion versus active gripping. Change surface adhesion energy while recording release energy with an external reference. The competing explanation is passive attachment mimicking success. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  A future successor might discover reversible release without cell carryover. Change release waveform while recording fully released target fraction with an external reference. The competing explanation is stuck targets excluded. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  The strongest claim is challenged by doublets and crowded-target selection. Change neighbor distance while recording doublet discrimination precision with an external reference. The competing explanation is segmentation of two cells as one. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  The next observable failure concerns flow-induced target displacement. Change cross-flow speed while recording post-flow location error with an external reference. The competing explanation is unrecorded hydrodynamic drift. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  A model becomes more honest when capture in off-axis depth. Change target z coordinate while recording out-of-plane error with an external reference. The competing explanation is false two-dimensional overlap. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  An especially revealing perturbation involves camera latency and active pursuit. Change frame delay while recording latency-adjusted residual with an external reference. The competing explanation is tracking compensation on test data. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  Before accepting a gain, examine posthandling delayed cell identity. Change postrelease incubation while recording independent identity match with an external reference. The competing explanation is stain detection altered by manipulation. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  A falsification program can isolate complete attempted-capture accounting. Change failed-start denominator while recording all-start success fraction with an external reference. The competing explanation is failed picks omitted from throughput. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  The hidden denominator often lives in phantom-based force and position calibration. Change reference bead stiffness while recording blind phantom residual with an external reference. The competing explanation is software-only calibration agreement. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  One cannot generalize without testing donor and geometry transfer challenge. Change donor and channel lot while recording out-of-lot localization error with an external reference. The competing explanation is cell-size selection under transfer. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  For F041, the minimum prototype is magnetically positioned inert reference beads followed by authorized in-vitro cell fixtures. The best immediate comparator is skilled manual cell placement and feasible optical tweezers; the primary witness is blind 3D fiducial microscopy combined with an independent calibrated stage. The stop condition is deliberately independent of the optimization algorithm: a force excursion, cell identity mismatch, residual microrobot, or failed independent localization audit. None of these instructions implies that a living-cell device has already been built or validated.  F042 — SOFT MICROGRIPPERS AND LOW-INJURY CELL TRANSPORT  The adjective soft is not a safety certificate. A compliant jaw may reduce instantaneous pressure while a long hold increases integrated mechanical exposure, and a release process can impose a second injury after successful transport. The second flagship therefore treats manipulation-induced injury percentage as an independently measured endpoint. It examines force-displacement calibration, stress relaxation, adhesion hysteresis, cell-size heterogeneity, thermal effects and late loss of cell function. A cell counted as alive immediately after movement may require a second blinded observation after an appropriate interval.  One research door opens at elastic jaw stiffness and force calibration. Change gripper spring constant while recording force calibration residual with an external reference. The competing explanation is tip deflection misread as cell indentation. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  Another sharp boundary appears in contact patch size and pressure localization. Change jaw contact radius while recording maximum local stress with an external reference. The competing explanation is average force hides local peaks. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  A useful negative case arises from viscoelastic cell relaxation during hold. Change hold time while recording relaxation recovery fraction with an external reference. The competing explanation is fast-only assay misses delayed strain. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  There is a less obvious question about force impulse rather than force peak alone. Change loading duration while recording time-integrated load with an external reference. The competing explanation is short peaks and long holds confounded. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  An independent laboratory should examine adhesion hysteresis during release. Change surface coating while recording release hysteresis energy with an external reference. The competing explanation is adhesion loss interpreted as safe release. Change shear rate while recording shear-adjusted injury with an external reference. The competing explanation is external flow damage attributed to grip. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  The strongest claim is challenged by vertical lift and settling collisions. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  An especially revealing perturbation involves soft-material extractables and cytotoxicity. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  Before accepting a gain, examine early membrane staining versus late viability. Change assay delay while recording twenty-four-hour viability with an external reference. The competing explanation is early green cells later lose function. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  A falsification program can isolate cell size dispersion and grip geometry. Change cell diameter while recording size-stratified injury with an external reference. The competing explanation is easy large cells dominate reported success. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  The hidden denominator often lives in sublethal signaling disturbance. Change mechanotransduction marker while recording posthandling stress reporter with an external reference. The competing explanation is normal membrane appearance masks altered state. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  One cannot generalize without testing multiple-handling cumulative exposure. Effective magnetic moment, field gradient, fluid viscosity, robot size and spatial confinement jointly determine motion. The third flagship measures three-dimensional placement error in micrometres rather than equating a field map with a spatial achievement. It challenges coil heating, magnetic chaining, scaffold deformation, axial misregistration and weak carrier recovery. A field reversal becomes a scientifically useful question when apparent placement might actually result from adhesion.  One research door opens at field-gradient map and coil calibration. F044 — COOPERATIVE MICROROBOTIC CELL-GROUP ASSEMBLY AND ERROR CONTROL  Cooperation creates new failure modes that do not appear in a single-robot experiment. Even if each agent is individually precise, the collective may exchange identities, collide, block the camera or assemble a structure with missing graph edges. The fourth flagship therefore evaluates multicell assembly defect rate with a volume-wide rather than a selected-view reference. Communication delay, task allocation, near-miss events, rollback operations and complete assembly attempts all enter the evidence ledger. The benefit of parallel operation must survive a fair comparison to sequential assembly with the same total budget.  One research door opens at agent identity and assignment ambiguity. Change agent identity confidence while recording identity-switch rate with an external reference. The competing explanation is duplicated tracks falsely increase throughput. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  Another sharp boundary appears in multi-agent collision prediction. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  Before accepting a gain, examine shared field interactions among robots. Change actuation cross-talk while recording cross-agent displacement with an external reference. The competing explanation is one command moves unintended agent. Change scaffold compliance while recording scaffold residual strain with an external reference. The competing explanation is assembly shape due to plastic deformation. Change failed run fraction while recording qualified assemblies per hour with an external reference. The competing explanation is fast local steps hide slow rework. The best immediate comparator is single-robot sequential assembly and skilled manual placement with identical material budgets; the primary witness is blind volumetric graph reconstruction and independent all-attempt event log. The stop condition is deliberately independent of the optimization algorithm: unlogged collision, incomplete assembly denominator, unsafe swarm density, or autonomous stop failure. None of these instructions implies that a living-cell device has already been built or validated.  F045 — JOINT OPTIMIZATION OF CELL-HANDLING PRECISION AND SURVIVAL  An engineering team can almost always buy a better headline by relaxing its tolerance, lowering its survival requirement or excluding a difficult population. The fifth flagship makes that temptation explicit and refuses to compress all performance into one unexplained score. Its primary quantity is qualified viable placements per minute, calculated from all attempts and subject to frozen spatial and biological thresholds. An admissible Pareto improvement requires that gains in speed or positioning not silently purchase greater injury, identity loss or posthandling failure. The frontier itself must be reconstructed under held-out conditions.  One research door opens at definition of a jointly qualified placement. Change discard probability while recording failure-inclusive improvement with an external reference. The competing explanation is unreported failed tracks boost throughput. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  Before accepting a gain, examine resource energy and material cost. Change energy per task while recording qualified units per joule with an external reference. The competing explanation is extra sensing cost omitted. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  A falsification program can isolate human authority and hard-stop margins. Change veto latency while recording independent veto lag with an external reference. The competing explanation is unsafe output allowed during uncertainty. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  The hidden denominator often lives in comparison against fixed pareto alternatives. Change benchmark frontier while recording frontier dominance with an external reference. The competing explanation is unoptimized manual comparator exaggerates gain. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  One cannot generalize without testing sample-size and rare-harm sensitivity. Change tail event frequency while recording upper confidence harm bound with an external reference. The competing explanation is small cohorts miss infrequent injury. If the outcome tracks this nuisance, the claimed mechanism fails; retain unsuccessful trials.  For F045, the minimum prototype is registered microcarrier positioning with inert references and independent viability surrogates before authorized cells. The best immediate comparator is optimized skilled manual workflows and optical tweezers with full all-attempt time accounting; the primary witness is third-party position calibration, blinded delayed live-cell assay and full operation-time ledger. The stop condition is deliberately independent of the optimization algorithm: any preregistered survival floor breach, invalid specimen selection, missed stop or unrecovered carrier. None of these instructions implies that a living-cell device has already been built or validated.  COUPLING THE FIVE FLAGSHIPS WITHOUT MERGING THEIR EVIDENCE  The interfaces between the projects are as important as the projects themselves. Capture determines which cell is initially selected; gentle transport determines whether that selection remains biologically defensible; magnetic positioning determines where it is placed; cooperative assembly determines the final spatial graph; and joint optimization decides whether the entire process produces qualified outcomes at a reasonable complete-experiment cost. Each interface therefore needs an identity key, a coordinate transform, a physical exposure ledger and a time stamp. If one part of the chain cannot be reconstructed, the combined headline must be downgraded rather than repaired by confident narration.  A second coupling concerns how measurement can distort the phenomenon it seeks to certify. Fluorescence intensity may change with focus and bleaching, membrane staining may be sensitive to treatment duration, and a tracking model may inherit the same training labels as its purported reference. These are not small statistical footnotes. They are alternative mechanisms that can make an apparently successful operation look precise and gentle. The family therefore requests orthogonal witnesses and blinded reference swaps. A positive simulation may teach investigators which parameter range merits testing, but simulation cannot confirm that cells retained their biological role.  The thirty candidate equations intentionally include both generic experimental contracts and a shared compliant-contact relation. Hookean force versus indentation is valid only over a measured local elastic range; it must not be used as a universal membrane-damage law. Normalized prediction error can be compared across instruments only when the reference scale remains frozen. Complete time must include setup, readout, calibration and failed-run review. A stop equation is not a safety guarantee unless a physically distinct human-authorized channel can actually enforce refusal.  FORTY-TWO RECONSTRUCTABLE SYNTHETIC SURFACES  A collection of three-dimensional mathematical surfaces gives this research a second, visual language. One group maps camera calibration and movement latency to localization error. Another depicts a toy force-duration injury-risk proxy, clearly separated from measured viability. A third maps magnetic gradients and medium viscosity into a drag-governed placement residual. A fourth explores how coordination delay and agent count can increase a toy assembly defect index. A fifth draws the constrained frontier of qualified placement rate against spatial tolerance and survival floor. Two integration surfaces illustrate joint risk and reconstruction completeness. They are deliberately synthetic and supplied with sample grids, axis units, assumptions and a runnable independent numerical check.  The Research Gates are presented as a civilization of questions rather than a catalog of confirmations. Two hundred different prompts ask what could counterfeit success, which signal a rival system would produce, and how the next laboratory might falsify the preferred interpretation. The thirty-three Phoenix concepts propose small instruments and evidence contracts, ranging from calibrated contact witnesses to magnetic carrier retrieval ledgers, graph-level assembly referees, independent human vetoes and open negative-case archives. An embryo is an invitation to test, not a device certification.  ETHICAL AND EPISTEMIC BOUNDARY  All of these designs are prospective and nonclinical. Beginning with nonliving microphantoms, maintaining material provenance and using only suitably authorized in-vitro research are necessary boundaries. No part of the atlas authorizes deployment in human subjects or automatic irreversible biological actuation. The research value is not measured by whether every bold idea is confirmed. A rigorous disconfirmation can teach the next generation which geometry, force budget, sensing pathway or coordination assumption should be changed. The durable artifact is the ability to repeat a question without inheriting an unearned claim of success. evidence_items.summary: STARLI | F091–F100 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume I · Collective Microrobotic Autonomy, Swarm Safety and Mission Continuity Author: 33 | Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.3 | English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This ten-volume collection closes the first hundred of the STARLI 300-theme research-design atlas. Research Unit I (F091–F095) examines autonomous sampling, local-to-global coordination, pheromone-like signaling, collision avoidance and collective energy allocation. Research Unit II (F096–F100) examines distributed planning, localization uncertainty, changing network topology, fault isolation and safe mission handoff. Each volume states prospective physical tests rather than completed experimental findings. The ten English working editions total 7,770 PDF pages: 300 candidate mathematical plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated investigations, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The v1.3 Gate-annotation pass contrasts mechanisms, physical witnesses, blinded falsifiers, rivals, stopping boundaries and successor interfaces. These editorial counts and text-screening results do not establish causal independence or scientific validation. The Ten Research Directions F091 Nanorobotic Collective Autonomy Sampling At The Limit — Proposes controlled tests of swarm sampling throughput and identity preservation. A concealed communication partition probes whether completion gains survive the loss of collective coordination, against a centralized full-state controller; collision events and consensus error remain explicit vetoes. F092 Microrobotic Local Collaboration And Global Mission At The Limit — Asks whether agent-to-agent collaboration improves global agreement when robots lack an unmetered global-state feed. Hidden adversarial-neighbor states test dependence on outside tracking; fixed behavior rules with matched energy provide the comparator.
evidence_items.title: STARLI | F091–F100 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume I · Collective Microrobotic Autonomy, Swarm Safety and Mission Continuity Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.3  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This ten-volume collection closes the first hundred of the STARLI 300-theme research-design atlas. Research Unit I (F091–F095) examines autonomous sampling, local-to-global coordination, pheromone-like signaling, collision avoidance and collective energy allocation. Research Unit II (F096–F100) examines distributed planning, localization uncertainty, changing network topology, fault isolation and safe mission handoff. Each volume states prospective physical tests rather than completed experimental findings. The ten English working editions total 7,770 PDF pages: 300 candidate mathematical plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated investigations, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. The v1.3 Gate-annotation pass contrasts mechanisms, physical witnesses, blinded falsifiers, rivals, stopping boundaries and successor interfaces. These editorial counts and text-screening results do not establish causal independence or scientific validation. The Ten Research Directions F091  Nanorobotic Collective Autonomy Sampling At The Limit — Proposes controlled tests of swarm sampling throughput and identity preservation. A concealed communication partition probes whether completion gains survive the loss of collective coordination, against a centralized full-state controller; collision events and consensus error remain explicit vetoes. F092  Microrobotic Local Collaboration And Global Mission At The Limit — Asks whether agent-to-agent collaboration improves global agreement when robots lack an unmetered global-state feed. Hidden adversarial-neighbor states test dependence on outside tracking; fixed behavior rules with matched energy provide the comparator. F093  Nanorobotic Collective Pheromone Communication At The Limit — Explores prospective chemical-trail or signal-mediated coordination with collision exposure as a primary outcome. Hidden actuator saturation and a matched-actuation single-agent baseline challenge claims that signaling, rather than redundancy or imposed motion, caused the improvement. F094  Microscale Robot Collective Collision Avoidance Control At The Limit — Examines collision-safe motion while monitoring spatial coverage, recovery time and communication burden. A blinded shared-localization bias tests whether apparent avoidance depends on erroneous common position estimates; safety-boundary crossings trigger rejection. F095  Nanorobotic Collective Energy Allocation At The Limit — Tests dynamic allocation of limited energy across agents during dropout and recovery. Hidden agent-loss clusters challenge energy accounting and recovery-time claims against fixed rules with an equal energy budget; persistent unsafe confidence is a stop condition. F096  Microrobotic Distributed Mission Planning At The Limit — Studies task planning without a central controller using communication load, work-per-task and selective abstention as prospective metrics. Hidden network partitions expose plans that depend on unavailable messages, while a matched-actuation single-agent system tests whether coordination adds value. F097  Nanorobotic Collective Localization Uncertainty At The Limit — Tests whether robots can act safely when position confidence is uncertain or neighbors provide deceptive state information. Energy per accepted task, abstention and completion are checked against a full-state centralized benchmark; unrecognized safety-boundary crossings invalidate the claim. F098  Microrobotic Collective Dynamic Topology Control At The Limit — Examines when changing neighbor connections should trigger reconfiguration or justified refusal to proceed. Hidden actuator saturation challenges topology decisions; fixed energy-matched rules and independent task and consensus measurements distinguish adaptive control from misleading internal agreement. F099  Nanorobotic Collective Fault Isolation At The Limit — Investigates recognition and containment of malfunctioning agents without allowing errors to propagate across the swarm. A blinded shared-localization bias tests whether fault labels confuse a common sensor defect with separate robot failures; recovery to a known-safe state is mandatory. F100  Microrobotic Collective Mission Handoff At The Limit — Designs a traceable transfer of task state and authority across agents after concealed dropout clusters. The study checks consensus error, collisions and coverage against centralized full-state control; an apparently successful handoff is rejected if safety invariants are violated. Scope, Falsifiability and Evidence Boundaries All ten volumes are prospective, nonclinical research-design working editions for traceable materials, authorized ex-vivo systems, synthetic phantoms and bench-scale microfluidic tests. Proposed comparisons require preregistered budgets, blinded perturbations, independent reference measurements, complete negative-trial denominators and explicit safety stops. No new experimental results, validated in-body autonomy or clinical benefit are claimed. Mathematical derivations, physical unit consistency, claim-level DOI linkage and substantive causal novelty still require specialist review; the automatic Gate-text distinctness audit cannot replace it. Selected Established Methodological References Yang & Zhang (2021) · Motion Control in Magnetic Microrobotics: From Individual and Multiple Robots to Swarms · DOI 10.1146/annurev-control-032720-104318   |   Farivarnejad & Berman (2022) · Multirobot Control Strategies for Collective Transport · DOI 10.1146/annurev-control-042920-095844   |   STARLI Flagship 13 mother-method ancestry · DOI 10.5281/zenodo.23318840 These identifiers and methodological descriptions come from the supplied source-archive evidence register. They are reference points for existing methods, not evidence that any STARLI-specific candidate device or proposed experimental advantage has been demonstrated. Independent source-to-claim verification remains necessary. We only hope that when they open it, they will find a little light to guide their way.

Conclusion: AI algorithms and 3D imaging should serve as transparent clinical decision-support tools under direct practitioner oversight.

evidence_items.summary: Accurately extracting and mapping road surface elements is crucial for applications such as high-definition maps, road asset management, and intelligent transportation systems. This study first provides a comprehensive review of the benchmark datasets for extracting and mapping road elements, encompassing overhead-to-perspective data, large-to-local scales, and coarse-to-fine details. Subsequently, we thoroughly review the relevant approaches for extracting road surface elements. However, we argue that existing datasets still require enhancements in semantic richness, data modality diversity, and scenario complexity. To bridge these gaps, this paper presents WHU-Road3D, a large-scale multimodal dataset for fine-grained road surface mapping to address these shortcomings. WHU-Road3D provides approximately 100 km of diverse Chinese highways and urban streets. It features a rich combination of MLS point clouds, associated panoramic images, vehicle trajectories, detailed vectorized annotations, and pointwise instance annotations for road surface elements. The dataset carefully annotates 15 distinct categories of road elements, including common markings like road boundaries, zebra crossings, lane dividers, stop lines, as well as 10 types of direction symbols. To our knowledge, WHU-Road3D stands as the first multimodal dataset for mapping such a comprehensive range of road surface elements, designed to facilitate cutting-edge research in instance segmentation, full-element extraction and mapping on road surfaces. Beyond these immediate applications, WHU-Road3D also provides a valuable source for hierarchical road topology reasoning, map updating, and street scene generation. The dataset, along with the code for our benchmark methods, will be made publicly available at \href{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}{https://github.com/WHU-USI3DV/WHU-Road3D.git}.

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used not only to power AI agents but also to build them. While many benchmarks assess the quality of LLM- powered agents, few ascertain how good LLMs are at building them. To this end, we introduce AppSci-Bench, where we construct a setting akin to how human Applied Scientists build agents for businesses - through eliciting task requirements from stakeholders, exploring the business's infrastructure, and scientifically improve the target agent by designing experiments and internal benchmarks. AppSci-Bench features seven realistic domains - five new ones (Slides Generation, Order-to-Cash, Compliance Review, Customer Call Insights, and CRM Insights) and two domains recast from tau3-bench (Yao et al., 2024; Shi et al., 2026b)(Airline and Banking) - each with a held-out evaluation suite customized for that task. We evaluate seven frontier models and find AppSci-Bench challenging: the best model, Claude Opus 5.0, only reaches a mean-minimum score of 59.1% across 3 build attempts; other models do significantly worse. Models struggle with eliciting task requirements (only 65% for Opus 5.0), build representative internal evaluations (models saturate their own evaluation 65% of the time but fail to solve the held-out task), presenting challenges for future research. The benchmark code is available here: https://github.com/sanjari-orb/appsci-bench.
evidence_items.title: AppSci-Bench: Can LLMs Build AI Agents and Make Them Better?

evidence_items.summary: This record contains the complete artifact bundle for the arXiv preprint ULM-Bench: A Preregistered Benchmark and Audit Protocol for Ontological Coherence in Language Models (Mark JJ McCormack, independent researcher).Contents: ULM v1.0 — a versioned Hegelian category graph (Logic → Nature → Spirit) with 654-slot grid, 555 uncontested verified slots, 53 pending, 28 gaps, 18 contested, 342 application mappings, and 24 cross-cutting Universals. Released as JSON (ulm v1.json), CSV position tables, raw exports, and JSON Schema. OMS Reference Implementation — deterministic Python reference for the Ontological Match Score (oms reference.py), computing direction, distance, and triad-integrity losses against the sequestered ULM graph. Semantic Logic Mapping (SLM) Specification — formal parser spec (PARSER SPEC.md), relation inventory, worked examples, failure taxonomy, and JSON Schema (slm.schema.json). ULM-Bench Benchmark Specification — three task families (Static Retrieval, Cross-Domain Normative Dilemmas, Ontological Rupture), item schema, four conditions (Ungrounded, BFO/CCO, GraphRAG, ULM), six controls, and eight primary endpoints. Preregistered Confirmatory Protocol — \$25k study design with hypotheses (H-01–H-19), power analysis (N=194/condition for 10pp effect), go/no-go gates (Parser F1 ≥ 0.85, κ ≥ 0.67, OMS AUC ≥ 0.80), and falsification criteria. Pilot Results — 200 items × 4 conditions; L condition 52% OMS pass (0.707 mean), U/B/G 100% abstain. Audit Scripts — ulm audit.py (14,940 checks, 0 errors), build ulm.py (deterministic builder). evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Large language models (LLMs) perform strongly on medical specialty board multiple-choice questions (MCQs) but underperform in complex medical reasoning. This gap indicates a need to improve LLM medical reasoning and evaluation paradigms. Objective This study aimed to develop and evaluate MedEvalArena, a dynamically regenerable benchmark for assessing medical reasoning in LLMs. Methods In a symmetric round-robin format, 6 frontier LLMs from the OpenAI, Grok, Gemini, Claude, Kimi, and DeepSeek families generated challenging board-style medical MCQs, adjudicated question validity on an ensemble LLM-as-judge panel, and answered the validated examination. Candidate items were generated until each model contributed 50 validated questions according to Association of American Medical Colleges (AAMC)/American Board of Medical Specialties (ABMS) physician specialty distributions, yielding a 300-question examination. Judges adjudicated candidate questions’ logical validity and medical accuracy. We compared question-generation validity rates, assessed leave-one-out judge agreement, and tested for self-judging preference. Questions were audited for overlap with public MedQA (medical question-answering) benchmarks. We tested question-answering (QA) accuracy across LLMs using a binomial-logit generalized linear mixed model likelihood-ratio test. A generator-stratified 90-question subset was completed by 5 board-certified physicians for paired human-LLM analysis. We evaluated inference cost-accuracy tradeoffs. Multiple comparisons were adjusted by the Benjamini-Hochberg (BH) procedure. Results Judge-panel validity rates were significantly higher for questions generated by OpenAI (94.8%, Wilson 95% CI 85.9%-98.2%), Gemini (92.3%, 95% CI 83.2%-96.7%), and Claude (83.3%, 95% CI 72.6%-90.4%) models than those generated by Kimi (63.8%, 95% CI 54.3%-72.4%), Grok (56%, 95% CI 45.8%-65.8%), and DeepSeek (46.0%, 95% CI 37.4%-54.7%).
evidence_items.title: Medical Reasoning in Large Language Models: Development and Evaluation of the MedEvalArena Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly evaluated for empiric antibiotic decision support, but it remains unclear whether contemporary systems behave similarly under the same clinical and stewardship constraints. We compared four LLM configurations on real internal medicine admissions using a common, auditable stewardship benchmark. Methods: This single-center, retrospective, paired, non-interventional shadow-mode study included 486 admissions from a previously published 493-admission internal medicine cohort. For each admission, the clinician-prescribed empiric regimen was compared with recommendations from OpenAI GPT-5.5, Anthropic Claude Opus 4.7, Google Gemini 2.5 Pro, and Mistral Large 2512; OpenAI GPT-5.2 was analyzed separately as a supplementary legacy bridge. All LLMs received identical clinical content, local epidemiology context, antibiotic ontology, and three-field output schema. The primary endpoint was any contextually unsupported broad-spectrum escalation, defined by the study’s prespecified guardrail rules; the key secondary endpoint was a weighted contextual escalation penalty. Results: Clinician regimens met the primary endpoint in 16.7% of admissions. Rates were 13.0% for GPT-5.5 (paired risk difference [RD] −3.7 percentage points; Holm-adjusted p = 0.216), 15.0% for Gemini 2.5 Pro (RD −1.6; Holm-adjusted p = 0.509), 29.8% for Claude Opus 4.7 (RD +13.2; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001), and 31.9% for Mistral Large 2512 (RD +15.2; Holm-adjusted p < 0.001). Mean weighted contextual escalation penalty was 0.288 for clinician prescribing, 0.173 for GPT-5.5, 0.165 for Gemini, 0.510 for Claude, and 0.348 for Mistral. Global heterogeneity across contemporary LLMs was significant for both endpoints (p < 0.001). Conclusions: Contemporary LLM configurations were not interchangeable under the same stewardship benchmark.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models Are Not Interchangeable for Empiric Antibiotic Recommendations Under a Stewardship Benchmark: A Paired Retrospective Multi-Model Study

evidence_items.summary: Large language models are increasingly deployed as reasoning and decision support components in intelligent systems, yet aggregate benchmark scores provide limited evidence about whether they can reliably access primitive operations, combine them compositionally, adapt to reformulated contexts, and preserve successful behavior under perturbation. We introduce PPC-Bench, a controlled behavioral benchmark comprising 5000 deterministic samples across mathematical computation, Python code execution, and rule-based reasoning. Nine open-source models are evaluated along five dimensions: Direct Accessibility, Compositional Utilization, Prompt Elicitation, Contextual Adaptation, and Robustness Consistency. To distinguish inaccessible primitive capability from failed composition, we further construct a separate paired set of 1800 samples organized into 240 matched task families. Each family aligns atomic probes with composition, prompted, contextual, and perturbed variants of the same task. Qwen3.5-27B correctly answers 839 of 840 atomic probes but successfully composes only 74 of 239 atom-accessible families. In contrast, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct correctly composes 132 of 164 atom-accessible families despite lower atomic accuracy. Gemma-3-1B-IT exhibits limitations in both atomic accessibility and compositional utilization. Step-by-step prompting recovers approximately half of the accessible-but-uncomposed families for Qwen3.5-27B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, while successful composition is preserved under perturbation in more than 91% of eligible families for both models. These results provide condition-specific behavioral profiles that distinguish initial composition success, recovery of composition failures, and correctness preservation within successful subsets. PPC-Bench combines broad model-level evaluation with matched-family conditional analysis, providing a basis for investigating model and prompt choices without inferring internal mechanisms from task accuracy.
evidence_items.title: A Controlled Behavioral Benchmark for Diagnosing Atomic Accessibility and Compositional Utilization in Large Language Models

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Routine dental imaging captures cumulative dentoalveolar and periodontal changes, offering a non-invasive window into both chronological aging and physiological senescence. While task-specific deep learning models have been widely explored in dental radiology, the zero-shot diagnostic performance of commercial Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) in adult populations remains underinvestigated. The aim of this study was to benchmark the zero-shot diagnostic accuracy and repeatability of a commercial MLLM against human clinicians of varying experience levels in estimating adult dental age and biological sex from panoramic radiographs (OPGs), using documented chronological age and biological sex as the ground truth. Methods: From 216 initially screened records, this retrospective single-center study included 127 standardized, anonymized OPGs from patients (74 men, 53 women; mean chronological age 55.5 ± 15.8 years, range 18–90 years) treated at the Clinical Department of Cranio-Maxillofacial Surgery, Military Institute of Medicine—National Research Institute in Warsaw. Each radiograph was independently evaluated across three trials by Gemini 3.1 Pro (Google, Mountain View, CA, USA) and once by two clinicians—a maxillofacial specialist (>10 years of experience) and a resident (<3 years of experience)—all blinded to clinical metadata. Results: Gemini 3.1 Pro demonstrated excellent repeatability across the three trials (ICC(A,1) = 0.926, ICC(A,3) = 0.974; p = 0.156) and moderate agreement with chronological age (ICC(A,1) = 0.604), but systematically overestimated age by a mean of 6.23 years. Mean absolute error (MAE) ranged from 12.91 to 13.03 years across the AI trials. The specialist achieved a significantly lower MAE (10.39 years) than all AI assessments (adjusted p ≤ 0.003), whereas the resident (MAE = 11.19 years) did not differ significantly from the AI (adjusted p = 0.282).
evidence_items.title: Comparative Accuracy of a Commercial Multimodal Large Language Model Versus Clinicians in Dental Age and Sex Estimation from Panoramic Radiographs: A Benchmark Study

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have become a cornerstone of modern generative artificial intelligence, demonstrating remarkable performance across a wide range of tasks, including machine translation, question answering, and dialogue generation. However, most existing reviews primarily emphasize theoretical foundations and training methodologies, and offer limited insights into real-world application performance and domain-specific deployment patterns. To address this gap, we conducted a systematic literature review following PRISMA guidelines, synthesizing the application of LLMs across diverse vertical domains. The review examines system architectures, technical approaches, and performance benchmarks reported in the literature. In addition, it analyzes core challenges associated with LLM deployment, such as hallucinations, explainability, value alignment, and data quality, along with targeted solutions. Finally, it identifies emerging research opportunities and future directions, contributing to a more coherent, application-oriented understanding of LLM development and impact.
evidence_items.title: Vertical Domain Large Language Models: Applications, Challenges, Future Prospects

evidence_items.summary: BACKGROUND Counseling a person about cancer screening requires more than factually accurate information. It must respond to the person's readiness to act, beliefs, barriers, emotions, and sociocultural context while conveying guideline-concordant recommendations. Large language model (LLM)–based health communication is often evaluated with general measures of fluency, coherence, or isolated factual accuracy, which may not show whether a multi-turn conversation is clinically accurate, complete, or patient centered. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to develop a theory-grounded framework for structuring and evaluating multi-turn LLM-based breast and cervical cancer screening communication and to apply it to identify where conversational quality diverges from clinically relevant and patient-centered quality. METHODS Constructs from the Transtheoretical Model and the Health Belief Model, intrapersonal and interpersonal (sociocultural) determinants of screening, patient-centered communication functions, and age-specific screening guidance were operationalized in a structured knowledge representation with patient and provider branches. Role-specific GPT-4o Patient and Provider Agents instantiated this representation as a controlled simulation testbed, with stage-aware provider communication, dialogue state tracking, and retrieval of guideline text, and generated 2000 synthetic patient-provider dialogues. The synthetic conversations were not assumed or validated to represent real patient-provider conversations. Dialogues were evaluated with Fine-grained Evaluation of Dialog (FED), rubric-based G-Eval, and human review of 100 selected dialogues by two annotators on six accuracy, completeness, and communication criteria, each scored from −1 to 1. RESULTS FED scores were highest for coherence (0.98), error recovery (0.97), and consistency (0.94) and lowest for likeability (0.45) and informativeness (0.47). G-Eval scores ranged from 2.34 to 2.50 on a 1-3 scale.
evidence_items.title: Theory-Grounded Evaluation of Multi-Turn Large Language Model Communication for Cancer Screening: Framework Development and Evaluation Study (Preprint)

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Reaction monitoring is central to chemical process development, but systematic evaluation of machine-learning models is limited by the scarcity and heterogeneity of experimental monitoring data. ReactionFormer provides a controlled and reproducible framework for evaluating machine-learning-based reaction-state inference from simulated infrared mixture spectra and molecular reaction context. The benchmark pairs reaction context with simulated spectral snapshots generated from computed and experiment-derived pure-component infrared spectra. The reaction-monitoring trajectories are not experimentally measured; they are simulated from pure-component spectra and represented as serialized sequences combining reactant and product simplified molecular-input line-entry system (SMILES) strings with discretized infrared mixture spectra. ReactionFormer supports reaction-progress regression, practical-completion classification, spectrum-only ablation, cross-source transfer, and low-data adaptation under matched reaction-level splits. The results show that infrared snapshots contain substantial reaction-state information, molecular context provides additional gains, and masked-language-model pretraining improves cross-source transfer and adaptation when only a limited number of labeled examples from the experiment-derived spectral variant are available. Beyond predictive performance, the study quantifies how molecular context, spectral-source variation, and self-supervised pretraining affect the robustness and transferability of learned spectroscopic representations.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Stroke is the leading cause of death and disability in Indonesia, yet clinical NLP tools for stroke triage support remain limited by the lack of annotated resources for patient-generated health text. We introduce StrokeID-NER, a stroke-specific named entity recognition dataset of 1,742 informal Indonesian patient queries annotated with 6,765 spans across four clinically grounded entity types: Symptom, Diagnosis, Temporal and Risk Factor. Inter-annotator agreement on 103 doubly annotated queries reached an entity-level F1 of 0.78 for exact spans and 0.96 for overlapping spans. We benchmark ten systems over three random seeds with query-level bootstrap confidence intervals: monolingual and multilingual transformers with linear and CRF decoders, and GPT-5.4 with zero-shot and five-shot prompting. XLM-RoBERTa-large with additional Indonesian NER training and a CRF decoder achieves the best macro F1 (0.792 ± 0.003). CRF decoding improves every encoder, whereas multilingual pretraining alone does not outperform monolingual pretraining of the same size. Five-shot GPT-5.4 (0.724) matches a fine-tuned base-size model but remains 6.8 points below the best system, with the largest gap on informal symptom expressions. StrokeID-NER, the annotation guideline, code and predictions are released publicly at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.23910283 .
evidence_items.title: An annotated dataset and benchmark for stroke named entity recognition in Indonesian patient health queries

evidence_items.summary: Background Cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic (CKM) disease integrates metabolic, renal, and cardiovascular systems. Learning in probability samples is challenged by rare outcomes, unequal sampling, clustered dependence, and miscalibration. This study aimed to develop a design-consistent, calibration-first framework for concurrent CKM multimorbidity classification in complex surveys and quantify the consequences of ignoring survey design. Methods We analyzed the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) 2017–March 2020 data for U.S. women aged 20–44 years. CKM multimorbidity was defined as the coexistence of at least two of the following: hypertension, diabetes mellitus, chronic kidney disease, and clinical cardiovascular disease. Five learners were compared using 20×5 whole-PSU design-aware cross-validation, fold-contained preprocessing, survey-weighted loss functions, and cross-fitted sigmoid recalibration. The evaluation used design-based and survey-bootstrap procedures across key performance metrics. A 6,000-replicate survey-plasmode benchmark was used to evaluate bias, RMSE, and 95% coverage against finite-population truth. Results Among 1,743 classifiable women, 44 unweighted cases yielded a survey-weighted prevalence of 1.97% (95% CI, 1.30%–2.65%). The elastic net minimized the calibrated weighted log loss (0.089) and achieved a ROC AUC of 0.797 (95% CI, 0.765–0.830), PR AUC of 0.062 (0.023–0.100), and calibration slope of 0.90. Naive random cross-validation yielded an absolute log-loss bias of 0.0539 and 30.2% coverage; weighted design-aware cross-validation with recalibration achieved 95.0% coverage. Conclusion For rare CKM outcomes in complex surveys, valid population-level performance estimation requires survey-aware resampling, proper scoring rules, cross-fitted calibration, and design-consistent uncertainties. The framework distinguishes investigator-defined multimorbidity from guideline-aligned CKM staging.
evidence_items.title: Design-consistent statistical learning for rare survey outcomes: a cardiovascular-kidney-metabolic multimorbidity plasmode benchmark in women

evidence_items.summary: Watershed-scale carbon assessments remain limited for humid subtropical reservoir catchments where heterogeneous land cover and terrain interact with climatic forcing and direct ecosystem-flux observations are scarce. To address this gap, we evaluated how modeled GPP, NPP, RH, and NEP differed among the 2015, 2020, and 2024 benchmark years in the Shanzai Reservoir watershed using an integrated Google Earth Engine framework. Results showed that the watershed remained predominantly forest dominated across the three benchmark years, although localized expansion of built-up land occurred mainly within the southeastern sector. Watershed mean NDVI was 0.771, 0.706, and 0.745 in 2015, 2020, and 2024, respectively, indicating non-monotonic differences in vegetation greenness among the three benchmark years. Modeled carbon productivity was lower in 2020 than in 2015 and higher in 2024, when watershed mean GPP, NPP, and NEP reached 1344.09, 726.59, and 513.28 g C m −2 yr. −1 , respectively. Modeled NEP remained positive across most of the watershed in each benchmark year, indicating net ecosystem carbon uptake potential under the adopted modeling framework. Terrain-stratified analysis further revealed spatial differences in vegetation productivity and carbon balance among elevation–aspect classes. Overall, the results demonstrate the utility of integrating remote sensing, ERA5-Land climatic forcing, external productivity benchmarking, and terrain-stratified assessment for watershed-scale carbon evaluation while avoiding inference of a persistent or field-confirmed carbon sink.
evidence_items.title: Spatial patterns and benchmark-year variability of ecosystem carbon productivity and carbon balance in the Shanzai reservoir watershed, southeastern China

evidence_items.summary: Abstract We benchmark a minimal latent world model on drought-to-pluvial transitions over North America. Using SPEIbase v2.11 (SPEI-1, 1980 to 2023, 4,817 land cells), we evaluate 335,106 held-out drought origins under blocked cross-validation. The world model (WM1) is compared with persistence, climatology, a logistic model, gradient boosting, and a ConvLSTM on flip probability, footprint, withheld flips, and counterfactual ENSO forcing. The logistic model leads, with Brier skill of 0.015 to 0.022. The ConvLSTM also beats climatology but not the logistic model. WM1 scores minus 0.234 to minus 0.178 and is badly overconfident. Its median footprint is empty at lead 6. Among the forecast models WM1 times flips best, at 1.62 months on a common subset, but a climatological timing rule is better at 1.36 months, and a deterministic ablation shows that the timing is largely an ensemble-noise effect. The companion concurrent drought-pluvial event catalog (Sokol 2026) provides geographic context. The collapse is specific to this minimal latent model, and event-focused benchmarks expose failures that mean-state scores hide.
evidence_items.title: Does a minimal latent world model know when drought breaks? A benchmark of drought- to-pluvial transitions over North America

evidence_items.summary: Large language model (LLM) agents no longer only answer questions; they now call tools, read databases and change the state of business systems. Orchestration frameworks such as LangGraph coordinate these agents well, but they leave execution governance to every application: who may write, whether a decision is still valid at the moment of writing, what happens when a call is retried, and how each effect is traced. This paper surveys the research that addresses parts of this problem: reasoning-and-acting agents, reliability and safety benchmarks, prompt-injection defences and guardrails, privilege control, transaction and compensation models, observability, and AI-risk governance standards. From this survey we derive a taxonomy of seven failure classes that occur on an agent’s write path and show that no single existing approach covers stale decisions, unauthorized actions, duplicate side effects and incomplete audit together. We then present AgentForge, a domain-agnostic tool-effect gateway built on the idea of harness engineering. In AgentForge an agent can only propose an action. The gateway validates it against typed contracts, current business state and declarative policy; obtains human approval bound to a cryptographic state fingerprint; enforces exactly-once effects with idempotency keys and optimistic concurrency; revalidates the action immediately before commit; verifies the post-condition; and records the whole journey as an OpenTelemetry trace. The framework is demonstrated on a simulated supply-chain procurement workflow. We specify a paired evaluation protocol (60 scenario templates × 3 runs per arm, judged on the final database state) with measurable targets: at least 90% fewer unauthorized commits, at most 1% duplicate effects, at least 95% of stale approvals blocked, at most 5% false blocks, at least 98% audit completeness and below 500 ms median overhead. We close with open challenges and a research agenda for trustworthy agentic infrastructure.
evidence_items.title: AgentForge: A Survey of Harness Engineering for Reliable Agentic AI and a State-Bound Action-Control Framework for Enterprise Workflows

evidence_items.summary: STARLI | F111–F120 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume II · Collective Microrobotics, Fault Resilience and Trustworthy Autonomy Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.2  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This collection presents ten prospective research-design monographs on distributed micro/nanorobotic collectives. Research Unit I (F111–F115) addresses limited communication, collaborative quantum sensing, consensus breakdown, dynamic task reassignment and joint human-machine authority. Research Unit II (F116–F120) examines misinformation propagation, graceful degradation, custody and mission integrity, cross-platform coordination and trustworthy autonomy. The ten studies propose falsifiable bench-scale experiments; none asserts demonstrated swarm intelligence, clinical efficacy or certified autonomous safety. The ten English working editions comprise 7,770 PDF pages in total: 300 prospective mathematical research plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated study sections, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Gate proposes six annotated research dimensions: causal mechanism, measurable witness, blinded falsifier, rival explanation, stopping boundary and successor interface. The counts describe publication architecture, not experimentally verified results or independently certified scientific originality. The Ten Research Directions F111  Nanorobotic Collective Limited Communication Control At The Limit — Investigates safe collective recovery when peer-to-peer messages are delayed, lost or limited. The proposed endpoint is time to independently confirmed safe recovery after communication loss, measured in seconds. Tests compare matched-actuation single-agent control against local coordination; task redundancy is a rival explanation. Failure to regain a known-safe state is a stopping condition.

Research Unit I (F111–F115) addresses limited communication, collaborative quantum sensing, consensus breakdown, dynamic task reassignment and joint human-machine authority. Research Unit II (F116–F120) examines misinformation propagation, graceful degradation, custody and mission integrity, cross-platform coordination and trustworthy autonomy. The ten studies propose falsifiable bench-scale experiments; none asserts demonstrated swarm intelligence, clinical efficacy or certified autonomous safety. The ten English working editions comprise 7,770 PDF pages in total: 300 prospective mathematical research plates, 820 chapter openings, 4,100 independently paginated study sections, 2,000 Research Gates and 330 Phoenix Answer Embryos. Each Gate proposes six annotated research dimensions: causal mechanism, measurable witness, blinded falsifier, rival explanation, stopping boundary and successor interface. The counts describe publication architecture, not experimentally verified results or independently certified scientific originality. The Ten Research Directions F111  Nanorobotic Collective Limited Communication Control At The Limit — Investigates safe collective recovery when peer-to-peer messages are delayed, lost or limited. The proposed endpoint is time to independently confirmed safe recovery after communication loss, measured in seconds. Tests compare matched-actuation single-agent control against local coordination; task redundancy is a rival explanation. Failure to regain a known-safe state is a stopping condition. F112  Microrobotic Collective Quantum Sensing Collaboration At The Limit — Proposes cooperative field sensing against independent calibrated reference measurements. Its candidate endpoint is normalized field-estimation error; the atlas also tracks communication load. A fully observed centralized controller is the comparator, and additional agent count may explain apparent improvement. Violation of registered safety invariants rejects the proposed collaborative sensing benefit. F113  Nanorobotic Collective Consensus Failure At The Limit — Examines whether distributed agreement remains justified when hidden partitions or corrupted information change the swarm's evidence. The candidate endpoint is the false-consensus acceptance fraction, with energy per task retained from the atlas. Fixed rules under equal energy challenge the proposal; leaked global tracking is a rival. Confidence maintained during a hidden partition triggers rejection. F114  Microrobotic Collective Dynamic Mission Reconfiguration At The Limit — Studies bounded mission reassignment following changing tasks, link loss or unavailable agents. The proposed witness is independently verified mission-reassignment success fraction, while selective abstention remains an atlas outcome. Matched total actuation controls for redundancy masquerading as adaptation. Failed return to a registered safe state is the hard stop. F115  Nanorobotic Collective Joint Human-Machine Oversight At The Limit — Tests whether collective task completion remains inside explicit human authorization and machine safety constraints. Authority-compliant task success fraction is the proposed endpoint, complemented by atlas task-completion records. A centralized full-state controller is the comparator; larger teams alone may explain any gain. Crossing a safety invariant overrides apparent task efficiency. F116  Microrobotic Collective Misinformation Propagation At The Limit — Addresses the spread of incorrect shared state estimates through a microrobotic collective. Its candidate observable is false-belief propagation rate, accompanied by the atlas consensus-error outcome. Equal-energy fixed behavior challenges the claimed mechanism, while hidden external state tracking may bias comparisons. Persistent confident agreement under concealed network partition is a rejection condition. F117  Nanorobotic Collective Graceful Degradation At The Limit — Evaluates whether a damaged or partially disconnected swarm retains bounded task capability rather than failing abruptly. Completion fraction under preregistered fault severity is the proposed witness; the atlas also records collision rate. Single-agent operation with matched total actuation tests whether redundancy alone explains resilience. Inability to return to a known-safe state stops the trial. F118  Microrobotic Collective Mission Integrity At The Limit — Proposes end-to-end custody and task-state audits for collective sampling missions. The measurable candidate is the valid sample-and-mission custody fraction, with coverage entropy retained from the original atlas. A centralized full-state controller anchors comparison; increased agent number can mimic benefits. Any violation of physical safety invariants invalidates the release claim. F119  Nanorobotic Collective Cross-Platform Collaboration At The Limit — Studies verified recovery and coordination across dissimilar robotic platforms with distinct sensing and control interfaces. Recovery latency in seconds is the proposed measurement and atlas recovery time is preserved. Matched-energy fixed rules are the baseline; external tracking that reveals global state is a rival. Confident consensus during a hidden communication partition is a stop condition. F120  Intelligent Nanorobotic Collective Trustworthy Autonomy At The Limit — Investigates whether autonomous collective decisions remain within defined authority and physical safety envelopes. The candidate witness is unsafe autonomous release fraction, alongside atlas communication load. A matched-actuation single-agent baseline tests purported benefits of collective intelligence versus redundancy. Failure to recover a known-safe state disqualifies the autonomy claim. The publication title follows the corrected source-introduction identity. Scope, Falsifiability and Evidence Boundaries These nonclinical research-design working editions are limited to traceable materials, calibrated sensing, physically bounded actuation, authorized reference systems and laboratory or simulated validation. Proposed endpoints supplement, rather than silently replace, the original atlas outcome fields. No laboratory results are reported. Equal-resource baselines, blinded disturbance tests, preservation of failed runs, raw evidence provenance and mandatory stop rules are required before claims of superiority. The source batch passes scripted PDF-structure checks; derivation-level physics, causal distinctness, individual DOI-to-claim relevance, exhaustive visual review and specialist peer review remain incomplete. evidence_items.summary: Agents increasingly operate software and even write it, yet they are almost always told what to achieve: given a goal, a mock-up, or a demonstration. We ask whether an agent can instead understand an unfamiliar product by using it, and then rebuild it. The agent sees only rendered pixels and acts through pointer and keyboard, without access to the DOM, source, logs, or back-end. Within this interface, it explores, generates a replica, and checks its own work before evaluation. We present SWE-Recreation, a benchmark of 54 real applications (28 websites and 26 Android apps) with 1,446 hidden requirements describing multistep, stateful workflows and explicit exclusions for behavior outside the reconstruction scope. A fixed judge grades workflows with pixel evidence; a separate post-hoc judge estimates exploration coverage. Across 54 evaluated applications, five frontier systems reach at most 0.530 weighted fidelity and 22.9% fully reproduced requirements under application-equal averaging. These descriptive results expose both exploration-evidence gaps and implementation shortfalls. Code and data are available at https://github.com/nologistic/recreateanything.
evidence_items.title: SWE-Recreation: Benchmarking Coding Agents for Software Recreation

evidence_items.summary: AI agents are increasingly expected to act as AI scientists, which requires three increasingly open abilities: carrying out a given computational workflow correctly, choosing the next measurements from a given design space, and designing their own experiments. Existing benchmarks mainly evaluate the first two abilities, in a terminal or in a closed loop that selects from predefined candidates. Evaluating the third ability requires reliably executing an experiment that an agent designs, with readings grounded in a real laboratory. We introduce TwinLab-Bench, which evaluates AI scientists on self-designed experiments in 52 tasks from laboratories in the physical sciences, the life sciences, and engineering. The benchmark supports more than 100 experimental action types, and the agent's report is scored by comparison with a hidden answer taken from real laboratory records. Each task has its own TwinLab agent, an agent that serves as the environment and executes the experiments that the tested agent designs, reading the raw materials of the laboratory and calling calculators that are built from its records. Compared with a language model that sees only the task description, the TwinLab agent almost eliminates readings that deviate from the real records and inconsistent answers to a repeated request, and closed-book probes control for answers recalled from memory. We find that these tasks remain hard for frontier models: the strongest, Claude Fable 5.2, averages a score of only 45.0, and we conduct an empirical study of where it fails.
evidence_items.title: TwinLab-Bench: Evaluating AI Scientists in Agentic Twins of Real Labs

authors: Jiaru Qian, Jiawei Li, Xiaolong Hu, Zheng Shen, LiMing Zhao, Xin Zhang, Siyuan Jiang, Yongqiang Wei, Dong Liu, Jianyang Li, Yihua Chen, Yangxu Liao, Yuxin Wu, Jing Liang, Bin Wen, Junjie Zhang, Yongsheng Han, Yihong Dong, Ge Li
evidence_items.summary: Design verification (DV) remains a major bottleneck in hardware development, with large-scale verification using the Universal Verification Methodology (UVM) being highly labor-intensive. Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) and agentic systems offer new opportunities for DV automation. However, existing benchmarks primarily construct mutually decoupled subtasks, which deviates from the real-world workflow. In this paper, we present DVBench, the first end-to-end benchmark for Real-World UVM design verification agents. DVBench comprises 95 tasks across 9 functional domains and 5 difficulty levels, covering diverse verification scenarios and design scales. Each task requires agents to independently complete the full verification workflow. DVBench evaluates final testbenches via compilation, coverage, and bug detection, while assessing intermediate artifacts including feature lists, test plans, and reference models. We evaluate frontier LLMs (e.g. Claude Opus 5.5, GPT-6 Astra) and agent frameworks (e.g. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode). Experimental results show that the best LLM-based agent (Codex \& GPT-6 Astra) can only achieve an overall success rate of 21.05\%, revealing substantial room for improvement in complex verification tasks.
evidence_items.title: DVBench: End-to-End Benchmark for Real-World UVM Design Verification Agents

evidence_items.title: STARLI | F121–F130 / 300 Flagship 13 Fission · Volume II · AI-Guided Sensing and Uncertainty-Aware Microrobotic Control Author: 33  |  Nonclinical Research Design Working Edition v1.1 / Gate Annotation v1.2  |  English Zenodo Ten-Volume Overview This ten-volume STARLI research-design collection studies the interface between AI-based physical sensing, model uncertainty, quantum-sensor calibration and micro/nanorobotic feedback. The first five flagships address sensor-driven closed loops, uncertain control, signal/artifact separation, active learning and drift compensation. The next five examine causal state estimation, multimodal fusion, safety control, anomaly detection and model-predictive action. These are proposed, falsifiable laboratory designs, not claims of measured scientific breakthroughs. Ten English working-edition PDFs each contain 777 pages, 30 candidate mathematical plates, 82 chapters, 410 separately paginated studies, 200 Research Gates and 33 Phoenix Answer Embryos: 7,770 pages, 300 formula plates, 2,000 Gates and 330 Phoenix across the collection. Gate annotation revision v1.2 records prospective mechanisms, measurements, blinded countertests, rivals, stop rules and successor interfaces. Document structure and distinct wording do not themselves validate scientific independence. The Ten Research Directions F121  AI-Driven Nano-Quantum Sensing Closed-Loop Systems At The Limit — Evaluates selective risk of accepted sensing decisions (normalized loss) against a preregistered design-of-experiments baseline. An equal-budget blinded material challenge must distinguish a genuine closed-loop contribution from extra trials or unmetered external assistance. Acting outside the registered authority envelope is a stop condition. F122  Microrobotic Uncertainty-Aware Control At The Limit — Studies field-referenced calibration error (normalized error) and the ability to abstain under hidden out-of-distribution states. Equal-trial expert tuning is the declared comparator; undisclosed human intervention is an alternative explanation. High-confidence action on unsupported cases invalidates the proposed safety claim. F123  AI Biological Signal and Mechanical Artifact Separation At The Limit — Asks whether biological response can be discriminated from mechanical artifacts using a preregistered misattribution fraction. A frozen open-loop policy supplies the baseline; training-test leakage could create false evidence of autonomous separation. The raw measurement-to-action sequence must remain independently replayable. F124  Nano-Quantum System Active Learning At The Limit — Tests active experimental selection while directly recording the fraction of constraints breached during learning. Preregistered design of experiments is the strong baseline. Gains must survive identical trial and resource budgets; extra experiments or any action outside the authorization envelope constitute rejection grounds. F125  AI-Driven Quantum Sensor Drift Compensation At The Limit — Uses post-correction offset on a blinded sensor standard, measured in tesla, to evaluate proposed drift correction. Equal-trial expert tuning challenges any apparent gain. Hidden manual adjustment, changed standards and confident out-of-domain correction are rival or stopping mechanisms, rather than evidence of robust autonomous calibration. F126  Microrobotic Causal State Estimation At The Limit — Frames causal-state inference through counterfactual physical-state prediction error on withheld interventions (normalized error). A frozen open-loop policy and matched observations protect against claims created by training-test leakage. Reconstruction of each raw observation, inferred state and subsequent action is a mandatory evidence condition. F127  AI Multimodal Microscale Signal Fusion At The Limit — Studies held-out multimodal inference calibration error when separate microscale sensing channels are combined. Preregistered experimental design serves as the comparison; extra trials or untracked sensor budgets can mimic improvement. Hidden distribution shifts and action-authority boundaries test whether confidence remains physically warranted. F128  Nanorobotic Closed-Loop Safety Control At The Limit — Measures safe-set violation fraction under bounded feedback in authorized bench-scale nanorobotic tasks. Matched expert tuning provides a conventional comparator, with hidden human correction treated as a live rival. High-confidence actions outside the calibrated domain trigger an explicit safety stop. F129  AI Quantum Sensor Anomaly Detection At The Limit — Examines severity-weighted missed-anomaly risk under blinded sensor changes and unselected cases. A frozen open-loop policy is the declared baseline; training-test leakage can produce misleading anomaly scores. The audit must preserve raw measurements, false negatives and the complete alert-to-action record. F130  Microrobotic Model-Predictive Control At The Limit — Uses independently measured prediction error, in metres, over a frozen control horizon to test microrobotic model-predictive control. Preregistered experimental design is the comparator. Equal budgets and hidden shifts must separate predictive value from extra experimentation; crossing the physical authority envelope is a hard stop. Scope, Falsifiability and Evidence Boundaries All ten monographs are prospective, nonclinical research designs using traceable materials, calibrated sensors, authorized ex-vivo specimens, simulations or closed-bench reference platforms. No experimental result, clinical outcome, quantum advantage, independently established safety benefit or completed peer review is asserted. Equal-budget baselines, withheld shifts, blind references, failed-run denominators, original measurement records and hard stop rules are required to evaluate proposed gains. The source batch reports a complete PDF-structure check but only partial physics, semantic distinctness and DOI claim-mapping review; its full-page visual review remains incomplete. (2026) · Control barrier functions under uncertainty · DOI 10.1109/TCYB.2025.3633800   |   Autonomous, multiproperty-driven molecular discovery (2023) · DOI 10.1126/science.adi1407 These references are listed in the supplied evidence register as established methodological context, not experimental proof of the STARLI proposals. Individual source-to-claim DOI links and physical derivations still require independent review. evidence_items.summary: The dataset contains temperature and moisture measurements collected during the early-age curing of concrete using a low-cost embedded sensor monitoring system. Five DS18B20 digital temperature sensors were individually embedded in concrete cubes A–E, while four capacitive moisture sensors were installed in cubes A, B, F, and G. The specimens measured 150 × 150 × 150 mm and were prepared using a nominal mix ratio of 1:2:4 and a water-to-cement ratio of 0.50. Measurements were recorded at nominal 10-second intervals using an ESP32-based data acquisition system and stored in CSV format. The original dataset comprises 26,042 timestamped observations recorded between 6 and 13 July 2026, while 14,611 observations were retained for the analysis presented in the accompanying manuscript. The records include missing sensor readings and interruptions in data acquisition arising from operational limitations of the monitoring system. The original dataset is provided to support transparency, reproducibility, and further investigation of early-age concrete temperature and moisture behaviour. This dataset accompanies the research manuscript "Development and Evaluation of a Low-Cost Embedded Sensor System for Monitoring Temperature and Moisture in Early-Age Concrete".

evidence_items.summary: This research repository contains data, source code, analysis results, and figures supporting an astronomy-inspired colour–colour diagram (CCD) approach for river turbidity assessment and indirect arsenic contamination screening in the Kok and Sai Rivers, Thailand. The approach adapts established principles of astronomical photometry and optical physics to Sentinel-2 multispectral surface reflectance observations. The repository includes 300 ground-based arsenic observations from 22 monitoring rounds conducted between March 2025 and August 2026, of which 296 were paired with turbidity measurements, and 45 exploratory satellite–ground observations from the Kok River. The accompanying materials include Google Earth Engine scripts, Python analysis scripts, spatial and temporal matching procedures, colour indices, cross-validation results, bootstrap confidence intervals, sensitivity analyses, and reproducible manuscript figures. The results provide preliminary insights into the potential of astronomical photometric techniques for environmental monitoring but do not establish reliable satellite-based arsenic screening. Contains modified Copernicus Sentinel data 2025–2026. OpenStreetMap data and other third-party datasets retain their original attribution and applicable licensing conditions. This repository supports reproducible research and future interdisciplinary investigations integrating astronomy, optical physics, and environmental remote sensing.
