evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Objective Accurately distinguishing between epileptic seizures (ES) and nonepileptic seizures (NES) remains a significant clinical challenge, typically requiring resource‐intensive inpatient video‐EEG monitoring. We developed a multimodal large language model (MLLM)‐based framework for automated extraction of semiological features from seizure videos, followed by classification of events as ES or NES. Methods We analyzed 90 seizure videos (45 ES, 45 NES) from 29 patients in an epilepsy monitoring unit. Each event was labeled using expert‐reviewed video‐EEG and annotated for 24 clinically relevant semiological features. An MLLM framework integrating open‐source vision‐language models (VLMs) and audio‐language models (ALMs) was used to extract these features automatically. The extracted features were then used to train classifiers (K‐Nearest Neighbors, XGBoost, and Deep Factorization Machine) to distinguish ES from NES. Model performance was evaluated using leave‐one‐patient‐out (LOPO) cross‐validation. Results Expert‐annotated features yielded near‐perfect classification using KNN (precision = 0.92, recall = 0.92, F1‐score = 0.92, AUC = 0.99). Compared to expert annotations, the MLLM pipeline achieved a mean recall of 0.71, accuracy of 0.58, and F1‐score of 0.51 for feature extraction. Using MLLM‐extracted features, the KNN classifier ( k = 7) achieved a precision of 0.77, recall of 0.76, F1‐score of 0.76, and AUC of 0.76, correctly identifying 68 out of 90 events. Conclusion Multimodal large language models can extract clinically relevant semiological features from seizure videos and support interpretable classification of ES versus NES. This approach offers a scalable, explainable tool to assist in video‐based epilepsy diagnosis.

evidence_items.summary: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.
evidence_items.title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation

evidence_items.summary: Video understanding, particularly with accompanying audio, remains a central challenge in multimodal intelligence. In this report, we introduce WeMM-Video, a family of Chinese-English bilingual omni-modal foundation models spanning 2B, 4B, 9B, and 35B-A3B variants. Centering on joint audio-visual perception and reasoning, WeMM-Video unifies text, image, audio, and video processing within a hybrid-thinking paradigm, seamlessly supporting both a non-thinking instruct mode for fast, direct responses and a thinking mode for explicit step-by-step reasoning. The models are trained on a large-scale multimodal corpus of approximately 1.2 trillion tokens through progressive pre-training and a multi-stage post-training pipeline incorporating multi-teacher OPD, anti-repetition MrDPO, and specialist RL. Evaluated across more than 120 benchmarks, WeMM-Video demonstrates superior performance in omni-modal video understanding and reasoning, while maintaining highly competitive capabilities across general audio, silent video, image, and text tasks. Specifically, in omni-modal video evaluations, our flagship WeMM-Video-35B-A3B establishes a new open-source state of the art, substantially outperforming proprietary models such as Qwen3.5-Omni-Flash and Seed2.0-Mini-0428 while narrowing the gap with the strong Gemini-3.0-Flash, and our compact WeMM-Video-9B surpasses the larger open-source Qwen3-Omni-30B-A3B-Instruct. We publicly release the WeMM-Video family along with our evaluation and reproduction pipeline to foster further research and development in the open-source community.
evidence_items.title: WeMM-Video: Pushing the Frontiers of Open-Source Omni-Modal Video Understanding

evidence_items.summary: Simulated manipulation benchmarks measure policy performance using hand-written success checkers that label each episode as a success or failure. Passing an expert demonstration shows that a checker accepts one way of completing the task. Learned policies, however, may stop after partial progress or complete the task in a different way. A checker may then accept an incomplete execution (phantom success) or reject an execution that satisfies the instruction (silent failure). In this paper, we introduce SimAudit, an LLM-based pipeline that audits success checkers against task instructions. SimAudit analyzes the instruction and checker code to identify scenarios where the two may disagree, recreates those scenarios in simulation, and runs the original checker. Multi-view renderings are then used to verify whether the observed behavior satisfies the instruction. Across RoboTwin 2.0, RoboCasa365, and RoboDojo, 183 simulated test cases produced the predicted checker verdict. Visual verification and deduplication yielded 61 distinct defects across 49 tasks, including 40 phantom successes and 21 silent failures. Most defects in RoboCasa365 accepted incomplete executions, most in RoboDojo rejected valid executions, and both error types were common in RoboTwin 2.0. These findings suggest that validating success checkers requires testing both incomplete executions and valid alternatives to expert demonstrations, and motivate more rigorous evaluation protocols for future benchmarks.
evidence_items.title: Phantom Success, Silent Failure: Auditing the Success Checkers of Simulated Manipulation Benchmarks

evidence_items.summary: Code-search benchmarks show dense encoders well ahead of BM25, yet coding agents do well with grep. What does this dense advantage measure? Existing benchmarks cannot tell: they use curated queries, old code and a handicapped BM25. To find out, we build Repo-Premium, a realistic repository-level code-search benchmark. It ranks files in real repositories, with curated and raw queries in Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Go, Rust and Java, pull requests from 2022 to 2026, and a preregistered test pool over 91 repositories. Our experiments trace the advantage to two sources: evaluation choices that favor dense retrieval, such as splitting files into chunks for BM25 and counting edited tests as relevant, and queries that lack the code's rare identifiers. Expanding the query with LLM-written identifiers (generate-then-grep) helps BM25 far more than dense retrieval, letting it match dense retrieval in every Python pool, even on pull requests opened after the LLM was released. No method we tried predicts which retriever will win on a given query. From these results we derive three guidelines: measure dense gains against a fair lexical baseline, fuse dense retrieval with BM25, and add the code's words to queries that lack them.
evidence_items.title: Embeddings vs. Grep: Rethinking the Dense Advantage in Code Search

evidence_items.summary: We present CompoundingKernel, a self-improving agent system that writes GPU kernels by search. As of 2026-11-11, its generated kernels rank #1 on the public L1, L2 and Quantization boards of SOL-ExecBench (NVIDIA B200). They have held #1 on L1 since 2026-10-27, albeit a short loss on 2026-11-07. All 235 problems have a site-verified correct kernel; on the 209 public-board problems they are 4.40x faster than the benchmark's reference baseline. The search starts from zero: agents get each problem's PyTorch definition but no reference kernels or official scores. A per-problem archive outside the model holds every correct kernel and its lineage. An LLM controller reads it, picks a parent or a new design, and gives each parallel child agent one direction. Checks outside the model decide correctness. At equal wall time, it beat a coded UCB style tree on 35 of 38 problems by making 2.4x as many correct attempts. Over a thousand agents ran at once, and one warm restart fix raised their evaluation rate 3.6x. We find that the rate of reliable measurements, not the number of agents, limits how far such a search scales. Our code and kernels are available on URL.
evidence_items.title: CompoundingKernel: Self-Improving from Zero to First

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence (AI) now underpins FinTech services that support digital financial inclusion and sustainable economic growth, yet AI-enabled fraud threatens users' trust in this innovation. Some users intend to discontinue AI-enabled FinTech services even when they are satisfied and habituated, a pattern that traditional continuance explanations do not explain. This study examines a Dual Evaluation Mechanism in which discontinuance intention forms through an internal path (confirmation, satisfaction, and habit) and an external path (vicarious exposure to AI fraud and perceived AI fraud risk), and tests whether perceived AI fraud risk moderates the relationship between habit and discontinuance intention. The study employs cross-sectional survey data from 507 Indian users of AI-enabled FinTech services, analyzed with partial least squares structural equation modeling and complemented by predictive, importance-performance, endogeneity, and necessary condition analyses. The results show that confirmation raises satisfaction (β = 0.648), satisfaction raises habit (β = 0.578), and habit lowers discontinuance intention (β = −0.330). Vicarious AI fraud exposure raises perceived AI fraud risk (β = 0.588), which raises discontinuance intention (β = 0.507), and the interaction between risk and habit is positive (β = 0.174); all paths are significant at p < 0.001. The model explains 39.9% of the variance in discontinuance intention and outperforms the indicator-average benchmark in out-of-sample prediction. The findings suggest that all six hypotheses are supported, that perceived AI fraud risk is the most important predictor of discontinuance intention (0.507) and weakens the protective effect of habit, and that no construct is a strong necessary condition for discontinuance (d ≤ 0.163). JEL Classification Codes: D91, G21, G23, G41, O33.
evidence_items.title: Dual evaluation mechanism of artificial intelligence enabled fintech discontinuance for sustainable financial inclusion in India

evidence_items.summary: Existing LLM reasoning benchmarks are largely static, single-turn, English-centric, and reliant on biased LLM-as-a-judge scoring. We present MTGBench, a bilingual (English/Russian) suite of seven multi-turn puzzle games—Wordle, Word Chain, Situation Puzzles, 20 Questions, Wheel of Fortune, 20 Features, and Alias—spanning deductive, semantic, lateral, consistency, and knowledge-retrieval reasoning. Four games use algorithmic checkers; the remaining three use a constrained LLM-as-a-rule-enforcer validated against human annotators, and episodes are regenerated natively per language rather than translated. Across 16 frontier models and a human baseline comprising 476 sessions we find that (i) rankings are highly task-dependent, (ii) chain-of-thought is near-essential for letter-level games but uneven on knowledge-driven ones, and (iii) the strongest reasoning-enabled LLMs match or exceed our collected Russian human baseline across the entire suite. Game scores align most consistently with cognitive batteries probing Causal Reasoning, Pragmatics, Planning, and Common-sense Reasoning, though these associations are game-specific rather than a single executive-function signal. Code and data are available in MTGBench github.
evidence_items.title: MTGBench: A Multi-Turn Game Benchmark for Diverse LLM Capability Assessment

evidence_items.summary: Public administration continuously issues official acts through official gazettes; however, their publication in unstructured formats hinders automated querying and computational reuse. This article investigates the ability of small language models (SLMs) to extract structured information from administrative acts into a unified JSON schema, comparing zero-shot and one-shot prompting regimes. A two-stage benchmark protocol is proposed and applied to acts from the Official Gazette of the State of Ceará: an exploratory evaluation of various models using 50 instances to assess structural compliance, followed by an evaluation involving 2,300 acts—measuring structural compliance, average inference time, and informational agreement with extractions produced by GPT-4o (used as an automated reference). The results reveal performance variations among the models across the evaluated dimensions. Qwen2.5-1.5B demonstrated the highest structural compliance, reaching 96.18% in zero-shot and 95.44% in one-shot settings, with average inference times of 33.04 and 36.91 seconds, respectively. Conversely, Qwen3-4B achieved the highest average informational agreement (0.465 in one-shot), performing particularly well in the similarity of summaries (0.788) and the comparison of complex lists, despite lower structural compliance (approximately 77%). It should be noted that the one-shot regime did not consistently improve model performance, and that structural compliance does not necessarily imply higher informational agreement. The study concludes that SLMs show potential for specific administrative information extraction tasks, provided that their selection process separately considers structural reliability and agreement with an automated reference.
evidence_items.title: A TWO-STAGE BENCHMARK OF SMALL LANGUAGE MODELS FOR STRUCTURED INFORMATION EXTRACTION FROM ADMINISTRATIVE ACTS

evidence_items.summary: This paper presents an economic study of a novel Thermal Energy Storage system, the Thermal Energy Storage and Exchange with Integrated Rotating Media Transport (T.E. Sandewirm, i.e. Sandewirm). The Sandewirm technology is a sensible energy storage device using solid particle media that is horizontally conveyed through an inner and outer annulus. This allows for a charging and discharging heat exchanger to reside within an endcap, where particles are moved between inner and outer annuli, eliminating the need for vertical conveyance systems that are necessary for two-tank systems. Sandewirm’s economic performance is evaluated in three potential applications—Gen3 concentrated solar power, long-duration energy storage, and industrial steam generation—through back-to-back levelized cost of storage (LCOS) comparison against incumbent TES technologies. An object-oriented Python cost analysis framework is constructed and facilitates the use of detailed and customized cost factors, Monte Carlo simulations, and financial models to most closely estimate each case’s LCOS. Results from this study show that the Sandewirm design is competitive with current state-of-the-art TES technologies for Gen3 concentrated solar power, long-duration energy storage, and solar steam generation cases, resulting in 7.7%, 4.2%, and 72% reduction in lifetime project costs, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Benchmark LCOS Analysis of the T.E. Sandewirm Technology

evidence_items.summary: This study investigates deep learning-based vehicle type classification from LiDAR point clouds in motorway traffic scenes. Using stationary, roadside LiDAR sensors, the work aims to distinguish vehicle categories such as motorcycles, passenger cars, vans, trucks, buses, and trailer combinations in a non-invasive, privacy-preserving, and weather-independent manner. In addition to model comparison, a major contribution of the work is the creation and validation of a project-specific LiDAR dataset, derived from an initial dimension-based CoMark pre-classification and subsequently verified through manual labeling. To assess the suitability of contemporary point cloud architectures, DGCNN with PAConv, PointNeXt, and Point Transformer V3 (PTv3) were trained on the manually validated dataset. The experimental results indicate that PointNeXt achieved the strongest overall performance, reaching 96.74% accuracy and an F1 score of 0.942, while also exhibiting the lowest model complexity among the best-performing methods. PTv3 attained similarly high classification accuracy but required substantially more parameters, whereas DGCNN with PAConv showed robust performance at the cost of significantly higher training effort. Class-wise analysis and confusion matrices reveal that the remaining errors occur primarily among structurally similar commercial vehicle classes, highlighting the geometric ambiguity inherent in the dataset. Overall, the findings demonstrate that deep learning on LiDAR point clouds offers a scalable and effective solution for vehicle classification in traffic monitoring applications, while careful dataset preparation, validation, and class-specific analysis remain crucial for robust real-world deployment. To support reproducibility, the dataset, data loader, and training instructions will be released in a public GitHub repository: https://github.com/xGeorg315/tls81-roadside-lidar-vehicle-classification.
evidence_items.title: A Real-World LiDAR Benchmark for Fine-Grained Vehicle Classification

evidence_items.summary: Protein functional-class classifiers are usually evaluated with random train–test splits, which can overstate performance when closely related (homologous) sequences fall in both sets. We re-evaluated a widely used benchmark derived from the Protein Data Bank, with 40,211 unique protein sequences in ten functional classes. Six models were compared under random splits and under identity-controlled splits, which keep sequences sharing more than a set identity (90% down to 20%) on the same side: three k-mer composition classifiers, a method that copies the label of the most similar training sequence found by alignment, and two classifiers built on embeddings from the protein language model ESM-2. Under random splitting, 86.5% of test sequences had a training sequence more than 30% identical to them, and a nearest-neighbour model that only copies labels scored in the same range as the learned models. With related sequences kept apart at 30% identity, the k-mer classifiers lost about two-thirds of their macro-F 1 . As a secondary observation, alignment-based label transfer beat an ESM-2 classifier when close training sequences were available, and ESM-2 did better when they were removed; at 30% identity its macro-F 1 advantage was small and not statistically significant. The reason is unclear: almost every benchmark sequence has a close match in UniRef50, the database used to pretrain ESM-2, leaving too few test sequences distant from both the training set and the pretraining data to test generalization beyond them. Random-split results on this benchmark should not be taken as evidence of functional generalization, and comparisons involving protein language models must also account for pretraining data.
evidence_items.title: Homology Leakage Inflates Performance on a Protein Functional-Class Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Machine-learning forecasts of financial returns are usually judged by whether they beat other models, but in low signal-to-noise settings such comparisons can mislead. We propose an evaluation protocol for neural return forecasts that combines four elements: a zero-return benchmark with loss-based block-bootstrap tests and confidence bounds on the panel mean out-of-sample R²; an exact decomposition of R² into squared forecast–return alignment and an amplitude penalty; calibration that uses only past data; and the certainty-equivalent return of a mean–variance investor after transaction costs. We apply it to N-BEATS, N-HiTS and N-BEATSx on daily returns of 19 commodity futures from 2015 to 2026. No neural model improves significantly on zero, and the upper 95% bound on the mean daily R² is 0.16%. Training one network on all commodities raises the mean R² by 3.32 percentage points relative to separate training, yet almost all of this gain comes from smaller forecasts rather than a detectable improvement in alignment, and past-only calibration reduces it to 0.06 points. Sector-based pooling does no better than random grouping. Several forecasts raise the investor’s certainty-equivalent return over a historical-mean benchmark before costs, but none beats equal-weight buy-and-hold, the gains vanish at one-way costs above about 4 basis points, and the training strategy with the lowest loss is not the one with the highest certainty-equivalent return. Lower forecast loss relative to another model should therefore not be read as evidence of predictability or of economic value.
evidence_items.title: Neural Forecasting of Daily Commodity Futures Returns Against a Zero-Return Benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Microlevel loss reserving can use claim-level information that aggregate methods such as chain ladder cannot exploit. This paper predicts individual ultimate claim amounts with a hybrid neural network that combines a feedforward network for static claim characteristics with a long short-term memory network for the payment history of each claim. The framework is evaluated on a simulated motor-insurance portfolio of claims closed at the final valuation date, so that predictions can be compared with known ultimates; the estimation of RBNS and IBNR reserves is outside the scope of the study. Severity strata are formed by k-means clustering of the ultimate amount, and covariates are selected with the Boruta algorithm, both fitted to the training claims only. With complete payment histories, the hybrid models produce much smaller aggregate deviations than chain ladder for recent accident years, while chain ladder remains competitive for mature ones. Boruta retains one or two covariates; the reduced set helps only the untuned full-portfolio model, whereas in the tuned severity-stratum models the full covariate set lowers the test MAE by one third to one half. In a backtest with payment histories truncated at December 2019, the hybrid models keep an accident-year MAPE of 2.1–3.0%, against 16.5% for chain ladder, but improve on the amount paid to date by only 10–15% for claims still open at that date. The results indicate that feature selection, segmentation, and model tuning should be evaluated jointly.
evidence_items.title: Predicting Individual Ultimate Claim Amounts with Hybrid Neural Networks and Claim Segmentation: A Benchmark for Microlevel Loss Reserving

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background: Insomnia is associated with a state of physiological hyperarousal rather thanwith a simple loss of sleep drive. Aromatherapy is used as self-care for this kind of sleepproblem, but its pharmacological basis is unclear. Linalyl acetate (LA) is a majorconstituent of bergamot and lavender oils. A recent study deposited brain transcriptomesfrom mice that inhaled LA and were sampled immediately after an acute stressor, andinterpreted a module of immediate-early genes (IEGs) as evidence of neurotrophin-drivenactivation, without reporting the direction of change. Methods: We reanalysed the deposited hippocampal and olfactory bulb microarrays(GSE316912, GSE316919; vehicle, 1% and 10% LA, n = 3 per group; tissue taken immediatelyafter the final tail suspension test) with a pre-specified 24-gene IEG set. Significance wasassessed with moderated t-statistics, competitive rank tests and exhaustive sample-labelpermutation (84 labellings). The LA profile was compared with public datasets for acutestress (GSE100236), sleep deprivation (GSE33302), chronic mild stress (GSE151807),chronic diazepam (GSE76700), chronic fluoxetine (GSE118669, GSE43261) and linaloolinhalation in rats (GSE19589, GSE90923). Results: Acute handling, restraint and cold swim each increased all 24 IEGs in thehippocampus, and sleep deprivation increased them. After LA inhalation the same geneswere decreased: 21 of 22 detected IEGs in the hippocampus and 22 of 23 in the olfactorybulb (label-permutation P = 0.012 and 0.024). LA therefore moved the stress-evokedactivation programme in the direction opposite to the acute stressors that induce it. Fourweeks of chronic mild stress, by contrast, also lowered these genes in all four brainregions examined, so the direction of the IEG programme depends on the duration of thestressor and does not by itself distinguish relief from chronic stress.
evidence_items.title: Olfactory receptor enrichment in fold-change rankings can arise without regulation: a null benchmark across 99 human transcriptomes

evidence_items.summary: Background/Objectives: Healthcare AI systems described as agentic may improve selected tasks, but gains can reflect models, information access, human support or complete intervention packages. We mapped clinical utility, safety and workflow consequences while distinguishing functional agency from evidence isolating its contribution. Methods: We searched PubMed, Embase, CINAHL, Scopus and Web of Science, supplemented by citation searches, through 11 September 2026. Eligible evidence comprised original empirical journal reports of healthcare systems described as agentic or demonstrating potentially agentic functions. Two authors independently screened records, and two independently extracted data, with adjudication. All four authors jointly assigned analytical classifications after a five-report pilot. A structured critical audit and descriptive Clinical Agency Evidence Chain informed synthesis. The review was not registered. Results: The corpus included 123 reports; 90 were classified as core or bounded functionally agentic. Within this subset, technical task performance was the endpoint category in 44/90 reports (48.9%), and clinical decision/process outcomes in 33/90 (36.7%). Three randomised reports in the broader corpus assessed patient health outcomes: one core, one boundary/non-agentic and one indeterminate. All evaluated bundled interventions. Evidence isolating agency and following its consequences within the same comparison was limited. Safety ascertainment, intended-user error correction and whole-pathway workload were incompletely reported. External or temporal validation occurred in 6/90 reports (6.7%), with partial validation in seven others. Predominantly retrospective, simulated or offline evidence limited clinical inference. Conclusions: Intervention-level benefit must be distinguished from the incremental contribution of agency. Technical gains and local or estimated time savings do not establish patient benefit or reduced total human work.
evidence_items.title: Agentic Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare: A Scoping Review of Clinical Value, Safety, and Human Oversight

evidence_items.summary: Enterprise agentic AI systems exchange contextual information across functional modules, creating governance challenges when information crosses operational and organizational boundaries. This study distinguishes organizational governance boundaries from information exchange boundaries and proposes an Inter-Module Information Contract (IMIC) architecture for purpose-bounded context exchange. IMIC evaluates provenance, semantic and temporal validity, permitted information scope, and applicable originating constraints before downstream execution, independently of language-model reasoning. We compare IMIC with full-context sharing, reduced-context sharing, and strengthened structured handoff. In a deterministic benchmark of 32 synthetic conditions, joint correctness is achieved in 3, 10, 28, and 32 cases, respectively. The four differences between strengthened structured handoff and IMIC arise from conditions testing onward-transfer permission, recipient, purpose, and field scope. A downstream integration experiment evaluates 14 selected conditions across four local language models and three seeds, yielding 168 case–model–seed blocks and 672 method-level records. IMIC achieves correct exchange actions and information boundaries in all 168 blocks and joint correctness in 165 across four local LLMs and three seeds. Three permitted executions produce incorrect downstream responses despite correctly governed exchanges, demonstrating that information-exchange correctness does not guarantee correct downstream task performance. These results support the functional feasibility of the implemented originating-contract inheritance mechanism under controlled synthetic conditions. Further study is required to evaluate generalizability to independent enterprise workflows and richer policy structures and to extend the architecture to multiple originating providers, policy conflicts, and derived information.
evidence_items.title: Purpose-Bounded Context Exchange in Enterprise Agentic AI Systems: An Inter-Module Information Contract Architecture

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Enterprises increasingly combine large language models, retrieval-augmented generation, and autonomous software agents with existing enterprise architecture, knowledge management, and analytics investments, yet these capabilities are commonly adopted as isolated point solutions without a shared architectural foundation for organizational knowledge, decision reasoning, human accountability, or continuous assurance. This fragmentation leaves organizations unable to explain how an automated recommendation was produced, to bound what an autonomous agent may do, or to demonstrate governance to auditors, regulators, and boards. This paper asks how enterprise knowledge, decision support, agent execution, and governance can be structured as one coherent architecture. Using a literature-grounded conceptual synthesis across enterprise architecture, knowledge management, retrieval-augmented generation, decision intelligence, agentic artificial intelligence, and artificial intelligence governance, the paper derives a consolidated research gap and proposes the Governed Cognitive Enterprise Architecture: six integrated layers, a human accountability boundary, a structural formal representation, an operational lifecycle, and a maturity model, the Cognitive Enterprise Readiness Index, for organizational self-assessment. The architecture is evaluated conceptually against explicit criteria for completeness, capability integration, and governance alignment, and is compared with the reviewed literature through a source-referenced framework rather than an experimental benchmark. The principal contribution is an integrated architectural vocabulary and structure that treats human accountability and continuous assurance as first-class concerns alongside knowledge and decision capability. As a conceptual reference architecture it has not been empirically validated in an operational enterprise; expert evaluation, case-study, and quantitative validation are specified as future work.
evidence_items.title: A reference architecture for governed cognitive enterprises combining knowledge memory and decision intelligence with agentic AI under continuous assurance

evidence_items.summary: NANOSENSING AND LOCAL MICROENVIRONMENTS AT THE LIMIT F056–F060 | STARLI | WHITE RAINBOW ERA | RESEARCH WORKING EDITION v1.0 A PROSPECTIVE, NONCLINICAL, FALSIFIABLE SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH ESSENCE There is a special scientific danger in an extraordinarily beautiful sensor map. The colors are continuous, the contour lines appear physically plausible, and a small patch seems to glow with biological meaning. Yet the local concentration that the image claims to reveal cannot be seen directly. It is reconstructed through a molecule-sensitive surface, an optical or electrical transducer, a moving fluid, a chip whose materials interact with the analyte, and a sequence of decisions about calibration. This new STARLI family begins at the fragile point where an instrument report becomes a claim about a living microenvironment. Its central principle is simple: the environment must not be defined by the device that wants to be congratulated for measuring it. Five flagship investigations carry distinct questions. F056 asks if a local nanosensor can report dissolved oxygen without consuming oxygen or mistaking thermal quenching for hypoxia. F057 studies whether a microrobot can map the spatial distribution of hydrogen-ion activity without stirring the gradient into a different state. F058 asks how glucose and lactate readings can be synchronized when electrochemical reactions, dead volumes and pumps each introduce delays of their own. F059 examines drift, surface adsorption, photobleaching and biofouling across long observation intervals. F060 asks whether the combined uncertainty of those measurements is honest in a new laboratory, under conditions that the calibration software has not already seen. These are five scientific objects, not five marketing descriptions of a single device. The supplied STARLI two-hundred-flagship atlas fixes the research identities and family boundaries.
evidence_items.title: NANOSENSING AND LOCAL MICROENVIRONMENTS AT THE LIMIT F056–F060 | STARLI | WHITE RAINBOW ERA | RESEARCH WORKING EDITION v1.0 A PROSPECTIVE, NONCLINICAL, FALSIFIABLE SCIENTIFIC RESEARCH ESSENCE  There is a special scientific danger in an extraordinarily beautiful sensor map. The colors are continuous, the contour lines appear physically plausible, and a small patch seems to glow with biological meaning. Yet the local concentration that the image claims to reveal cannot be seen directly. It is reconstructed through a molecule-sensitive surface, an optical or electrical transducer, a moving fluid, a chip whose materials interact with the analyte, and a sequence of decisions about calibration. This new STARLI family begins at the fragile point where an instrument report becomes a claim about a living microenvironment. Its central principle is simple: the environment must not be defined by the device that wants to be congratulated for measuring it.  Five flagship investigations carry distinct questions. F056 asks if a local nanosensor can report dissolved oxygen without consuming oxygen or mistaking thermal quenching for hypoxia. F057 studies whether a microrobot can map the spatial distribution of hydrogen-ion activity without stirring the gradient into a different state. F058 asks how glucose and lactate readings can be synchronized when electrochemical reactions, dead volumes and pumps each introduce delays of their own. F059 examines drift, surface adsorption, photobleaching and biofouling across long observation intervals. F060 asks whether the combined uncertainty of those measurements is honest in a new laboratory, under conditions that the calibration software has not already seen. These are five scientific objects, not five marketing descriptions of a single device.  The supplied STARLI two-hundred-flagship atlas fixes the research identities and family boundaries. The uploaded F18 organ-on-chip monograph supplies an essential inheritance: engineering success and physiological function are different kinds of claims. This new family extends that lesson to metrology. A nanosensor may be accurately fabricated and still report the wrong concentration; a device may reconstruct its own synthetic surface exactly while the entire model is physically wrong; a well-controlled chip may remain a poor representation of an intact human organ. These cautions are not reasons to abandon imagination. They allow researchers to imagine more freely without confusing imagination with evidence. All curves in the accompanying book are explicitly synthetic, and no experiment, living organ improvement, clinical efficacy or regulatory approval is claimed.  The integrated research design combines five stages of work: freeze the physically meaningful measurand, build a transparent model, challenge it under an adverse perturbation, transfer the observation to an independent reference, and preserve the counterexample in an open successor archive. The result of every stage may be failure, narrowing, or abstention. A laboratory cannot repair such a verdict by changing the units, discarding inconvenient sensors, moving the analysis window or calling post hoc retuning a prospective prediction. The limits are part of the scientific result.  F056  —  OXYGEN: THE SENSOR MUST NOT CREATE ITS OWN HYPOXIA NANOSENSOR MEASUREMENT OF LOCAL OXYGEN CONCENTRATION AT THE LIMIT  Dissolved oxygen is not merely another colored channel. It participates in cellular metabolism and its transport is affected by perfusion, channel geometry, diffusion length, gas permeability and temperature. Optical oxygen indicators can change lifetime or intensity with quencher concentration; an electrochemical electrode may consume a fraction of the oxygen it is attempting to read. The primary outcome is a difference between a localized estimate and an independent dissolved-oxygen reference, expressed in micromoles per litre. A small signed mean bias alone is insufficient, because positive and negative local errors can cancel. Depth mismatch and delayed response can also make an appealing spatial gradient false.  The first hidden question is not always the most photogenic one. One part of oxygen-lifetime Stern–Volmer calibration against a blind standard is tested when investigators fit a lifetime or intensity ratio to certified dissolved-oxygen standards. In that controlled world, photobleaching shifts an intensity ratio while oxygen stays fixed. But oxygen-probe consumption in a diffusion-limited boundary layer tells a different story: the decisive probe must quantify oxygen consumption at the live electrode surface with a zero-bias control, even though the sensor generates the very oxygen depletion it claims to observe. The decisive endpoint is local dissolved oxygen bias [µmol/L], evaluated against established optical oxygen probe and electrochemical dissolved-oxygen reference with identical spatial, time and calibration budgets.  A second frontier emerges when the chip itself becomes part of the instrument. One part of gas permeability of the chip roof and package seals is tested when investigators switch gas-impermeable and gas-permeable chip roofs at fixed perfusion. In that controlled world, atmospheric oxygen enters through the package rather than through biology. But microbubble nucleation near the sensor footprint tells a different story: the decisive probe must trigger controlled microbubbles and quantify reference fluctuations, even though optical scattering around a bubble is misread as oxygen change. The decisive endpoint is local dissolved oxygen bias [µmol/L], evaluated against established optical oxygen probe and electrochemical dissolved-oxygen reference with identical spatial, time and calibration budgets.  Consider an adversarial experiment instead of a perfect-looking demonstration. One part of relative height of the probe and cell surface is tested when investigators translate a calibrated spot between channel heights and reconstruct fiducials. In that controlled world, the reference samples a different depth than the target sensor. But flow reversal and upstream downstream asymmetry tells a different story: the decisive probe must reverse flow and compare upstream and downstream spots without re-registration, even though transport asymmetry is assigned to sensor gain. The decisive endpoint is local dissolved oxygen bias [µmol/L], evaluated against established optical oxygen probe and electrochemical dissolved-oxygen reference with identical spatial, time and calibration budgets.  Another quiet source of error lives in the reference chain. One part of oxygen saturation drift during reservoir change is tested when investigators change reservoir oxygen under an independently timed reference step. In that controlled world, gas exchange during a valve switch contaminates the oxygen trace. But inlet-outlet oxygen mass balance closure tells a different story: the decisive probe must reconcile inlet and outlet oxygen with independent sample aliquots, even though unmeasured gas diffusion falsely appears as metabolic consumption. The decisive endpoint is local dissolved oxygen bias [µmol/L], evaluated against established optical oxygen probe and electrochemical dissolved-oxygen reference with identical spatial, time and calibration budgets.  The final challenge is whether a successor can reproduce the unfavorable world. One part of time response after an imposed oxygen step is tested when investigators inject a reference oxygen step whose time is hidden from the controller. In that controlled world, probe lag is incorrectly interpreted as a slow biological response. But held-out sensor relocation and second-laboratory transfer tells a different story: the decisive probe must freeze calibration while moving the probe to a new chip at another lab, even though local remapping is mistaken for transferable nanosensor accuracy. The decisive endpoint is local dissolved oxygen bias [µmol/L], evaluated against established optical oxygen probe and electrochemical dissolved-oxygen reference with identical spatial, time and calibration budgets.  The minimum prototype is cell-free sealed channel with certified oxygen-equilibrated standards, controlled flow, two external reference spots and switchable sensor bias. The primary operational claim is that a localized oxygen nanosensor can estimate dissolved oxygen with lower blind-reference bias than a matched established optical or electrochemical probe without consuming or altering the sample measurand. Yet oxygen consumption at an electrode, temperature-dependent quenching, illumination artifacts and probe-location differences can imitate local oxygen gradients. The independent witness is traceably calibrated optical-lifetime oxygen spot and independently sampled dissolved-oxygen reference with inlet/outlet mass balance; measurements must include drift, failure and calibration provenance. If the outcome demands that we suspend acquisition when local oxygen reference disagreement exceeds the preregistered bound, probe-induced oxygen depletion is non-negligible, or authority and sample identity are lost, this is a scientifically productive stop rather than a reason to hide data.  F057  —  pH: AN ACTIVITY GRADIENT IS NOT A MOVING CAMERA GRADIENT MICROROBOT-ASSISTED SPATIAL MAPPING OF PH GRADIENTS AT THE LIMIT  The pH of a microenvironment is the negative base-ten logarithm of hydrogen-ion activity. The relevant chemistry therefore depends on ionic strength, buffer capacity, temperature and liquid junction potentials. Mapping pH is not equivalent to stacking raw fluorescence frames: a mobile microprobe changes the flow field, and robot-induced mixing may erase an acidification front faster than the device can record it. The principal observable is spatial pH-map root-mean-square error in pH units, calculated against held-out references with fixed spatial coordinates. Robot speed, sample spacing and drift matter at least as much as the final displayed image.  The first hidden question is not always the most photogenic one. One part of Nernst-slope calibration at controlled temperature is tested when investigators measure electrode voltage across certified pH buffers at fixed temperature. In that controlled world, junction potential drift is mistaken for a buffer transition. But hydrogen activity versus nominal concentration tells a different story: the decisive probe must compare activity-based pH against concentration-based calculations, even though ionic strength changes activity coefficient without changing nominal H concentration. The decisive endpoint is pH map root-mean-square error [pH units], evaluated against fixed ratiometric fluorescence array and standard microelectrode raster scan under matched spatial/time sampling.  A second frontier emerges when the chip itself becomes part of the instrument. One part of buffer-capacity-induced suppression of true gradients is tested when investigators add identical acid pulses to buffers of measured capacity. In that controlled world, strong buffering flattens the field while the probe response is unchanged. But mobile robot stirring of weak-buffer zones tells a different story: the decisive probe must track dyed inert robot mixing at two commanded speeds, even though robot motion destroys the pH gradient being measured. The decisive endpoint is pH map root-mean-square error [pH units], evaluated against fixed ratiometric fluorescence array and standard microelectrode raster scan under matched spatial/time sampling.  Consider an adversarial experiment instead of a perfect-looking demonstration. One part of spatial sampling density and inverse-map ambiguity is tested when investigators withhold spatial reference points and calculate interpolation RMSE. In that controlled world, a dense smooth map is interpolated from too few independent samples. But dye ratiometry and wavelength-dependent bleaching tells a different story: the decisive probe must change dye exposure time and compare ratiometric channels, even though unequal photobleaching changes the apparently measured pH. The decisive endpoint is pH map root-mean-square error [pH units], evaluated against fixed ratiometric fluorescence array and standard microelectrode raster scan under matched spatial/time sampling.  Another quiet source of error lives in the reference chain. One part of microchannel wall surface charge effects is tested when investigators measure changes in wall surface charge under controlled ionic strength. In that controlled world, surface electrostatics is attributed to tissue-generated acid. But path-dependent hysteresis of a moving pH probe tells a different story: the decisive probe must repeat a trajectory forward and backward through the same buffer, even though hysteresis is mistaken for spatial asymmetry. The decisive endpoint is pH map root-mean-square error [pH units], evaluated against fixed ratiometric fluorescence array and standard microelectrode raster scan under matched spatial/time sampling.  The final challenge is whether a successor can reproduce the unfavorable world. One part of cross-instrument pH map interpolation error is tested when investigators reconstruct a blinded fixed grid with an independent pH microelectrode. In that controlled world, algorithm smoothing lowers apparent error while creating bias. But frozen calibration transfer to another chip geometry tells a different story: the decisive probe must repeat an unseen reference profile at a second chip geometry, even though a good map requires undocumented retuning for every device. The decisive endpoint is pH map root-mean-square error [pH units], evaluated against fixed ratiometric fluorescence array and standard microelectrode raster scan under matched spatial/time sampling.  The minimum prototype is acellular buffered microchannel containing two known pH zones and a commanded inert mobile marker tracked by an independent microscope. The primary operational claim is that microrobotic spatial sampling can reduce held-out pH-map error without stirring, heating or contaminating the buffer microenvironment. Yet probe movement may alter the local buffer, and dye photobleaching or ionic-strength mismatch can fabricate apparent pH heterogeneity. The independent witness is stationary calibrated ratiometric pH references and a separately masked microelectrode transect; measurements must include drift, failure and calibration provenance. If the outcome demands that we stop when reference dye ratio leaves calibration, when mixing induced by the robot exceeds tolerance, or when spatial registration cannot be independently reconstructed, this is a scientifically productive stop rather than a reason to hide data.  F058  —  METABOLITES: CLOCKS, ENZYMES AND THE INVENTORY OF LOST MOLECULES MULTIPOINT REAL-TIME MEASUREMENT OF MICROENVIRONMENTAL METABOLITES AT THE LIMIT  In glucose and lactate sensing, apparent metabolic changes can arise inside the instrument: an enzyme consumes a cosubstrate, a membrane slows diffusion, the electrode reacts with an interferent, or a droplet waits in tubing before its concentration can be read. A sensor installed upstream is not measuring the same chemical time as one located downstream. The flagship outcome is temporal lag in seconds, independently verified with a known concentration pulse and clock. Multipoint sensing is useful only if the locations, dead volumes, sample dilution and signal processing histories are separately traceable.  The first hidden question is not always the most photogenic one. One part of glucose oxidase oxygen-dependence of amperometric signals is tested when investigators vary oxygen at fixed glucose and audit oxidase-generated current. In that controlled world, oxidase cosubstrate depletion is mislabeled as glucose loss. But lactate cross-talk and electrode-potential isolation tells a different story: the decisive probe must spike glucose and lactate separately into identical medium, even though potential-dependent cross-talk creates a false metabolite pair. The decisive endpoint is metabolite map temporal lag [s], evaluated against sequential off-chip metabolite assays and calibrated integrated electrochemical array matched on recovery, sample use and total elapsed time.  A second frontier emerges when the chip itself becomes part of the instrument. One part of dead-volume residence time under pulsed flow is tested when investigators vary tubing dead volume and reconstruct inert dye lag. In that controlled world, fluid residence delay is interpreted as slower metabolism. But mass transport to a planar electrochemical electrode tells a different story: the decisive probe must change boundary-layer flow while holding analyte concentration, even though electrode transport limitation is mistaken for consumption. The decisive endpoint is metabolite map temporal lag [s], evaluated against sequential off-chip metabolite assays and calibrated integrated electrochemical array matched on recovery, sample use and total elapsed time.  Consider an adversarial experiment instead of a perfect-looking demonstration. One part of reference assay recovery after tubing adsorption is tested when investigators recover known tracer after exchanging tubing materials. In that controlled world, polymer sorption hides incoming metabolite mass. But temperature response of enzyme activity tells a different story: the decisive probe must vary temperature under fixed standard concentration, even though enzyme kinetics alters readout gain without metabolite change. The decisive endpoint is metabolite map temporal lag [s], evaluated against sequential off-chip metabolite assays and calibrated integrated electrochemical array matched on recovery, sample use and total elapsed time.  Another quiet source of error lives in the reference chain. One part of metabolite gradient smoothness versus spatial spacing is tested when investigators change sensor spacing across a known stable concentration field. In that controlled world, spatial interpolation creates an artificial metabolite gradient. But matrix interference from albumin-rich medium tells a different story: the decisive probe must spike albumin-rich medium and compare external chromatography, even though matrix interference resembles a metabolic reaction. The decisive endpoint is metabolite map temporal lag [s], evaluated against sequential off-chip metabolite assays and calibrated integrated electrochemical array matched on recovery, sample use and total elapsed time.  The final challenge is whether a successor can reproduce the unfavorable world. One part of lactate and glucose joint mass balance is tested when investigators reconcile glucose uptake and lactate release with all inflows/outflows. In that controlled world, unclosed material recovery is proclaimed altered cell metabolism. But blinded transfer between metabolite reference standards tells a different story: the decisive probe must blindly exchange analyte reference standards between laboratories, even though a calibration transfer gains accuracy only after privileged adjustment. The decisive endpoint is metabolite map temporal lag [s], evaluated against sequential off-chip metabolite assays and calibrated integrated electrochemical array matched on recovery, sample use and total elapsed time.  The minimum prototype is cell-free glucose/lactate pulse mixer with dye-time fiducials, separate electrochemical probes and external reference aliquots. The primary operational claim is that multipoint oxygen-glucose-lactate readouts can resolve transient metabolite changes with shorter verified timing error than one-point sequential sampling under equal analyte and reference budgets. Yet tubing dead volume, diffusion, enzyme exhaustion and sensor-clock skew can imitate a metabolic phase lag or localized gradient. The independent witness is synchronized outlet reference sampling with calibrated external glucose/lactate assays and a nonreactive timing tracer; measurements must include drift, failure and calibration provenance. If the outcome demands that we stop when analyte mass closure fails, enzyme capacity saturates, cross-talk exceeds limit or the timebase cannot be independently aligned, this is a scientifically productive stop rather than a reason to hide data.  F059  —  DRIFT AND BIOFOULING: THE INSTRUMENT CHANGES WHILE THE ORGAN CHIP LIVES NANOSENSOR DRIFT AND BIOFOULING CONTROL AT THE LIMIT  A sensor that initially reports well may deteriorate through surface protein adsorption, membrane aging, photobleaching or electrode polarization. Fouling may shift the zero point, change sensitivity, and increase response time by different amounts. The reference measure here is an oxygen-equivalent drift slope in micromoles per litre per hour. Lower apparent drift can be achieved deceptively by replacing bad sensors, rejecting failed runs, or allowing an algorithm to erase slowly varying real oxygen signals. Such a strategy makes a nice performance graph at the cost of losing the scientific measurand.  The first hidden question is not always the most photogenic one. One part of protein adsorption kinetics on an exposed nanosensor is tested when investigators measure surface protein loading against exposure duration. In that controlled world, a fouling layer changes transport even when baseline appears flat. But steric barrier performance after repetitive flow cycles tells a different story: the decisive probe must repeat flow cycling before and after polymer passivation, even though a coating passes an immediate test but peels after shear cycles. The decisive endpoint is oxygen-equivalent sensor drift slope [µmol L⁻¹ h⁻¹], evaluated against unmodified reference sensor with preregistered calibration interval and matched passive antifouling coating.  A second frontier emerges when the chip itself becomes part of the instrument. One part of surface functional group hydrolysis and sensor aging is tested when investigators quantify surface chemistry aging with independent spectroscopy. In that controlled world, chemical instability is confused with recoverable sensor drift. But electrode polarization and baseline recovery tells a different story: the decisive probe must switch electrode polarization and record baseline relaxation, even though an electrochemical history effect resembles biological aging. The decisive endpoint is oxygen-equivalent sensor drift slope [µmol L⁻¹ h⁻¹], evaluated against unmodified reference sensor with preregistered calibration interval and matched passive antifouling coating.  Consider an adversarial experiment instead of a perfect-looking demonstration. One part of photobleaching of optical oxygen indicators is tested when investigators expose optical indicators to matched cumulative illumination. In that controlled world, bleaching is misinterpreted as oxygen depletion. But stochastic fouling patches and spatial hot spots tells a different story: the decisive probe must inspect spatial fouling patches across the sensor array, even though only surviving clean pixels are used to report low drift. The decisive endpoint is oxygen-equivalent sensor drift slope [µmol L⁻¹ h⁻¹], evaluated against unmodified reference sensor with preregistered calibration interval and matched passive antifouling coating.  Another quiet source of error lives in the reference chain. One part of accelerated thermal aging and real-time equivalence is tested when investigators compare accelerated thermal exposure to real-time aging. In that controlled world, thermal equivalence is falsely assumed without kinetic support. But long-term oxygen sensor response delay tells a different story: the decisive probe must fit response time before and after controlled protein deposition, even though a slowly responding probe disguises a sharp event. The decisive endpoint is oxygen-equivalent sensor drift slope [µmol L⁻¹ h⁻¹], evaluated against unmodified reference sensor with preregistered calibration interval and matched passive antifouling coating.  The final challenge is whether a successor can reproduce the unfavorable world. One part of sensor cross-lot and sterilization exposure is tested when investigators swap sterilization cycles and reagent material batches. In that controlled world, a favorable antifouling result applies to one unreported lot. But external laboratory replay of stored drift history tells a different story: the decisive probe must transfer calibration histories to a blinded external analysis team, even though calibration relies on undocumented operator overrides. The decisive endpoint is oxygen-equivalent sensor drift slope [µmol L⁻¹ h⁻¹], evaluated against unmodified reference sensor with preregistered calibration interval and matched passive antifouling coating.  The minimum prototype is acellular microchannel cycled through certified standards and surrogate protein solutions with retained sensor blanks. The primary operational claim is that reference-aware antifouling and drift correction can reduce blind post-exposure oxygen-equivalent drift without erasing real microenvironment change or altering living-cell compatibility. Yet silent recalibration on the test sample, sensor replacement selection and slow true oxygen change can masquerade as less drift. The independent witness is before/after multi-point external calibration combined with surface microscopy and protein-adsorption mass assay; measurements must include drift, failure and calibration provenance. If the outcome demands that we stop when calibration history is incomplete, sensor response becomes non-monotone, residual foulant breaches a material criterion or a supposed correction removes a known injected standard step, this is a scientifically productive stop rather than a reason to hide data.  F060  —  UNCERTAINTY: A RIGHT TO SAY WE CANNOT MEASURE THIS MEASUREMENT UNCERTAINTY IN LOCAL PHYSIOLOGICAL SENSING AT THE LIMIT  Reporting a point estimate without a defensible uncertainty interval is often an invitation to overinterpretation. In a small organ-on-chip geometry, the reference standard, timebase, position, temperature, calibration curve, sensor interactions and local gradient all contribute to uncertainty. Independent errors may be combined by root-sum-square only when the independence assumption is defensible. Shared calibration standards introduce covariance and can make two apparently agreeing sensors wrong together. The principal endpoint is expanded local oxygen calibration uncertainty in micromoles per litre, checked against the empirical coverage of withheld reference values.  The first hidden question is not always the most photogenic one. One part of traceability chain from certified solution to local concentration is tested when investigators rebuild calibration with a traceable two-standard chain. In that controlled world, both standards share a hidden systematic offset. But Type A repeatability versus Type B reference uncertainty tells a different story: the decisive probe must separate repeated reading scatter from reference certificate contributions, even though repeatability is presented as total uncertainty. The decisive endpoint is expanded local oxygen calibration uncertainty [µmol/L], evaluated against standard independent error-propagation budget and uncorrected reference sensor with external coverage checking.  A second frontier emerges when the chip itself becomes part of the instrument. One part of covariance between optical and electrochemical oxygen sensors is tested when investigators introduce a common offset into optical and electrochemical sensors. In that controlled world, correlated errors masquerade as independent agreement. But nonlinear calibration uncertainty at range boundaries tells a different story: the decisive probe must challenge calibration at the lower and upper standard range, even though a central-range fit understates edge uncertainty. The decisive endpoint is expanded local oxygen calibration uncertainty [µmol/L], evaluated against standard independent error-propagation budget and uncorrected reference sensor with external coverage checking.  Consider an adversarial experiment instead of a perfect-looking demonstration. One part of temporal uncertainty from clock misalignment is tested when investigators shift timestamps across a known oxygen step. In that controlled world, clock misalignment creates concentration error. But parameter-identifiability limits under correlated drift tells a different story: the decisive probe must perturb simultaneous slope and offset drift, even though the inverse problem is not identifiable despite a narrow reported interval. The decisive endpoint is expanded local oxygen calibration uncertainty [µmol/L], evaluated against standard independent error-propagation budget and uncorrected reference sensor with external coverage checking.  Another quiet source of error lives in the reference chain. One part of finite replicate sampling and donor clustering is tested when investigators reduce the number of independent reference lots. In that controlled world, nominal sample count overstates effective information. But heteroscedastic residuals at low oxygen concentration tells a different story: the decisive probe must test near-zero oxygen standards with known added variation, even though constant-variance intervals undercover the low range. The decisive endpoint is expanded local oxygen calibration uncertainty [µmol/L], evaluated against standard independent error-propagation budget and uncorrected reference sensor with external coverage checking.  The final challenge is whether a successor can reproduce the unfavorable world. One part of external coverage frequency under withheld offsets is tested when investigators hide calibration offsets during an external coverage audit. In that controlled world, reported intervals miss the reference more often than claimed. But cross-lab portability of a full uncertainty certificate tells a different story: the decisive probe must provide a frozen uncertainty certificate to another lab, even though claimed portability depends on local retuning and shared standards. The decisive endpoint is expanded local oxygen calibration uncertainty [µmol/L], evaluated against standard independent error-propagation budget and uncorrected reference sensor with external coverage checking.  The minimum prototype is open oxygen and pH calibration phantom with hidden reference offsets and two blinded instrument operators. The primary operational claim is that a multicomponent and auditable uncertainty budget can provide valid out-of-sample coverage for spatial oxygen estimates under blind calibration and adverse transfer without hiding correlated bias. Yet shared reference standards, correlated sensor drift and post-selection calibration can falsely narrow uncertainty intervals. The independent witness is two independent oxygen reference families, calibration certificates and a blinded held-out coverage audit; measurements must include drift, failure and calibration provenance. If the outcome demands that we stop when held-out coverage falls below preregistration, covariance becomes unidentifiable, traceability breaks or the reporting software suppresses unresolved measurements, this is a scientifically productive stop rather than a reason to hide data.  FROM FIVE MEASUREMENTS TO ONE BOUNDED LOCAL ENVIRONMENT  The five flagships exchange information, but no cross-flagship arithmetic should ignore units. Oxygen concentration estimates are in micromoles per litre; pH reconstruction error is in pH units; metabolite arrival times are in seconds; drift is concentration per time; uncertainty is concentration with a declared reference frame. A system designer can formulate a conjunction of acceptable states—for example, a valid oxygen reference, a tolerable pH-map error, a metabolite lag below a preregistered limit, stable sensor calibration and acceptable held-out uncertainty coverage. It is not acceptable to let an excellent oxygen score numerically compensate for a missing pH reference or an unreported contamination event. Such a trade would create a scalar performance illusion rather than a valid scientific integration.  A physical coupling experiment should keep the causal directions distinct. Changing perfusion can alter real oxygen delivery while changing sensor transport lag; it can also shift pH and dilution. A moving microrobot may improve spatial sampling but stir the local fluid. Added electrochemical sensors can improve spatial coverage while consuming oxygen or introducing cross-analyte interference. A protective anti-fouling layer may extend sensor lifetime but increase diffusion resistance. Better calibration can increase the honest uncertainty interval rather than narrow it. The whole point is to learn which benefit survives after each of these opposing tendencies has been independently observed.  A synthetic three-dimensional mathematical atlas can help make such conflicts visible. The forty-two reduced response surfaces in the companion research PDF are built from transparent equations for oxygen bias, pH-map error, metabolite lag, fouling drift and expanded uncertainty. They deliberately vary flow, temperature, buffer capacity, dead volume, surface coverage, exposure duration, reference scatter and position error. Their CSV values and reconstruction script are attached to the PDF. Reproducing the numbers proves that the file faithfully computes its own declared assumptions; it does not prove that a particular instrument or biological tissue follows those assumptions. Any future experimental study must estimate its coefficients, test the physical domain, and publish a failure when the predicted surface does not appear.  Two hundred Research Gates in the main monograph are arranged to invite a later researcher into the strongest unresolved question rather than merely displaying a checklist. A gate might ask whether a sensor still measures oxygen after the electrode bias is silently reversed; whether a pH map survives a hidden buffer-strength swap; whether a lactate spike arrives late only because the tubing is longer; whether an antifouling correction deletes a true local oxygen transient; or whether a low uncertainty bound misses the reference standard more often than advertised. Each proposed gate carries an origin, an extreme counterfactual world, a concrete successor test, a strong comparator and a stopping condition. The accompanying concept and counterfactual diagrams are not results; they visualize which physical path could fail.  Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos then propose small nonclinical instruments that future teams might actually construct: a hidden oxygen-standard cabinet, a robot-mixing sentinel, a dual-pH reference map, an enzyme-interference mirror, a drift-exposure carousel and a covariance-based uncertainty coverage auditor, among others. None has been built merely because it is described. Every prototype should begin with a certified acellular phantom, retain the full failed-run denominator, and carry a physical or operational veto. The strongest open scientific legacy may be a precise negative result that retires an attractive mechanism and prevents the next generation from repeating its error.  WHAT THIS WORK DOES AND DOES NOT ESTABLISH  This research working edition is prospective, nonclinical and falsifiable. It proposes sensor measurement protocols and synthetic models; it does not provide biological measurements, verified cell-function improvement, medical efficacy, autonomous treatment approval or a regulatory-compliant device. In a scientific field where visualizations can become persuasive before calibration is complete, the right to decline a conclusion is an indispensable design property. A new laboratory that reconstructs a failure with independent standards contributes more to the programme than one that reproduces its terminology without a transparent test. evidence_items.summary: This replication package contains the anonymised post-treatment survey dataset (N = 84; Group A Plain Text Control: n = 12; Group B HTML Treatment: n = 72), the Python reproducibility script (reproduce analysis.py), and the official aggregate campaign reports from Brevo (N = 622 randomised recipients; 7-day observation window from 30 June 2026, 19:43 CEST to 7 July 2026, 19:43 CEST) supporting the study "Optimising Conversion Rates in Direct Email Marketing: A Field Experiment Based on the C-TAM-TPB Model with Master's Students in Albania". Per-recipient tracking logs were permanently deleted upon closing the seven-day observation window on 7 July 2026 (19:43 CEST) in compliance with Albanian Law No. 124/2024 on Personal Data Protection.

That gap between apparent geometrical success and independently measured function motivates this research family. The prospective system combines robot-assisted cell placement, microvolume ink release, photocuring, cooperative stacking and strong-baseline functional verification. The objective is not to celebrate microrobots as a technological synonym for progress. It is to specify the physical circumstances under which the additional robotic complexity earns its place, where the gain can be measured without contaminating the test, and which evidence could compel a future laboratory to abandon the preferred explanation. No simulation here is a bioprinting experiment, no attractive plot demonstrates tissue maturation, and no mathematical formula substitutes for the identity and history of the specimens that would ultimately have to be tested. The family inherits two disciplines. The uploaded 200-topic STARLI atlas assigns the five flagship identities and six candidate mathematical roles to each study. The F18 organ-on-chip monograph insists that manufacturing precision does not yet establish physiological function. This distinction remains absolute: a printed cell can be in the right place and yet be dead, stressed, phenotypically changed, poorly connected, or incapable of a specific biological response. Every proposed improvement is therefore conditional on separate witnesses for geometry, material transport, cell state, and if relevant organ-specific function.

THE FIVE-DIMENSIONAL ENGINEERING COUPLING A future integrated station might position cell cargo, meter ink, crosslink a hydrogel, arrange stacked layers, and decide whether the resulting organ-on-chip is independently qualified. The coupling is meaningful only if the interfaces are physically explicit. Where did the cell go? How much material did the system really release? What photon exposure reached each depth, rather than what the lamp was commanded to deliver? How far did the layer drift during settling? Did an independent physiological readout pass after the robot had finished acting? These questions must be asked in their own units and combined only by a declared decision rule. A composite score that allows outstanding geometry to compensate for dead cells should fail before it is ever published.  MATHEMATICS, RECOMPUTABLE SURFACES AND EVIDENCE DISCIPLINE The revised thirty candidate plates now separate five physical problems: landing and contact physics, bioink hydrodynamics and mass closure, photocuring and viability limits, cooperative stacking mechanics, and function-qualified throughput with risk accounting. Each relation has its own dimensions, operating assumptions, geometric reading and falsification test. The shared wall-shear approximation from the mother blueprint remains documented as a common starting point, not repeated as five allegedly independent discoveries. Forty-two three-dimensional numerical surfaces make assumptions visible by exposing two independent inputs against an observable such as landing error, dose error, viability loss, layer offset or function-qualified throughput. Every CSV row, model parameter and reproducing Python expression is intended to be available in the research PDF. These graphics are synthetic response surfaces, not measurements, empirical fits or guarantees of an optimum. Their scientific purpose is to make it easier for a subsequent experiment to falsify the relationship.  THE RESEARCH GATES AND PHOENIX PRINCIPLE The two hundred Research Gates invite a future generation to construct explicit counterworlds: a chip with a hidden height defect, a carrier leaving residue, a photopolymer that appears strong but suppresses survival, a robot stack made orderly by selective exclusion of failed layers, and a production pipeline whose apparent speed disappears once readout and rejection time are counted. Each gate carries a core question, an origin, an extreme extrapolation, a concrete next experiment, and a stopping condition. Thirty-three Phoenix Answer Embryos then translate some questions into minimum bench instruments: mass-balance ledgers, independent dose mirrors, fail-closed relays, calibration passports, blinded negative-world archives and reproducibility kits. None is declared constructed merely because it has been diagrammed. Their value lies in allowing future teams to build the smallest discriminating test, observe an unfavorable outcome, and publish the result without rewriting the original claim.  FROM RESEARCH WORKING EDITION TO OPEN SUCCESSOR SCIENCE The strongest inheritance is not a monument to continuous success. It is an auditable set of decisions and failures: which samples were excluded and why, which materials were used, what the separate witness measured, where the calibration failed, what the hard veto did, and whether the purported robot advantage survived a fully matched comparator. Laboratory replication is not assumed; it is a test to perform. A result may be negative, inconclusive, or restricted to a narrow phantom environment without diminishing the value of a well-posed question. The collection remains prospective and nonclinical; no description should be interpreted as demonstrated organ manufacture, animal or human intervention, medical effectiveness, regulatory authorization, or a validated autonomous bioreactor. STARLI's scientific invitation is to begin with a precise question and make it possible for a stranger to prove it wrong. evidence_items.summary: Critical reading is an essential skill for future English language teachers because it enables them to understand not only the literal meaning of a text but also the intentions, attitudes, and emotions expressed through language. Stylistic analysis provides an effective approach to developing this skill by examining how lexical choices, figurative language, repetition, contrast, and sentence structure influence interpretation. This article explores the role of stylistic analysis in developing critical reading skills among future English language teachers. It adopts a qualitative, descriptive approach based on theoretical literature and the analysis of illustrative English-language examples. The discussion demonstrates how stylistic features can guide learners towards deeper textual understanding, evidence-based interpretation, and independent thinking. A practical framework consisting of five stages is proposed: observation, identification, interpretation, evaluation, and reflection. The article argues that integrating stylistic analysis into English language teacher education can strengthen linguistic awareness and analytical competence. It also emphasizes the importance of contextual interpretation and teacher guidance in developing effective reading strategies.
evidence_items.title: DEVELOPING CRITICAL READING SKILLS THROUGH STYLISTIC ANALYSIS IN ENGLISH LANGUAGE TEACHER EDUCATION

evidence_items.summary: Research data obtained in epidemiological studies are important for generating new knowledge in medical research. When the data is managed according to the FAIR¹, their value enhances significantly². However, in the health data environment, it is also necessary to establish a clear data collecting and sharing process as part of comprehensive data management, addressing legal and ethical risks and ensures compliance with the GDPR³. The process was created and implemented in cooperation of several departments of St. Anne's University Hospital. The hospital organizes responsible data sharing through a transparent workflow. Requests are submitted via the REDCap4 web application and goes through a structural approval process. The Kardiovize Brno population study5 serves as a pilot dataset for testing and validating process. The implemented procedure is flexible, accomodating large cohort studies and smaller projects that maintain data in an exportable format with a corresponding codebook. A transparent and auditable procedure for exchanging sensitive data is the main advantage of this process. The active involvement of the Data Protection Officer and legal experts guarantees adherence to all relevant regulations. REDCap provides a reliable, cost-effective solution. Cooperation with the Biostatistics Department provides extensive methodological support to researchers throughout the entire data management lifecycle.
evidence_items.title: Workflow for Sharing Sensitive Data at St. Anne's University Hospital Brno
