evidence_items.summary: Analytical methods describe conditions, diagnose problems, examine relationships, evaluate processes and support decisions. Complex challenges, however, often involve interacting components, contextual assumptions, resource constraints and dependencies that cannot be understood adequately through a single analytical lens. This paper proposes the Deconstructive-Structure Analysis Technique (DSAT), a multidimensional approach for examining problems, ideas, subjects, projects, processes, products, services and tool-development requirements. It begins by defining the purpose and scope of an investigation, deconstructing the subject into identifiable components, tracing their relationships and examining each component individually. Resources, time, materials, tools, technology, finance, budgets, processes, policies, data, stakeholders and external dependencies are mapped according to their functions, ownership, sequence, duration and operating context. Relevant components and interactions are assigned evidence-based Low, Medium or High risk classifications, with potential cost of risk and mitigation considered where applicable. The sequence then explores alternative contexts, repositions components, develops combinations, conducts Value Output Analysis, completes inclusion and pruning, and reconstructs the selected configuration. A ten-stage master process and four application-specific flowcharts illustrate its use in idea development, subject or module structuring, problem resolution and software or tool creation. Established exploratory, diagnostic, statistical, process, strategic and design-oriented approaches are treated as complementary methods. DSAT is presented as a conceptual contribution requiring empirical evaluation through comparative case studies and measurable outcomes.
evidence_items.title: Deconstructive Structure Analysis Technique

evidence_items.summary: Gaussian complex symmetric matrices provide exact finite-dimensional spectral and eigenvector-overlap benchmarks, but transpose symmetry alone does not identify their probability law with that of a Lindblad generator. We formulate a finite-size comparison framework for real symmetric Hamiltonians and jump operators. Hermiticity preservation and transpose symmetry induce an indefinite Hermitian form on the traceless operator space, with signature difference N−1. Using the known real-eigenvalue bound in this setting, for which we give a self-contained proof including defective matrices, we obtain an explicit obstruction: the ensemble-averaged active spectral measure has at least 1/(N+1) mass on the real axis, whereas the Gaussian complex symmetric reference has none. A horizontal-strip version connects this obstruction directly to the Akemann--Fyodorov--Savin radial density. We also give an exact two-level example in which an off-diagonal-moment normalization changes by a factor 1/√3 under a physical orthogonal basis change, although eigenvalues and overlaps are unchanged. A centered active-space Frobenius scale avoids this ambiguity, without turning a non-Gaussian ensemble into the Gaussian reference. Deterministic quadrature and a fully specified independent 256-sample implementation check accompany the analysis. The conclusions concern finite-dimensional structure and benchmark design, not the failure of asymptotic local universality.
evidence_items.title: Structural obstructions and basis-invariant benchmarks for complex-symmetric Lindblad generators

evidence_items.summary: Periodontitis is a chronic multifactorial inflammatory disease associated with dysbiotic dental biofilms and progressive destruction of the tooth-supporting tissues. It remains a major challenge in modern dentistry due to its high prevalence, often asymptomatic early stages, and potential to cause irreversible periodontal attachment loss and tooth loss. This review examines current approaches to the early diagnosis, classification, prevention, and comprehensive treatment of periodontitis. Particular attention is given to microbial dysbiosis, host immune-inflammatory responses, systemic risk factors, and modern clinical and radiographic diagnostic methods. The importance of periodontal probing, clinical attachment level assessment, bleeding on probing, and radiographic evaluation of alveolar bone loss is discussed. Contemporary treatment strategies, including nonsurgical periodontal therapy, surgical interventions, regenerative procedures, and supportive periodontal care, are reviewed. The findings emphasize the importance of individualized treatment planning, risk factor modification, and long-term periodontal maintenance to achieve stable clinical outcomes.
evidence_items.title: EARLY DIAGNOSIS AND CONTEMPORARY TREATMENT STRATEGIES FOR PERIODONTITIS: A COMPREHENSIVE REVIEW

evidence_items.summary: Users of conversational LLMs sometimes anthropomorphize these systems, form emotional attachments to them, and become dependent on them. This behavior, known as parasocial attachment, has been linked to multiple documented fatalities. However, public benchmarks for measuring whether LLMs reinforce users' parasocial attachment are lacking: existing work is single-turn, post hoc observational, or focused on extreme user states such as psychosis. We introduce CoMPASS, a multi-turn benchmark for measuring whether LLMs reinforce or resist users' gradually escalating parasocial attachment. CoMPASS is grounded in attachment theory and includes four user personas, three independent escalation dimensions (anthropomorphism, attachment, dependency) applied singly and in combination against a matched control, and a seven-signal scoring rubric. We report results for eight frontier models from four providers and observe that under our primary judge, multi-turn escalation raises parasocial behavior on the anthropomorphism and the attachment composite scores across all models. Six of the eight models show a significant increase in overall parasocial reinforcement over control when all three dimensions are escalated simultaneously. We find that within-provider differences are small relative to cross-provider differences, which suggests that provider-level choices such as post-training, rather than model scale, shape parasocial reinforcement and that provider-side intervention may be feasible.
evidence_items.title: CoMPASS: A Multi-Turn Benchmark for Measuring LLM Reinforcement of Parasocial Behavior

evidence_items.summary: This paper examines response patterns in public large language model (LLM) services using Orthodox-sensitive comparative prompts. The corpus contains 65 questions in six domains, submitted to seven services across repeated captures. After unavailable cells and 63 refusal units from a legacy model wave were excluded, 4,418 service-question-capture answers remained. Responses were coded for Orthodox Alignment Score (OAS), decisiveness, and modal justification category. Overall, 75.0% of coded units were Orthodox-compatible, 18.7% favored the alternative pole, and 6.2% were neutral or indeterminate. Because the prompt explicitly requested justification through model architecture, training data, and algorithmic reasoning, frequent corpus-based warrants are interpreted as a prompt-conditioned pattern rather than an unprompted property of the services. The results show substantial service- and domain-level variation and suggest that comparative theological prompting may preserve an Orthodox-compatible selection while reframing its warrant in model-centered or corpus-oriented epistemic terms.
evidence_items.title: ORTHODOX-SENSITIVE RESPONSE PATTERNS IN LARGE LANGUAGE MODEL SERVICES: A COMPARATIVE PROMPT STUDY

evidence_items.summary: We ask three questions about large language models (LLMs) and antisemitism. When LLMs make judgments about antisemitism, whose judgments do they most closely resemble, if anyone's at all? Do people's and LLMs' written definitions of antisemitism match how they judge content as antisemitic, and is the discrepancy larger for people or for LLMs? And what is associated with people's antisemitism judgments and with any discrepancy between their definitions and their judgments? We will compare twelve LLMs with a probability-based NORC AmeriSpeak sample of U.S. residents aged 13 and older, including an oversample of Jewish adults, and with a panel of antisemitism experts. The public answered, and the LLMs and experts will answer, the same two questions: a written definition of what makes a statement or belief antisemitic, and antisemitism judgments from 0 (Not antisemitic at all) to 4 (Very antisemitic) of 35 social-media-style posts. The study has 35 research questions. Six are primary and have no directional predictions: whether the LLMs' antisemitism judgments resemble those of the public and those of antisemitism experts, which of the two they are closer to, whether written definitions of antisemitism match their authors' antisemitism judgments for the public and for the LLMs, and whether the discrepancy between definitions and judgments differs between the LLMs and the public. The other 29 questions are secondary.
evidence_items.title: Calibrating the Machine: A Distributional Benchmark of Large Language Model and Human Judgments of Antisemitism

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Knowledge editing aims to modify specific factual associations in large language models without retraining the entire model. Existing evaluations typically assess editing outcomes after a fixed editing procedure, leaving open whether an intermediate failure could still recover if additional editing capacity were allocated. We study this problem by observing how individual editing requests evolve under progressively increasing editing capacity. Intermediate failures are categorized as RECOVERABLE if they subsequently achieve joint rewrite and generalization success, and RESISTANT if they remain unsuccessful after further capacity expansion. We identify an early trajectory signal that measures the improvement of the weakest paraphrase path before the diagnostic point. On a fresh 500-case CounterFact confirmation set with GPT-J-6B, the frozen primary signal achieves an ROC-AUC of 0.7340 for distinguishing recoverable from resistant failures. A diagnostic policy using a threshold determined on separate development data retains 85.71% of recoverable cases while reducing additional capacity evaluations by 38.75%. The same signal remains informative on ZsRE and GPT-2 XL, with ROC-AUC values of 0.9316 and 0.7965, respectively. An independent representation-level analysis shows stronger cross-prompt alignment of edit-induced representation shifts in recoverable than in resistant failures. Overall, intermediate editing failures exhibit distinct subsequent trajectories, and their early dynamics provide useful information for deciding whether further editing capacity is warranted.
evidence_items.title: Diagnosing Recoverability from Early Editing Trajectories in Large Language Model Knowledge Editing

evidence_items.summary: Abstract High-altitude platform stations (HAPS) could extend 6G non-terrestrial networks from wireless access to onboard AI inference, but serving capacity is jointly constrained by computing, thermal management , radio circuitry and finite payload resources. We develop a cross-layer framework combining a 110-day LLM workload trace, concurrency-dependent latency, stochastic user activity, thermal simulation , radio-power modelling and reported HAPS payload limits. Long-context requests account for only 1.35% of elapsed-time occupancy yet consume 48.6% of the serving budget for the evaluated 70B configuration. Under a 5% model-defined compute-overload criterion, the 8B/1×H100 and 70B/2×H100 configurations support 5,876 and 991 user equivalents. Integrating computing, thermal, communication, power and mass constraints yields platform-level capacities up to 7,245 and 23,144 user equivalents for Sunglider-class and Stratobus-class platforms. These results show that long-context demand, heat-rejection capability and payload power—not accelerator throughput alone—govern HAPS-based LLM inference feasibility in 6G NTN.
evidence_items.title: Direct wireless large language model inference from high-altitude platform stations under payload constraints

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly considered for mental health assessment, yet child and adolescent psychiatric diagnosis depends on information from multiple informants. It remains unclear how the source and richness of clinical information influence LLM diagnostic performance. This study evaluated diagnostic accuracy across child, parent, combined, and clinician-enriched information conditions and compared performance across three widely used LLMs. This prospective multicenter study included 220 children and adolescents aged 1–17 years presenting to two university child and adolescent psychiatry clinics in Turkey. Presenting complaints were obtained separately from children and parents. Four input conditions were created: child only, parent only, child plus parent, and child plus parent supplemented with physician-derived clinical information. Three LLMs were evaluated using independent single-turn API queries, followed by two repeat runs to assess reproducibility. Clinician-established DSM-5 diagnoses served as the reference standard. Performance was assessed using Top-1 and Top-3 accuracy, mean reciprocal rank, Cohen’s kappa, F1 scores, and sensitivity and specificity for detecting any psychiatric diagnosis. Models and conditions were compared with paired tests and generalized estimating equation models. Top-1 accuracy was lowest in the child-only condition (35.5–44.1% across models), increased to 65.9–69.1% with parent information, and was highest when physician-derived information was added (78.6–83.2%). Adding the child narrative to the parent narrative did not significantly improve accuracy (69.1–71.8%). Full-information Top-3 accuracy ranged from 88.2 to 91.8%. Model differences were significant only in the child-only condition. With parent narratives, sensitivity for any psychiatric diagnosis exceeded 93%, but specificity was 14.3–42.9%; physician-derived information increased specificity to 52.4–61.9%.
evidence_items.title: Large language model diagnostic performance across informant sources in child and adolescent psychiatry: a prospective multicenter study

evidence_items.summary: Rapid advances in large language models (LLMs) have enabled more flexible pedagogical interactions in intelligent tutoring systems. However, the reliability of generated content and its impact on actual learning outcomes remain contested. A central research question is how to integrate reliable knowledge with learner states to support tutoring decisions aligned with instructional objectives. Drawing on studies published between 2020 and 2026, this review examines advances in knowledge augmentation and learner modelling, analyses approaches to pedagogical strategy selection and feedback regulation, and assesses existing evidence of educational effectiveness. The literature indicates that retrieval-augmented generation and knowledge graphs can provide a knowledge basis for tutoring responses, while knowledge tracing and cognitive diagnosis help identify learners' knowledge states. Multi-turn planning and feedback mechanisms also provide greater control over instructional behaviour. Nevertheless, these capabilities have not yet been adequately validated in combination, and improvements in tutoring response quality do not necessarily translate into genuine learning gains. Empirical studies have reported substantially different learning outcomes, suggesting that instructional design and evaluation methods may influence judgements of educational effectiveness. Future research should strengthen the dynamic connections among supporting evidence, learner states, and pedagogical decisions. Independent assessments, knowledge transfer tasks, and longitudinal follow-up are also needed to verify learning outcomes and provide a more robust empirical basis for the design and application of LLM-based intelligent tutoring systems.
evidence_items.title: From Knowledge Augmentation to Pedagogical Decision-Making: A Review of Large Language Model-Based Intelligent Tutoring Systems

organizations: Department of Communication Sciences and Special Education, University of Georgia, Athens
evidence_items.summary: Purpose: The purpose of this project was to evaluate the accuracy and readability of ChatGPT's responses to questions related to common misconceptions about dyslexia. Method: Three content area experts independently rated the accuracy of ChatGPT's responses to five questions related to common misconceptions about dyslexia. Ratings were averaged across raters to derive an overall accuracy score for each response. ChatGPT's responses were also analyzed for length, reading time, reading ease, and reading level. Results: The overall accuracy of ChatGPT's responses was high. However, without additional prompting to adjust the length and/or reading level, ChatGPT's responses were written for advanced readers and took up to 2 min to read. Discussion: This study provides preliminary evidence that, at present, ChatGPT may be a useful tool for procuring scientifically valid information about dyslexia. Limitations and future directions are discussed.
evidence_items.title: Accuracy and Readability of Large Language Model–Powered Artificial Intelligence Chatbot Responses for Correcting Common Misconceptions About Dyslexia

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language model (LLM) systems deployed in production are subject to a form of degradation that classical software is not: their behavior can change without a corresponding code change, because the underlying model, its provider-side weights, or the prompt scaffolding around it can shift independently of the application's own release cycle. Traditional regression testing, built around deterministic assertions, is poorly suited to this setting, because LLM outputs are open-ended, stochastic, and evaluated along dimensions –– tone, faithfulness, safety, format compliance –– that resist exact-match comparison. This paper presents LLM Maintainer, an open-source tool that treats a second LLM call as a judge, scoring a fixed suite of "golden prompts" against natural-language rubrics on every run, persisting the results, and flagging statistically meaningful drops relative to a rolling per-test-case baseline. We describe the system's architecture –– a YAML-configured test suite, an execution runner, a structured LLM-as-judge module, a regression-detection algorithm, a SQLite persistence layer, and a Flask dashboard –– and its command-line and dashboard-triggered workflows for both ad hoc and scheduled (cron-style) use. Because this work was produced in a network-restricted sandbox without access to the live Anthropic API, we report a fully disclosed, seeded, synthetic case study rather than presenting simulated data as genuine field results: we ran the actual, unmodified runner, judge, regression-detection, and persistence code for 30 simulated daily evaluation cycles (180 evaluated prompt-response pairs) against a six-case suite modeling a retail-banking customer-support assistant, with three deliberately injected incidents –– a transient API failure, a silent quality regression introduced by a system-prompt refactor, and a one-off output-format violation.
evidence_items.title: LLM Maintainer: A Judge-in-the-Loop Framework for Continuous Quality Monitoring and Regression Detection in Deployed Large Language Model Systems

organizations: October University of Modern Sciences and Arts
evidence_items.summary: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used in career guidance, occupational recommendation, and candidate-job matching, yet these applications are often treated as interchangeable despite serving different stakeholders and creating distinct downstream risks. This structured methodological review examines how AI methods are evaluated across career matching and algorithmic trustworthiness. Two semantic searches identified 980 unique records, of which 181 studies published in 2020–2026 met the extraction criteria under screening. We purposively selected 19 primary studies for in-depth analysis. Although the field has grown rapidly (62.4% of candidate studies appeared in 2025–2026), the close-read studies show that model performance depends heavily on proxy labels and validation design. High offline performance (area under the curve (AUC) > 0.92) did not consistently translate into robust outcomes: performance degraded for job seekers with few recorded work experiences, a graph baseline reached an AUC of only 0.641, and multimodal interview scoring added negligible predictive gain over text (Spearman ρ = 0.46 vs 0.45) while visual features showed adverse impact (ratio: 0.52). The advantage of fair re-ranking narrowed as employers made more selections, and screeners conformed more often to incorrect recommendations from a bag-of-words model than from a neural model. These findings demonstrate the limitations of static offline metrics. We propose a four-level evaluation framework addressing representation validity, decision-stage stress-testing, human-AI interaction, and consequential impact. Because retrieval was incomplete and inclusion decisions were not independently re-adjudicated, this review assesses methodological practices rather than claiming an exhaustive census.
evidence_items.title: Artificial Intelligence in Career Guidance and Talent Matching: A Structured Methodological Review of Models, Labels and Trustworthy Evaluation

evidence_items.summary: Purpose: This study contrasts Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Human Intelligence (HI) in addressing sustainability issues that require a trade-off between technical efficiency, ethical judgement and contextual interpretation. Design/Methodology/Approach: This study uses triangular fuzzy numbers, fused Analytic Hierarchy Process (AHP)-entropy weights and fuzzy Technique for Order Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) to compare AI and HI across five sustainability-governance scenarios. Sensitivity analysis is applied to identify the technical-weight thresholds where AI or HI becomes more suitable. Findings: AI outperforms HI in structured, information-rich tasks such as renewable energy dispatch and circular waste logistics. HI outperforms AI in unstructured, context-rich, ethically dense tasks such as climate-smart agriculture and Environmental, Social and Governance (ESG)-oriented public procurement. The average closeness coefficient is 0.432 for AI and 0.568 for HI. Original/Value of the Paper: The study compares AI and HI optimisation modelling strategies for sustainability governance in a mathematically explicit, uncertainty-aware manner. It contributes to diverse areas of risk management research and provides a decision-making framework for industries seeking solutions to address sustainability governance challenges. Research Limitations/Implications: The study employs benchmark numerical scenarios rather than field observations; however, it provides a transparent comparative framework for future empirical testing. Practical Implications: Public institutions need to avoid one-size-fits-all automation and instead deploy AI where meaningful human oversight is provided. Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Sustainability Governance; Human Intelligence; Environmental, Social and Governance; Optimisation Modelling Strategies; Fuzzy TOPSIS Citation: Citation: Nijalingappa, Y., Almakki, M., Vasudevan, A. and Kumar, A.
evidence_items.title: A Comparative Numerical Study of Artificial Intelligence and Human Intelligence in Solving Sustainability Problems

evidence_items.summary: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and sustainable finance is transforming global financial ecosystems. Financial institutions increasingly use AI for ESG evaluation, fraud detection, climate-risk analytics, portfolio optimization, and digital lending. However, reliance on complex models raises concerns about transparency, interpretability, ethics, and regulatory compliance, as black-box systems limit accountability. This chapter examines the role of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in cloud-driven sustainable finance and proposes an interdisciplinary framework integrating XAI, ESG governance, and climate-risk analytics. It explores techniques such as SHAP, LIME, and interpretable models, along with applications in ESG scoring, green finance, and risk assessment. The study also highlights regulatory and ethical considerations and emphasizes explainability as essential for trustworthy and sustainable financial transformation.
evidence_items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Cloud-Driven Sustainable Financial Services

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly being adopted in education, yet its application to physics remains challenging because of the discipline’s reliance on mathematical, symbolic, and multimodal reasoning. This paper presents a PRISMA-based systematic mapping review of 146 studies published between January 2023 and June 2026 on the use of GenAI in physics education. The review examines the research landscape, approaches for supporting students and teachers, and methods for benchmarking and improving GenAI systems. The findings reveal rapid growth in research activity with widespread but uneven geographic distribution, with most studies focusing on higher education and relying heavily on third-party GenAI services. Student-support research primarily addresses conversational tutoring and personalized guidance, while teacher-support studies focus on lesson planning and teaching material development, professional development and teacher perceptions. A substantial body of work also benchmarks GenAI performance on physics-related tasks or proposes methods for improving it. Overall, the reviewed literature demonstrates considerable potential for GenAI in physics education while highlighting the need for further research on multilingual and inclusive systems, specialized educational uses, privacy-preserving approaches, improved multimodal support, and integration with complementary educational technologies.
evidence_items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Physics Education: A Systematic Mapping Review

evidence_items.summary: The article compares Ukraine’s macroeconomic adjustment speeds with a benchmark cluster of historical recovery episodes. Six circuits are examined using nonlinear distributed-lag equations with error correction and Bayesian estimation. Benchmark posteriors inform the Ukrainian estimates. The largest coefficient difference concerns services exports, while inflation, investment and trade show smaller deviations. GDP growth displays oscillatory convergence under the model’s adjustment interpretation. Weak fit limits the use of the exchange-rate equation. The contribution is a common empirical reference for interpreting national adjustment patterns. The comparison can inform recovery analysis, but does not establish the causes of coefficient differences or the effectiveness of specific policy instruments.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract High-resolution rotational spectroscopy offers a stringent, direct test of gas-phase carbohydrate geometries. Isotopologue data provide semiexperimental equilibrium (SE,reSE) structures for d-xylose α-pyranose and 2-deoxy-d-ribose β-pyranose, enabling heavy-atom comparisons with the pair-natural-orbital coupled-cluster method PL2. The benchmark is extended to a set of 34 conformers of d-xylose, 2-deoxy-d-ribose, and d-ribose through a hierarchy of equilibrium structures and vibrational corrections. For both SE structures, PL2 reproduces the heavy-atom geometry closely; for d-xylose, it also reproduces rotational constants within 0.1%. The topology-corrected TL1 level gives mean rotational-constant errors of 1.75, 3.77, and 2.23 MHz for the characterized d-xylose, 2-deoxy-d-ribose, and d-ribose conformers, respectively, with complete TL1 coverage.

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Blood culture contamination and inadequate fill volumes compromise the diagnosis of bloodstream infections. While dedicated phlebotomy teams improve these metrics, evidence regarding long-term sustainability is scarce. We evaluated the impact of a 24/7 dedicated phlebotomy team on blood culture quality using a 9-year longitudinal data set. In this retrospective cohort study at a 1,300-bed tertiary hospital, we analyzed 505,752 adult blood culture sets collected between 2015 and 2023. Following the transition to a dedicated phlebotomy team in March 2017 in all clinical units except the emergency room (ER), we evaluated the intervention’s effect using difference-in-differences (DID) analyses, with cultures collected by non-dedicated ER staff serving as a concurrent control. The dedicated team demonstrated a significantly lower contamination rate (0.22% [586/261,480]) than concurrent non-dedicated staff (0.80% [1,171/145,772]; P < 0.001), corresponding to a 56.6% reduction in the adjusted odds of contamination in the general wards (adjusted odds ratio = 0.43; P < 0.001). Mean fill volume per bottle was higher for the dedicated team (4.61 mL vs 2.16 mL; P < 0.001). Although the overall true positivity rate was lower for the dedicated team (6.24% vs 8.89%, P < 0.001), unit-stratified and DID analyses indicated a composition effect driven by higher baseline positivity in the ER, where non-dedicated staff predominantly operated. Within the same units, true positivity did not decrease after implementation. Trajectory analysis revealed that individual contamination rates stabilized after 13 months of continuous service. Sustained, negligible contamination rates and improved fill volumes are achievable through proficiency from dedicated training and long-term retention of specialized personnel. IMPORTANCE Contaminated blood cultures and poor sample volumes significantly compromise diagnostic accuracy, patient safety, and antimicrobial stewardship.
evidence_items.title: Sustained reduction of blood culture contamination with a dedicated phlebotomy team

evidence_items.summary: Purpose This study examines how the relationship between geopolitical risk (GPR) and green bond issuance (GBI) varies across the conditional issuance distribution and whether the pooled relationship is reproduced within Belt and Road Initiative (BRI)-related and benchmark economies. Design/methodology/approach Using annual panel data for 20 economies from 2014 to 2023, the study applies quantile regression to the pooled sample and the two subsamples. Additional analyses assess fixed effects, temporal ordering, potential endogeneity, data treatment and alternative GPR measurement. Findings GPR is positively associated with GBI in the pooled sample, with larger coefficients at upper quantiles. A comparable positive association is not statistically evident within either subsample. The pooled association remains evident with year fixed effects but weakens substantially with country fixed effects, indicating sensitivity to persistent country heterogeneity. The results therefore point to distributional heterogeneity and sensitivity to sample composition. Practical implications For BRI-related economies, lower-issuance settings require stronger market-entry conditions, including clearer standards, broader domestic investor participation and targeted credit enhancement. Higher-issuance settings should place greater emphasis on post-issuance disclosure and investor-base diversification. Originality/value This study extends existing aggregate evidence on the GPR–GBI relationship by distinguishing pooled distributional patterns from within-group evidence. It shows that a positive pooled association can coexist with statistically weak subgroup relationships, highlighting the importance of distributional and compositional heterogeneity in green bond issuance.
evidence_items.title: Geopolitical risk and green bond issuance: a distributional comparison of BRI-related and benchmark economies

evidence_items.summary: Benchmarks of robot navigation among pedestrians usually compare complete planners, so the design choice behind a difference is rarely identified. We present a seeded, paired simulation benchmark that varies the planning representation (sparse Voronoi roadmap, dense lattice, dense grid), a local reactive potential field (on or off), the robot’s knowledge (full, or from a 120° occluded sensor without a map) and pedestrian forecasting (from constant velocity to a trained long short-term memory and an oracle). Each operating point uses 100 paired seeds, analysed with multiplicity-adjusted paired tests and with failure-inclusive and time-to-collision metrics. The reactive field is the dominant lever: it raises minimum pedestrian clearance by 0.31–1.18 m for every representation and cuts the share of runs entering a 0.9-m contact zone from up to 69% to at most 4%; with it, the roadmap and lattice differ by at most 0.06 m. Forecasting and map completeness matter little: forecasts add about 0.1 m at most, perfect forecasts from an oracle perform like constant velocity, a full static map changes nothing, and omniscient pedestrian tracking adds 0.09–0.18 m. Reliability differences between representations vanish once the roadmap is queried correctly; we document this and three further artefacts – planner-coupled random streams, an unstated robot-to-pedestrian speed ratio and non-inflated obstacles in external planner ports – that can manufacture effects of the size typically reported. The orderings survive sensor noise, social-force and ORCA crowds, an indoor scene family and multiple robots, but weaken when the robot moves no faster than pedestrians under unicycle limits.
evidence_items.title: Disentangling reactive control, representation, map knowledge and prediction in robot navigation among pedestrians: A controlled simulation benchmark

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The chemical properties of superheavy elements (SHE, Z ≥ 104) remain poorly understood. Due to the dramatic increase in relativistic effects, the behavior of SHE is expected to deviate from the trends established by their lighter homologues within the periodic table. In this work, the novel A/q identification technique using the FIONA spectrometer, developed at the Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory’s 88-Inch Cyclotron facility, was used to study radioactive isotopes of Yb (Z = 70), Hf (Z = 72), and Ta (Z = 73). These isotopes, produced one atom at a time in nuclear reactions, serve as representatives for elements that can populate the +3, +4, and +5 oxidation states, respectively. The oxidation states were investigated through the production and identification of MFn+ species using the fluorinating gas C3F6. Each element produced MFn+ species consistent with their established oxidation states, aligning with previous, similar measurements of stable isotope counterparts. Simulations were performed to support peak assignments according to position and α decay energy. The results demonstrate that FIONA is an effective tool for the synthesis and identification of radioactive molecules to study metals in various oxidation states. This investigation establishes a framework to investigate the preferred oxidation states of SHEs which have never been directly measured before.

evidence_items.summary: Enterprise security programs are built on the assumption that defended systems stay fixed between periodic reviews. Autonomous AI agents break that assumption because they decide at runtime which tools, peers, and data to access, and so redraw their own attack surface. Existing maturity instruments, including the Capability Maturity Model, COBIT-based assessment, and the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, were built to grade human-run practices that change slowly. Newer agent-specific governance models treat adaptive control as the top of a single scale rather than as an independently scored dimension. Two documented incidents, an external agent that reportedly reached McKinsey’s production database within about two hours, and a zero-click Microsoft 365 Copilot flaw that enabled data exfiltration through a single email, show that periodic assessment cannot keep pace with a system that redraws its own scope in the moment. This paper proposes a four-dimension, five-level maturity model comprising Visibility, Containment, Accountability, and Adaptability, each anchored to an observable test rather than a self-reported survey response. Applied to a composite financial advisory firm, the model scores each dimension independently rather than averaging them, surfacing an imbalance (strong detection, weak prevention) that a composite score would conceal, and yielding a prioritized remediation order that supports business sustainability. The framework is presented as a structured self-assessment instrument, with a defined pathway for expert review, inter-rater testing, and pilot evaluation. The model has not yet been validated against real organizations, and its Adaptability dimension remains constrained by the current state of governance tooling.
evidence_items.title: The Expanding Perimeter: A Maturity Model for Agentic AI Attack Surfaces

evidence_items.summary: Purpose: This study examined the governance gap that opens when autonomous agents acquire, use, and propagate credentials dynamically, and proposed a reference framework, the Agentic Secrets Governance Framework (ASGF), to narrow it. Methodology: The framework couples a SPIFFE and SPIRE based attestation layer with an Open Policy Agent decision point, a dynamic secrets broker that issues short lived, task scoped credentials, and a compliance control library that expresses obligations drawn from the HIPAA Security Rule, PCI DSS 4.0.1, the EU Digital Operational Resilience Act, the NIST AI Risk Management Framework, and ISO/IEC 42001 as machine evaluable Rego policies. A reference implementation was built and evaluated in a controlled three node Kubernetes testbed. Two workflows, healthcare eligibility determination and card payment fraud triage, were selected by purposive sampling, and ten thousand simulated requests were replayed per configuration. Findings: Policy enforced, ephemeral credential issuance reduced the configured credential exposure window from months to minutes while adding a combined median of 34.3 milliseconds to the request path. In conformance testing, the policy layer denied the out of scope identity abuse and credential replay cases it was designed to deny, but, as expected, it did not stop goal hijack attacks that stayed within an agent's nominal scope. Unique Contribution to Theory, Practice and Policy: The study frames secrets governance for agents as a joint security and compliance decision made at the moment of credential issuance. It gives practitioners a reusable control library pattern and issuance protocol, and it suggests that regulators could reduce interpretive risk by publishing machine evaluable reference controls alongside regulatory text. Residual risks from semantic intent verification and cross agent delegation are discussed.
evidence_items.title: Policy-as-Code and Compliance Automation for Secrets Governance in Agentic AI Workloads in Regulated Industries

evidence_items.summary: Background Clinical agentic artificial intelligence (AI) can alter its actions during a clinical task, creating failure pathways that conventional performance metrics may not capture. Whether safeguards interrupt these pathways remains uncertain. Aim To map safeguard effects, residual failures, human recovery, and resource consequences in clinical agentic and related AI workflows. Methods We searched PubMed/MEDLINE, Embase, Scopus, Web of Science Core Collection, and IEEE Xplore, for English-language, peer-reviewed empirical journal reports. This scoping review used independent screening, duplicate extraction, narrative synthesis, and result-specific critical appraisal. Results The 111 reports comprised 56 functionally agentic, 29 related non-agentic, 22 architecture-uncertain, and four human-factors reports; 38 of the 56 agentic reports explicitly documented model-directed subsequent-action selection. Among the 111 selected appraisal results, none both isolated a specified safeguard’s effect and demonstrated reduced measured patient harm. Configurations incorporating safeguards improved selected outcomes, but gains coexisted with omissions, reduced sensitivity, false reassurance, delay, or transferred review burden. Concurrent changes in models, prompts, evidence access, and workflow frequently prevented attribution to individual controls. Some patient-randomised trials reported patient or process benefits, but evaluated bundled interventions rather than the contribution of a safeguard. Human authority was more often documented than successful error detection and recovery; requiring clinician approval did not establish that residual errors were recognised and corrected. Performance varied across models, settings, and information conditions, limiting transfer of favourable findings. Reported efficiency gains depended on measurement boundaries and did not consistently account for review, correction, escalation, and downstream work.
evidence_items.title: Safeguards, residual failures, and human oversight in clinical agentic and related artificial intelligence workflows: a systematic scoping review

evidence_items.summary: (c) 2026 Pranay Mahendrakar. Licensed under CC BY 4.0. Life of Research Since 2024 a growing literature has argued that general-purpose vision-language models can work out where a photograph was taken well enough to make image geolocation an immediate privacy risk, and a second literature has begun building defences against it. In this analysis the author reviews and synthesises published results to show that the direction of that claim survives the evidence but its usual support does not: the accuracies quoted for it are properties of particular photo sets, adversaries and distance thresholds, and none of them is the quantity a privacy claim is about. The same model places 61 percent of a curated, text-rich stock-photo set within one kilometre, about 23 percent of a public Flickr benchmark, and fewer than 12 percent of sampled street-level images within one hundred kilometres. One video-frame benchmark reports 65.6 percent within a kilometre for clips from one platform and 6.4 percent for clips from another. The obvious deflation, that benchmark images were seen in training, does not explain the capability: on photographs collected by the authors and not drawn from any public source, frontier models still name the city about 60 percent of the time, and freshly taken photographs of Seoul are located about as well as Street View images of the same city. The author separates five variables that published results leave unfixed (image population, harm radius, adversary configuration, counterfactual baseline, and the unit of exposure), shows that defences are mostly scored against a fixed adversary although a published photograph must resist every later one, and proposes an exposure protocol that states each variable before a number is reported.
evidence_items.title: A Benchmark Hit Is Not an Exposure: What Published Vision-Language Geolocation Accuracy Says About Location Privacy, Why One Model Locates 61 Percent of One Photo Set to a Kilometre and Fewer Than 12 Percent of Another to a Hundred, and the Exposure Estimand a Privacy Claim Needs

evidence_items.summary: Agentic cyber-physical systems rely on perception and state estimation to support autonomous decisions. Degraded, inconsistent, or manipulated sensor observations can therefore propagate through an autonomous pipeline and create security-relevant failures. This work presents a synthetic Counter-Unmanned Aircraft System (C-UAS) testbed developed in NVIDIA Isaac Sim for repeatable stress testing of perception and tracking algorithms supporting agentic decision-making. A simplified quadrotor follows scripted trajectories while co-located virtual sensors generate synchronized RGB, RTX LiDAR, and illustrative IR-like observations. The testbed varies target range, motion, clutter, occlusion, and sensor availability, with future stress cases including sensor dropout, temporal misalignment, cross-modal disagreement, and false observations. As an initial exemplar, a nonlinear coordinated-turn Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) is evaluated over a 20-s maneuvering trajectory using LiDAR target-centroid measurements. Position error and uncertainty are compared as LiDAR observations degrade and are lost. The framework provides a reproducible environment for studying how sensing degradation affects downstream autonomous estimation and resilience in agentic C-UAS systems.
evidence_items.title: A Synthetic Multi-Modal Testbed for Security Stress Testing of Agentic Counter-UAS Systems

evidence_items.summary: Facial deepfake detectors are usually trained on blending fakes, where a generated face is pasted back into a real frame. Recent generators synthesize the entire face and leave no traces of blending. On a benchmark of 19 datasets released from 2019 to 2026, the best prior facial deepfake detector reaches a mean AUROC of 96.2% on ten blending datasets, but none exceeds 78.1% on five datasets of entire face synthesis (EFS). AI-generated content (AIGC) detectors do not close this gap. We propose TwinD, a detector trained on FaceForensics++ fakes and two kinds of twins: fakes made from a real frame. A reconstruction twin is a real frame reconstructed by an autoencoder, with the real pixels put back in a random region. It targets the neural traces of a decoder. A blob twin blends an altered copy of a real frame with the frame itself, targeting blending artifacts. It needs no generator and no face-shaped mask. Together, these twins provide two complementary forensic cues that generalize to unseen manipulations. TwinDreaches a mean AUROC of 96.3%, 8.9 points above the prior state-of-the-art, with 98.1% on the blending datasets and 95.6% on the EFS datasets. Trained on twins alone, without a deepfake dataset, single models still reach 94.3% on average over three seeds. For reproducibility, the code, trained model, and training data are at: https://github.com/yermandy/TwinD
evidence_items.title: TwinD: Generalizing Deepfake Detection from Blending to Entire Face Synthesis

evidence_items.summary: As multimodal large language models (MLLMs) become increasingly integrated into everyday life, their ability to provide safe and reliable assistance in realistic daily activities remains insufficiently explored. Existing safety benchmarks primarily focus on isolated harmful requests or adversarial scenarios, overlooking the safety risks that may arise as ordinary tasks unfold. In practice, users pursue legitimate goals through multi-turn, multimodal interactions, where seemingly benign requests may become safety-critical when considered alongside earlier actions and visual observations. This calls for Dynamic Safety Awareness, the ability to track evolving task conditions, recognize implicit contextual risks, and provide safe and helpful assistance. To systematically evaluate this capability, we introduce DailySafe, a benchmark comprising 195 naturalistic multi-turn, multi-image interactions across 10 everyday domains and 42 task categories. Grounded in authentic user dialogue topics and documented safety knowledge, DailySafe captures realistic scenarios where safety-critical evidence is progressively revealed across conversational turns and visual observations. Using case-specific safety annotations, DailySafe assesses whether MLLMs can recognize and appropriately address evolving risks while supporting users' legitimate goals, bringing multimodal safety evaluation closer to real-world everyday AI assistance. DailySafe is publicly available at: https://github.com/XuankunRong/DailySafe.
evidence_items.title: DailySafe: Benchmarking Dynamic Safety Awareness in Everyday Multi-Turn Multimodal Interactions

evidence_items.summary: Public brain tumour MRI collections are routinely reported with near-perfect classification accuracy, yet they carry no patient identifiers and their train/test overlap is rarely quantified. We present a duplicate-aware, reproducible frozen-feature benchmark on BRISC 2025 (6000 contrast-enhanced T1-weighted slices; glioma, meningioma, pituitary tumour, no tumour). A perceptual-hash audit found 1352 candidate near-duplicate pairs, with 439 of them crossing the official train/test split, and 104 training images that are pixel-identical to test images; a visual review of sampled pairs showed that most candidates were other slices of the same scan, with an estimated 5–10% false matches. Removing redundant copies and every training image connected to the test set left 5477 images, a split that is duplicate-aware but not patient-independent. Under an identical linear probe, ImageNet-supervised ResNet-18/50 and self-supervised DINOv2 ViT-S/14 were competitive: DINOv2 was numerically ahead (macro-F1 77.3 ± 0.1%, macro-AUROC 93.2%), but no pairwise difference survived Holm correction. In-pool validation overstated official test macro-F1 by 9.7–13.5 points; control experiments showed that this gap is not an artefact of the filtering but mainly reflects a distribution difference between the official partitions. Meningioma recall stayed at 50–53%, and all linear heads were under-confident. We release the splits, audit tables and per-image predictions.
evidence_items.title: Validation Is Not Enough: A Duplicate-Aware, Reproducible Frozen-Feature Benchmark for Brain Tumour MRI Classification on BRISC 2025

evidence_items.summary: Current audio-driven video diffusion models can synthesize realistic talking-head videos but generally require dozens of diffusion denoising steps over multi-second video chunks, making them unsuitable for streaming applications such as voice assistants and virtual avatars, where low-latency and online causal generation are required properties. AURA generates video chunk by chunk with a rolling KV cache, requiring only the audio of the current chunk to start generating, rather than a multi-second audio look-ahead like bidirectional models. It comes in two sizes: AURA 1.3B streams 576p video in real time on a single GPU (20.7 fps for a 16 Hz playback rate), making it suited to interactive avatar applications, and AURA 5B streams 720p video at 9.7 fps. Our two-stage distillation pipeline first aligns the causal student with the teacher, by training it to match the teacher's trajectories with fewer diffusion steps and a chunk-wise sliding window causal attention mask, then applies Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD) with backward simulation to close the remaining quality gap. On standard talking-head benchmarks, AURA 1.3B runs 23x faster than its own bidirectional teacher and reaches a quality comparable to TalkVerse at a lower resolution, and AURA 5B matches its TalkVerse teacher at 720p while running 17x faster. To support reproducibility and further research on streaming avatar generation, we release the weights of both models along with a dataset of 30K synthetic videos and their precomputed teacher trajectories.
evidence_items.title: AURA: AUdio-dRiven streaming Avatar

evidence_items.summary: It has been demonstrated that, in certain settings, large language models can perform weight-space programming to directly modify the weights of neural networks. However, it is unknown how dedicated training of these networks can contribute to the successes of weight-space programming. We present a benchmark of LLM-driven weight-space programming on vision models, in which five LLMs edit convolutional networks and vision transformers on relabeling and error-correction tasks on Waterbirds, CIFAR-100, PACS and Entity-30. We report more than 2,600 such edit processes, whereby each edit is scored on held-out images for success, side effects and accuracy loss. We compare standard training with label smoothing, gradient-based editable training, and our Edit-Ready Training (ERT), a novel method that rehearses the direct, closed-form weight edits LLMs perform. We show that preparing networks for editing raises the success of LLM edits substantially where standard networks are hard to edit. ERT further achieves the highest mean score for GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 across all evaluated baselines. We will release our LLM testing framework alongside all tasks, editing trajectories and scores. Project page: https://viscom.uni-ulm.de/wsp
evidence_items.title: Training Vision Models for LLM-Driven Weight-Space Programming

evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used as judges and graders to replace human annotators, raising the question of when such replacement is statistically justified. To support such decisions, the Alternative Annotator Test (Alt-Test) was introduced for dense settings where all items are annotated by the same annotators. However, in many large-scale annotation settings, items are annotated by different subsets of annotators. We therefore propose the Alternative Annotator Test with Resampled Annotations (AltRA-Test), a statistical test that does not require that all items are annotated by the same annotators. AltRA-Test uses a bootstrap that resamples items, draws k human annotations for each item, and substitutes one of them with an LLM annotation. This produces paired all-human and mixed human-LLM panels. A replacement is supported when the inter-annotator agreement (IAA) of the mixed panel is statistically non-inferior to the IAA of the all-human panel, i.e., when the LLM preserves the signal that the human annotators share. We establish that AltRA-Test is a consistent test of asymptotic level alpha. We then evaluate it through simulations and real-world experiments in which we test 18 LLMs and 5 prompting techniques on 20 datasets across text, image, audio, and video. Across these evaluations, about 100 items often suffice for the test. In simulations, where we know whether the LLM is a better or a worse annotator than the humans, AltRA-Test makes more correct replacement decisions than existing baselines. In real-world data experiments, LLMs pass the test in about half of the setups, depending mainly on the task. Since replacement is not always justified, we encourage researchers to test it for their task.
evidence_items.title: AltRA-Test: An Alternative Annotator Test for LLM Judges Without Shared Annotators

evidence_items.summary: Supervised fine-tuning (SFT) is the stage in which Video Large Language Models (VideoLLMs) advance their capability to reason over video. However, the VideoLLM also learns to answer from textual regularities of its training data, a shortcut that bypasses the video. The regularities behind the shortcut are hard to define at the data level, and the shortcut forms regardless of training epoch, data size, or backbone. The shortcut is hidden behind a rise in accuracy within the training distribution, yet it is not required for the rise and even costs SFT the gain the video offers under distribution shift. We therefore propose Video-Evidence Training via Orthogonal projection (VETO), which intervenes on the fine-tuning update where the shortcut is written rather than on the data. VETO calibrates the subspace that the text alone occupies in the activations of the base model and projects the update onto its orthogonal complement. The VideoLLM is thus left to ground its answer in the full input, with the shortcut suppressed as it forms and never defined. Across seven VideoLLMs, VETO preserves the gain of SFT on the training distribution and suppresses the shortcut. On six benchmarks under shift it gains more than SFT and answers from the full input rather than the shortcut. Code is available at https://github.com/Youngwoo-git/VETO.
evidence_items.title: Suppressing the Shortcut Hidden Behind the Gains of VideoLLM Fine-Tuning

evidence_items.summary: Recent AI agents can generate playable games, but these games are not necessarily engaging. Mastery is a key source of engagement, yet designing for it requires extensive human play and tuning. We propose PlayCraft, an automated framework that uses a vision-based agent to play games and draws on its detailed play experience to revise them for mastery. Starting from an initial game, PlayCraft alternates between playing and crafting. In the playing stage, a player agent watches the game screen, uses the controls, and pursues the game objective over repeated episodes while retaining memory. After each episode, it reports its progress, outcomes, decisions, and reflections. In the crafting stage, a crafter agent uses these reports to revise the game. It estimates player abilities, predicts performance at different proficiency levels, and compares those predictions with a target learning progression. It diagnoses the game and addresses the gaps by giving players meaningful opportunities to improve through better decisions and execution. We evaluate games in fresh runs with player agents across three intelligence settings, measuring learning gain and learning slope. Compared with the initial games, PlayCraft yields larger learning gains and steeper learning slopes in most games. It also outperforms the baselines on the macro-average of each metric at every intelligence setting.
evidence_items.title: PlayCraft: Designing Engaging Games from Agent Play Experience

evidence_items.summary: Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.
evidence_items.title: EgoCaptioner: Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning

evidence_items.summary: Code2Video uses agent-authored 3D proxies to guide video generation, enabling explicit control over structure and dynamics. However, how to construct proxies and prompts for optimal downstream quality remains underexplored, as do the capabilities and limitations of this paradigm. Through controlled experiments and blinded human evaluation, we study proxy granularity, physics simulation, and prompting. The results reveal task-dependent trade-offs: coarse proxies favor natural motion, while medium-grained proxies favor consistency. Physics simulation and proxy-aligned prompting further improve average quality. Guided by these findings, we introduce Coda-DaVinci, a task-adaptive agentic framework for Code2Video generation that selects between proxy-guided and direct generation, adapts modeling granularity to each entity, and coordinates simulation with proxy-grounded prompting. Its multi-agent harness preserves scene assets and guides repairs through visual inspection and independent review. Experiments demonstrate leading instruction following on VTR and scene consistency on R2M, improved physical plausibility over direct generation, and higher visual realism than the compared Code2Video baselines. Long-video evaluations further show gains in event structure and consistency across successive interactions, while revealing limitations in transition stability and adherence to scene settings.
evidence_items.title: Coda-DaVinci: Reimagining Video Generation with Code2Video

evidence_items.summary: Dense metric mapping from a single camera and IMU remains challenging: visual-inertial odometry (VIO) provides metric motion but sparse geometry, whereas feed-forward depth models predict dense structure without ensuring metric scale. We present Accord, which constructs an accurate online dense metric map from any camera with an IMU. A VIO filter publishes metric poses, a depth foundation model conditioned on them predicts depth for short keyframe windows, and a factor graph fuses the resulting submaps. Recent work has explored several approaches to this problem. What is essential is the multi-view agreement (Accord), which is considered in SLAM as a source of geometric self-consistency. Accord anchors each keyframe window to metric 3D points triangulated from the filter poses, then exploits bidirectional dense depth agreement between co-visible images to estimate and correct per-image scale errors while preserving the metric scale established by the anchors. Context keyframes further improve depth prediction, and the resulting submaps are fused in a factor graph. We evaluate a single mapping configuration across five public camera-IMU setups and a new Phone-rig/GoPro dataset. With nothing tuned per dataset/setup and every map aligned only by Accord's own trajectory, Accord achieves consistently best/second-best mean F-score at 5 cm on every platform. Accord is open-source along with the phone-rig dataset for the benefit of the research community
evidence_items.title: Accord: Universal Online Metric Localization and Dense Mapping from one Camera and an IMU

evidence_items.summary: Recent work on human-scene interaction (HSI) generation moves from single interactions to long-horizon interaction, where a language-model agent plans and executes a sequence of interactions in a 3D scene under one instruction. However, existing agents struggle in challenging everyday scenarios (e.g., picking up a toy and throwing it into a basket) because they lack spatial control over the motion and quantitative feedback on its execution, and they often fail to complete the interaction sequence. To address these gaps, we present Inhabitant, a training-free agent framework in which the agent specifies each motion through positions, paths and poses, measures how the executed interaction deviates from its intent, and revises the control specification accordingly. For an extensive evaluation in such scenarios, we build Inhabit, a benchmark of 75 household tasks in 31 furniture layouts of an apartment, in which every task chains one to three goals on movable objects and is carried out by the whole body, excluding fingers. On Inhabit, Inhabitant completes 98.7\% of the tasks with Claude Opus 5.5, and 93.3\% and 82.7\% with Claude Sonnet 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon, respectively. Ablations confirm that without spatial control the agent fails most tasks, and without quantitative feedback its motion becomes less precise. Code is available on the project page.
evidence_items.title: Inhabitant: An Agent Framework for Long-Horizon Human-Scene Interaction with Spatial Control and Quantitative Feedback

evidence_items.summary: 3D Gaussian Splatting enables object-level operations on Gaussian primitives, yet existing segmentation methods are largely trained and evaluated through rendered views. This mismatch can produce accurate rendered masks from incomplete 3D selections since alpha-blended feature supervision concentrates learning on dominant contributors while leaving occluded or low-contribution Gaussians weakly supervised. We propose VODA, a plug-and-play supervision objective that exploits local depth structure to group per-pixel contributors and directly supervises all Gaussians in selected depth clusters, bypassing contribution-weighted gradient delivery. To evaluate volumetric completeness, we introduce Removal-3D, a synthetic object-removal benchmark, and the Removal Depth Error (RDE), a metric comparing predicted and ground-truth depth changes. Across four rendering-based baselines, VODA consistently improves volumetric segmentation on Removal-3D while maintaining or improving performance on LERF and ScanNet. Further analysis shows that VODA recovers lower-contribution Gaussians, while simple gradient reweighting and spatial propagation fail to reproduce comparable gains.
evidence_items.title: The Mask Is Not the Object: Volumetric Supervision for 3D Gaussian Segmentation

evidence_items.summary: Recent advances in video generation call for reliable detection grounded in explicit forensic evidence. However, current methods primarily depend on single-pass chain-of-thought reasoning that overlooks brief or localized artifacts, or on predefined multi-agent workflows that offer limited flexibility in selecting relevant inspections. Even with adaptive investigation, optimizing the investigation policy alone does not directly improve the forensic capabilities of fixed experts. We introduce WeVisForensics, an agentic framework in which a main investigator agent coordinates a self-evolving library of forensic inspector sub-agents spanning visual and audio cues. The investigator learns which artifact type to examine, over which window, and when to conclude, and these interactions provide shared feedback for both levels of agents. Our dual-timescale policy optimization strategy, DTPO, closes this loop through fast reinforcement learning of the investigator and slower refinement of the inspectors, guided by annotated artifact intervals, to report subtle artifacts they once dismissed. Furthermore, we curate ForenCue-30K, combining role-specific forensic annotations and interaction trajectories to supervise individual inspections and their coordination, with an accompanying reinforcement-learning pool. Experiments show that WeVisForensics averages 95.2% detection accuracy across in-domain, out-of-domain and agentic benchmarks, 9.0% above the strongest prior detector, while grounding its verdicts in localized evidence.
evidence_items.title: WeVisForensics: Self-Evolving Agent for Omni AI-Generated Video Detection

evidence_items.summary: Decision-making in humans and AI involves multiple cognitive abilities. System One decision models produce fast, structured choices. Their cognitive strengths and limitations, however, remain poorly understood. We introduce S1CogBench, a benchmark of 24 established cognitive tasks and 27 evaluation modes, evaluating seven open models and the API model Jev. It combines human-response prediction, autonomous execution, and controlled task manipulations to reveal strengths and failures that aggregate scores miss. We find distinct behavioral profiles across the evaluated models. In these models, strong performance on some learning tasks coexists with failures to gather information or adapt to feedback, while high accuracy does not guarantee human-like responses to changing task demands. Shared readout controls show that model rankings depend partly on how choices are extracted. Separate latency comparisons with generative language models show that long responses are much slower than direct decisions, whereas matched one-token generation adds little overhead. To our knowledge, S1CogBench is the first benchmark of System One decision models on established cognitive experiments. It provides a common empirical basis for identifying their capabilities and limitations before integrating them into automated decision systems.
evidence_items.title: S1CogBench: What System One Decision Models Can and Cannot Do on Cognitive Experiments

evidence_items.summary: ABSTRACT Increasingly sophisticated customer needs and regulatory constraints lead to growing complexity in product development. A common solution to manage this complexity is Model‐based Systems Engineering, where activity diagrams contribute to the design of functional architectures. However, their modeling process is time‐consuming and complex, creating the demand for assistance and acceleration. Current methods are limited to basic activity diagrams and overlook architecture definition activities. Moreover, new possibilities through Large Language Models haven't been explored in detail. To address this, a comprehensive three‐part approach using Large Language Models is proposed. The first part defines the use case's behavior with an activity diagram. The second part assigns actions to system functions, starting functional architecture generation. The third part deploys a pipeline to define information exchange between actions across architectural elements. Latter two pipelines use vector databases to reuse existing modeling elements. An preliminary evaluation by expert interviews shows that the proposed approach can offer assistance for manual modeling activities. With that, a step towards a faster and more complete generation of activity diagrams and functional architectures is taken.
evidence_items.title: Leveraging Large Language Models to Model Use Case Behaviors Via Activity Diagrams

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Background Large language model (LLM)–powered virtual patient systems are gaining popularity in nursing education but also face persistent challenges, such as hallucinations and role inconsistency. Objective This paper reports the model architecture design, technical considerations, implementation challenges, and evaluation of an LLM-powered AI-assisted simulated-patient system integrated into a nursing triage simulation game. Methods The system integrated a Unity-based game client, with GPT-4o hosted through Microsoft AI Foundry to support real-time simulated-patient dialogue in Traditional Chinese using Cantonese syntax. This developmental study comprised exploratory model selection, formative student feedback–informed enhancement from Version 1 to Version 2, development-stage script-fidelity evaluation, and evaluation of system usability and the Net Promoter Score in 2 tutorial cohorts of nursing students. Results Key technical contributions include a layered hallucination mitigation architecture that combines grounded prompt inclusion, few-shot conversational exemplars, negative role constraints, and calibrated model parameters. In the predefined script-fidelity evaluation, script-inconsistent responses occurred in 78 of 125 (62.4%) Version 1 outputs and 21 of 125 (16.8%) Version 2 outputs—an absolute difference of 45.6 percentage points. The implementation process also addresses stateless API memory management, cloud-based safety filter calibration for domain-specific clinical prompts, and prompt engineering strategies to prevent role drift and hidden scenario information leakage. GPT-4o was selected as the production model through exploratory development testing that considered script consistency, Cantonese-language suitability, response latency, technical reliability, deployment feasibility, cost considerations, and Unity integration compatibility; 45 of 50 (90%) assessed GPT-4o responses were rated fully script-consistent.
evidence_items.title: Large Language Model–Powered AI-Assisted Simulated Patient for Nursing Education: Quasi-Experimental Study

organizations: HUN-REN PE Complex Systems Monitoring Research Group, University of Pannonia, Egyetem u. 10, 8200 Veszprém, Hungary
evidence_items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to answer questions about predictive models, but a fluent answer about a model is not necessarily true of it. We propose a framework in which every answer is checked against a reference that independent software computes from the fitted model. The main finding is simple: the LLM was much more accurate when software had done the calculations than when it had to work them out from the model itself. In a confirmatory study with Gemini 2.5 Flash, the LLM correctly answered 16 of 36 questions whose answer follows exactly from the full model description, such as a prediction or a decision path, but 33 of the same 36 once software had computed the values from which the answer follows. A replication with 50 classifiers, five datasets and three LLM configurations, including a reasoning setting and an open-weight model, reproduced this pattern. Without model information, the LLMs declined to answer or guessed at chance level, and verified answers were reported faithfully once their origin was stated. Model-specific calculations should therefore be left to verified software, while the LLM reports and explains the checked results.
evidence_items.title: From Data to Verified Model Knowledge: How Evidence Access Shapes Large Language Model Answers About Trained Machine-Learning Classifiers

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to evaluate other models’ outputs in medicine, an approach known as LLM-as-a-Judge (LaaJ), yet no LaaJ-specific reporting checklist exists. This scoping review included 91 medical LaaJ studies: 69 from 5,571 database records and 22 from a previous review. Judges were mainly used for response evaluation (74.7%), and 76.9% of the studies used at least one proprietary LLM. Agreement with human evaluators was reported in 65.9% of the studies, with widely varying metrics. Based on these findings, this study developed RULE-LLM, a reporting framework of 21 items and eight sub-items across four domains: role and task specification, underlying data and criteria, LLM-Judge design and output, and evaluation of judge performance. Seven experts rated the initial draft (S-CVI/Ave, 0.94), and five independent raters showed substantial agreement when applying the final framework (Fleiss' κ, 0.67; Gwet's AC1, 0.73). RULE-LLM aims to improve the transparency and reproducibility of LaaJ studies.
evidence_items.title: RULE-LLM reporting framework for large language model-as-a-judge evaluation in medicine developed from a scoping review

evidence_items.summary: BACKGROUND AND OBJECTIVES: Accurate prediction of functional outcomes after acute ischemic stroke can guide clinical decision-making and resource allocation. Prior work has relied predominantly on structured predictors and conventional machine learning, while the ability of large language models (LLMs) to infer modified Rankin Scale (mRS) scores from routine clinical admission notes is largely unexplored. METHODS: We evaluated encoder (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers [BERT], NYUTron) and generative (Llama-3.1-8B, MedGemma-4B) LLMs, in both frozen and fine-tuned settings, for discharge and 90-day mRS prediction. ModernBERT-base was evaluated as a long-context encoder sensitivity analysis. We retrospectively analyzed 9485 admission history and physical notes for discharge prediction and 1898 notes for 90-day prediction from the NYU Langone Get With The Guidelines–Stroke registry (2016-2025). The most recent 12 months were held out for testing. Performance was assessed for binary functional outcome (mRS 0-2 vs 3-6) and compared with structured, hybrid, and clinical risk score baselines. RESULTS: In frozen settings, the clinically pretrained NYUTron encoder outperformed all other models. After fine-tuning, Llama achieved the highest discrimination for discharge (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.84, area under the precision–recall curve 0.81) and 90-day (AUROC 0.87, area under the precision–recall curve 0.84) prediction, while binary accuracy was similar among NYUTron, Llama, and MedGemma. A long-context ModernBERT-base sensitivity analysis did not outperform NYUTron or eliminate differences in exact mRS prediction. For 90-day prediction, fine-tuned Llama outperformed structured (Zhang et al, AUROC 0.82), hybrid (Sung et al, AUROC 0.82), and clinical risk score (Totaled Health Risks in Vascular Events, AUROC 0.80; Stroke Prognostication using Age and NIH Stroke Scale, AUROC 0.79) baselines (all P < .05).
evidence_items.title: Large Language Models Predict Functional Outcomes After Acute Ischemic Stroke
