evidence_items.summary: Abstract Immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis (ICI-M) is a rare but often fatal immune-related adverse event. Large language models (LLMs) have provided new opportunities for patient education, yet whether they can effectively support patient education in ICI-M remains unknown. In this study, we submitted 20 standardized ICI-M-related patient questions to five LLMs (ChatGPT-5.5, Gemini-3.5 Flash, DeepSeek-V4, Qwen 3.7, and Doubao), generating 100 responses. Model performance was evaluated using the Global Quality Score (GQS), modified DISCERN (mDISCERN), Quality Analysis of Medical Artificial Intelligence (QAMAI), Ensuring Quality Information for Patients (EQIP), Patient Education Materials Assessment Tool understandability and actionability scores (PEMAT-U and PEMAT-A), and six readability indices. Significant inter-model differences were observed across most quality and readability metrics, and no single model outperformed the others across all dimensions. DeepSeek-V4 achieved the highest mDISCERN score [5.00 (IQR, 4.00–5.00)], whereas ChatGPT-5.5 achieved the highest PEMAT-A score [40.00 (IQR, 35.00–45.00)]. Readability was suboptimal, with a mean FKGL of 16.60 ± 2.64. Correlation analyses demonstrated information quality, usability, and readability represented correlated but distinct evaluation dimensions. While LLMs may serve as adjunctive tools for ICI-M patient education, substantial optimization of content accessibility and actionability is required prior to clinical implementation.
evidence_items.title: Quality, reliability, and readability of large language model responses to questions about immune checkpoint inhibitor-associated myocarditis: A cross-sectional study

evidence_items.summary: Introduction: What people with kidney concerns or disease and their families struggle with between visits may not surface in clinic. We mapped the needs and burdens they express online by clinical context and author. Methods: A large language model read all 22,170 posts reached by a chronic kidney disease tag or kidney lexicon on a Taiwanese forum and 3 ask-a-physician services (1995-2026), applying a companion friction framework with kidney-specific fields, author (patient or family) and clinical context. A second vendor re-read 11,010 posts; 2 physicians labelled relevance, author and context in 200. Results: Among 6,023 kidney-related posts, the reproducibly measured fields most often voiced on the forum were information needs (79%), emotional burden (48%), system navigation (34%) and worry about progression (24%). After abnormal tests, 54%-56% of posts quoted a laboratory value, nearly always with a question or stated uncertainty; renal-diet burden peaked with diagnosed disease; caregiver burden rose to 29% of dialysis-or-transplantation forum posts. Family-written posts more often voiced navigation difficulty and caregiver burden. Most fields agreed with the second vendor (kappa 0.65-0.98). On the model's labels, family members wrote 25% of forum posts about kidney concerns and 74% about dialysis or transplantation; on a 139-post sample, physicians' labels gave 47%-48% for dialysis or transplantation (model 71%). Conclusion: Kidney-related posts carry context-specific information needs and emotional and practical burdens, many voiced by relatives. They suggest candidate responses (test-result explanation, diet support, family-directed information and support) that need evaluation. Keywords: chronic kidney disease; dialysis; patient experience; caregivers; social media; large language models
evidence_items.title: Patient- and Family-Expressed Needs and Burdens in Kidney-Related Online Discussions in Taiwan: Large Language Model-Based Analysis Across Clinical Contexts

evidence_items.summary: Objective: To describe and evaluate a framework for using a large language model (LLM) as the primary coder in health content analysis, and to propose reporting items for LLM assisted studies, because no reporting standard exists. Methods: An LLM coded 6,982 Instagram and TikTok posts using a human written, human calibrated instrument. The framework has six components: human authorship of the instrument; two round human calibration; source discipline; quote anchored coding; verification in a representative and an outcome enriched sample, blinded in both directions; and per variable reliability reporting against a prespecified threshold, with the consequence of failure fixed in advance. Agreement was measured with Gwets AC1, prespecified because the outcome distribution was heavily skewed. Results: Agreement between the two human coders on the primary outcome rose from AC1 0.456 to 0.977 after two ambiguous rules were rewritten. LLM human agreement was 0.847 in the representative sample (N = 150) and 0.868 in the enriched sample (N = 50). Five of eight conditional variables fell below the 0.80 threshold and became exploratory: variables asking whether a defined textual feature was present met it, whereas those requiring graded judgement did not. The human coder identified misinformation more often than the LLM, so prevalence estimates are likely underestimates. Agreement on female targeting was lower for self-identified ethnic minority creators (0.744 versus 0.902). Conclusion: LLM coding cannot be computationally reproduced, so its reliability must be shown empirically: per variable agreement with independent human coding, the direction of remaining error, and a prespecified response to shortfall. The authors propose 18 reporting items for LLM assisted content analysis.
evidence_items.title: Using a large language model as the primary coder in health content analysis: a verification framework, per-variable reliability and proposed reporting items.

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Reliable preoperative classification and outcome prediction could improve management of locally advanced colorectal cancer. We retrospectively studied 879 participants from two centers, including 741 patients with locally advanced colorectal cancer and 138 with benign colorectal lesions. Clinical, radiomics, deep learning, and early fusion models were trained at center A ( n = 615) and independently tested at center B ( n = 264) using pretreatment contrast-enhanced computed tomography and clinical data. The clinical-radiomics nomogram achieved a test AUC of 0.957 for benign-malignant classification. For 3-year and 5-year overall survival, radiomics achieved test AUCs of 0.874 and 0.898, while fusion achieved 0.870 and 0.899, respectively. These findings identify CT radiomics as a promising digital biomarker for colorectal cancer stratification and show that early deep learning fusion offers limited incremental value over an optimized radiomics baseline.
evidence_items.title: Multicenter evaluation of radiomics and multimodal artificial intelligence for colorectal cancer diagnosis and survival prediction

organizations: Faculty of Education Sciences, Universidad Internacional de Valencia (VIU), Calle Pintor Sorolla 21, 46002 Valencia, Spain

evidence_items.summary: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping doctoral education, yet few empirically evaluated pedagogical models integrate AI literacy with research and teaching competence. This study examined changes associated with implementing the Dr. I.D.E.A. Model, which positions doctoral candidates who are also university teachers as co-researchers of their own research and teaching practice under an explicit responsible-AI framework. A participatory action research design with convergent triangulation was implemented during the 2025–2026 academic year. Thirty-four doctoral candidates participated in four collaborative virtual workshops organised through cycles of planning, action, observation and critical reflection. Self-report measures administered at three time points were integrated with interviews, focus groups, observation notes, reflective logbooks and independently verified academic products. Self-reported research competence, AI-supported digital competence and creative-pedagogical competence increased significantly between each pair of measurement points (pre–post dₐᵥ = 1.83, 2.10 and 1.69, respectively). All participants integrated generative AI into at least one university course, and 76.5% implemented a sustained course redesign. Because the design lacked a comparison group and relied on perceived competence, maturation, testing effects, response-shift bias and the programme’s ordinary activities may also account for the changes. The findings are therefore associative rather than causal and constitute preliminary evidence that warrants controlled replication in other doctoral contexts.
evidence_items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence in Doctoral Education: A Participatory Action Research Evaluation of the Dr. I.D.E.A. Model

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Literacies are not static competencies. They are dynamic; situated historically, politically, and socially; and fundamental to driving and responding to change in communication environments. Something has shifted as platforms have turned to their massive, accumulated datasets of user content and interactions to train artificial intelligence (AI) models while integrating new AI-driven features and content, processes that are fundamentally changing how people engage with platforms—or refuse to play. Users of social media platforms have had to adapt to the demands of data extraction, consider and defend their privacy and their intellectual property, or leverage evolving attention metrics for visibility and profit. As platforms integrate a diverse range of new data-driven AI features, users also have to renegotiate how they engage critically and competently. With the visibility and engagement game evolving, what does this mean for the development of new critical data literacies? In this chapter we explore the emerging implications this has for data and AI literacies and where they are heading.
evidence_items.title: Social Media Data Literacy in the Age of Artificial Intelligence

evidence_items.summary: Artificial intelligence has become a central component of society and its technological development, affecting all aspects of public, professional and private life. Computational tools and systems analyze data, generate predictions, and support decision-making across domains, shaping how problems are defined, how evidence is evaluated, and how actions are carried out. Many of these applications, and their consequences, involve animals. The use of artificial intelligence in domains impacting animals introduces new challenges for ethics and law that will be important in shaping society for decades to come. This chapter provides an introductory overview of artificial intelligence, animal ethics, and animal law as a foundation for understanding the issues involved in each, and at their emerging intersections.
evidence_items.title: An Introduction to Artificial Intelligence, Animal Ethics, and Animal Law

evidence_items.summary: Household food-waste surveys describe reported practices and attitudes but do not measure respondent-level wasted-food mass or composition. This study used a deliberately simple online questionnaire to examine digital engagement through a two-layer, benchmark-anchored framework. Among 386 respondents, 193 acknowledged household food waste: 49 ever-users of food-waste-related applications, 109 interested never-users, and 35 non-interested never-users. The observational layer examined associations with reported ever use and stated future interest through adjusted logistic regression. A separate, explicitly conditional modeling layer combined a published edible-food-waste mass benchmark, 12 external category shares and impact coefficients, and question B3 identifying the food category wasted most frequently. Reported ever use was associated with a fresh-produce B3 response (adjusted OR = 8.29; 95% CI: 2.95–23.29); the future-interest model showed limited cross-validated discrimination (AUC = 0.606). At the illustrative scenario setting τ = 2, modeled economic and carbon intensities were 2.85% and 3.24% lower for ever-users than for non-interested never-users. Excluding rare B3 responses attenuated the economic and carbon contrasts by 40.6% and 47.1%, respectively; the basic bootstrap carbon interval included zero. These conditional contrasts reflect the selected frequency-to-composition assumption and common mass benchmark, not observed changes in food-waste mass or demonstrated benefits from application use. The framework provides a transparent, reproducible exploratory bridge between questionnaire profiles and published environmental parameters.
evidence_items.title: Digital Engagement and Household Food-Waste Profiles: A Two-Layer Framework for Benchmark-Anchored Economic and Carbon Impact Scenarios

evidence_items.summary: Abstract The interpretation of neutron scattering data remains a major bottleneck in materials discovery, as it demands an iterative cycle of data reduction, modeling, and refinement. That is too time-consuming for experts and too complex for novices. Here we introduce DrSai-Rongzai, an autonomous agent built on a large language model (LLM) that perfoms joint neutron powder diffraction (NPD) and pair-distribution-function (PDF) analysis without human intervention. Deployed at the China Spallation Neutron Source (CSNS), the agent orchestrates established refinement software through a hierarchical “Reasoning + Acting” framework. Its core innovation, Agentic Context Operation (ACO), maintains a coherent ‘working memory’ of file paths, intermediate results, and domain-specific rules across entire processing steps, even when the underlying large language model undergoes context compression. Across reference materials (Si, CsAgTe and Bi2MoO6), the agent refined structural parameters statistically indistinguishable from expert-derived solutions, while requiring markedly fewer iterative cycles. In an exhaustive 18-run factorial ablation study on two high-entropy alloys, we systematically evaluated the MemoWrite and CoreSkillWrite in ACO mechanisms with and without 50k-token context compression, quantifying the necessity of each component. Memo improved both mean composite performance and repeatability even without compression (+ 20.2% and + 11.3%, respectively). Under compression, Memo improved these metrics by + 10.7% and + 17.0%, and retaining CoreSkill provided a further + 12.5% and + 6.6% improvement, yielding a mean composite score of 0.9316 and repeatability stability of 0.9905 for full ACO. The agent is integrated with a permission-controlled CSNS data interface, enabling secure, on-demand analysis of user-proprietary data with automatic archiving.
evidence_items.title: An agentic AI neutron scattering data scientist at the China Spallation Neutron Source

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) analysis relies on computational methods that shape biological conclusions. Developing new methods requires identifying computational operations that address problem constraints to produce intended effects. Here we investigate coordinated agents that extract methodological reasoning from full-text literature and reuse it as prior knowledge for method hypothesis generation. We instantiate this approach as scHypothesizer, a knowledge-grounded agentic framework that uses Mechanism-centered Generation (MCG) to formulate hypotheses from literature-derived Research Primitive Knowledge Graphs (RPKGs) and subjects them to early empirical assessment. We show that coordinated agents recover source-supported reasoning and that full-text RPKGs preserve more complete reasoning than abstract-only representations. In time-filtered retrospective evaluation of 2,429 Problems, MCG achieved the best ranking performance among compared retrieval methods, with a query-macro AUROC of 0.783 and Hit@10 of 69.1%. Finally, scHypothesizer supported early empirical assessment of four researcher-approved hypotheses, providing informative evidence regarding intended Effects, the settings in which they hold, and associated limitations. Together, these results suggest that coordinated agents can make methodological reasoning from prior studies reusable as source-traceable knowledge for generating new method hypotheses and informing their early empirical assessment.
evidence_items.title: A Knowledge-grounded Agentic Framework for Single-cell RNA Sequencing Method Hypothesis Generation

evidence_items.summary: Abstract Agentic artificial intelligence transforms self-correction from a localized answer-revision problem into a system-level reliability and recovery challenge. In autonomous, stateful, and long-horizon systems, early errors can propagate through reasoning, planning, retrieval, tool use, external actions, multi-agent interaction, and persistent memory. However, existing research often treats self-correction as either response-level refinement or a capability within broader agent architectures. This study develops an agent-level perspective that connects these fragmented views. It distinguishes reasoning, reflection, verification, correction, and adaptation, emphasizing that reasoning or critique alone does not constitute self-correction unless evaluative information produces a subsequent behavioral change. The study introduces a unified corrective lifecycle covering anomaly detection, error diagnosis and localization, corrective evidence acquisition, repair, validation, commitment or rollback, memory updating, and continuation, termination, or escalation. Existing approaches are organized across five dimensions: correction target, feedback source, temporal scope, persistence, and control architecture. A comparative synthesis shows that self-correction is not uniformly beneficial: repeated reflection can improve performance, stagnate, or degrade initially correct behavior. More reliable gains generally arise when feedback is task-relevant, informative, and at least partially independent of the process that produced the error. The study also identifies key failure modes, including missed errors, unsuccessful repair, over-correction, error amplification, memory contamination, and objective misalignment. These findings motivate research on calibrated intervention, memory integrity, verification, rollback, cost-aware correction, human escalation, and resilience under distribution shift.
evidence_items.title: Self-Reflection and Self-Correction in Agentic AI: A Critical Review of Feedback, Verification, Memory, and Failure Modes

evidence_items.summary: Vision Language Models (VLMs) have shown remarkable capabilities in qualitative spatial reasoning, but remain limited in quantitative spatial reasoning. Current work leverages the VLM agent to invoke external vision tools to perform computation. However, these methods usually bind each functional requirement to a single predefined vision specialist, implicitly resulting in fixed and rigid tool pipelines. In practice, addressing diverse spatial scenarios and tasks demands a broader diversity in pipeline orchestration and vision specialist selection to achieve robust spatial reasoning. However, such diversity leads to a combinatorial execution space, making it challenging for the agent to orchestrate the optimal pipelines and specialists for different scenarios. In this work, we propose SpatialMem, a memory framework that enables a VLM agent to accumulate tool-use experience and leverage that memory to orchestrate vision specialists to solve the spatial reasoning problem. SpatialMem builds a two-level memory structure, with task memory capturing tool orchestration and scene memory capturing tool selection. It further introduces a dual-state trajectory optimization process to preserve successful tool experiences and refine suboptimal ones. Moreover, existing spatial reasoning benchmarks suffer from quality issues and limited coverage of scene types and tasks. To address these gap, we propose MetricBench, a benchmark covering both indoor and outdoor scenes and three quantitative spatial reasoning tasks. Our method achieves state-of-the-art results on MetricBench, Q-Spatial, and SpatilRGPT-Bench, outperforming best VLM baselines by 32% on MetricBench. Additionally, the memory design yields a 9.1% absolute gain over a memory-free agent on MetricBench.
evidence_items.title: SpatialMem: Building Quantitative Spatial Reasoning Agents with Hierarchical Memory

evidence_items.summary: --> （＊日本語は英文の後に） Sakana AI is launching the Security Research Group, an independent R&D team studying collective, AI-driven cyber defense and the security and safety of AI itself. Our research starts from the idea that intelligence and resilience emerge from collectives, like a school of fish rather than a single swimmer. As a company building frontier AI, we also believe we share responsibility for the security of the society that uses it. Separate from our commercial business, the group’s mission is to serve the public interest: publishing research, reproducible benchmarks, and practical guidelines, and working with government, industry, and academia on research to improve cybersecurity. What We Are Seeing Frontier AI’s ability to find flaws in software is growing, and the number of disclosed flaws is climbing. 1 NIST reports that CVE submissions rose 263% between 2020 and 2025, and that early 2026 ran nearly a third above the same period a year earlier. 2 JVN iPedia, which provides vulnerability information in Japanese, also registered nearly twice as many entries in the latest quarter as a year earlier, most of them from the NVD. 3 AI is widely suspected to play a part, though there is still more to confirm: FIRST points to AI-assisted discovery alongside administrative factors, and NIST staff say AI-based discovery tools have added to their workload. 4 Japan’s government now treats the trend as a national security matter. 1 The strain is already showing. NIST has stopped routine analysis of older records and now prioritizes flaws known to be exploited. 5 Japan’s financial regulators have asked institutions to treat the response as a management issue, with top management directly involved. 6 Flaws are being found at machine speed and fixed at organizational speed, and we suspect the people in between are the ones bearing the cost. The other side is changing too. Attackers are using AI agents, running intrusions against many targets at once.
evidence_items.title: Introducing Sakana AI’s Security Research Group

evidence_items.summary: Learning and inference on time series can pose significant statistical challenges, including autocorrelated observations, distribution shift over time, and the curse of dimensionality. These challenges complicate the practical application of causal discovery algorithms, which already suffer from high computational and sample complexity in the general case. To mitigate these issues, this work introduces Iterative Temporal Parent Discovery (ITPD): a sound and complete constraint-based procedure for causal structure learning on multivariate time series with causal nonstationarity. ITPD takes a local-to-global learning approach that discovers the global graph by sequentially discovering the parent set for each variable. ITPD exploits temporal structural priors, graph partitioning, and the local Markov condition to swap higher-order conditional independence tests for lower-order alternatives. With an exact oracle, ITPD performed the least number of tests and used the smallest average conditioning set sizes relative to baselines. In benchmarking simulations, ITPD sat on the Pareto frontier with respect to F1 and wall-clock time and was faster than baselines on large graphs (geq 1000 nodes). For graphs with 2000 nodes, ITPD ran 2.3times, 9.1times, and 40.9times faster than iterative IAMB, DF-PC, and PCMCI, respectively.
evidence_items.title: Time Series Structure Learning with Local Causal Parent Discovery

evidence_items.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse tasks from visual observations and language instructions. While prior work has explored task suppression and refusal, stopping prohibited behavior once execution is underway and controlling the resulting physical response remain challenging. Our evaluation reveals that policies which suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway through execution. Even when the task remains unfinished, the robot may drop a held object, making non-completion an incomplete measure of safety. To address these challenges, we introduce State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative response. SAFI comprises two stages, (1) fallback target construction, which assigns stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, and (2) joint policy adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. This supervision teaches an explicit alternative response at intermediate execution states while maintaining the robot's other skills. Extensive experiments with OpenVLA-OFT across LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks evaluate prohibited completion, physical incidents, and retained-task performance. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduces aggregate target success after takeover to 1.3\%, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while preserving high retained-task success.
evidence_items.title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models to Stop Safely

evidence_items.summary: An assistant monitoring a person performing a procedure is most useful when it can detect mistakes while there is still time to recover. This requires judging actions against task instructions as the video unfolds, identifying the attempted step, locating it in time, and assessing its execution. Existing online detectors do not use the instruction text, while instruction-conditioned methods operate offline. In this paper, we study online, instruction-conditioned mistake detection in egocentric videos. Using only observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions, our model identifies and localizes completed action attempts and classifies them as correct, modified, slip, corrections, or additions; omitted steps are determined after the video ends. We compare a modular pipeline, with separate step identification, temporal localization, and execution verification, to a joint model that predicts all outputs in a single step. To support supervised learning from mistakes, we repartition EgoPER to include erroneous videos in all splits. The approaches achieve similar step-segmentation F1@0.5 (93.6% and 92.1%), while the joint model achieves higher binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 (84.1% vs. 80.7%), with its largest gain on slips (56.4% vs. 37.5%). Component-level analysis suggests that error propagation between stages contributes to the modular approach's lower detection score. On test videos containing mistakes, both designs outperform released AEM and ESTANet checkpoints under our evaluation protocol.
evidence_items.title: Online Mistake Detection in Instruction-Conditioned Procedural Video

evidence_items.summary: Recently, video world models have advanced interactive generation, with large models offering higher quality and smaller models enabling faster inference. Existing speculative methods combine their strengths through fast draft generation and selective target regeneration guided by rewards on decoded frames. However, verification covers only the external scorer's evaluation dimensions and adds decoding and scoring costs. Moreover, these scores provide no correction, requiring costly target regeneration for rejected drafts. To address these limitations, we propose Speculative World Model (SpecWM), a unified, training-free inference framework for streaming world models. It verifies draft chunks using the target's latent velocity field. Verification also yields a reusable correction; two thresholds select Accept, Refine, or Reject. Specifically, one-step refinement reuses it to improve perceptual quality, while three-step refinement strengthens camera following and trajectory consistency. These findings motivate transition-aware refinement. On WBench Navigation, SpecWM improves visual quality at 1.63times speedup over the target and raises NavScore from the draft's 75.99 to 85.63, achieving the best quality-speed-control trade-off. Additionally, our LongSpecBench shows sustained quality and control over long, multi-turn rollouts, while experiments on Hy-Nomas validate SpecWM across backbones and denoising budgets.
evidence_items.title: SpecWM: Turning Verification into Refinement for Streaming World Models

evidence_items.summary: World models aim to predict environment dynamics under actions, enabling the prediction of action consequences without executing them in the real world. Yet despite producing increasingly realistic videos, current world models often fail to capture how small action changes affect future observations. This limits their use in tasks such as robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning, where nearly identical actions can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. To address this, we propose AFFECT, an auxiliary training objective for learning the distribution of visual changes induced by action perturbations. Specifically, we inject temporally correlated noise into the actions of a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation. We then train the world model so that its generated videos respond to this noise as the recorded videos do, without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state. Across OGBench simulation and real-world DROID and ALOHA-2 setups, AFFECT makes world-model rollouts more faithful to real outcomes. On DROID, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates in the world model and on the real robot rises from 0.47 to 0.79, alongside up to 23% lower FVD. These gains carry over to planning, where selecting actions with AFFECT-trained world models improves task success by up to 8.3%.
evidence_items.title: Learning What Actions Change: Action Effect Matching for Dynamics-Faithful World Models

evidence_items.summary: Representative vision-language navigation (VLN) methods typically couple a vision-language model (VLM) brain with a learnable action head and fine-tune the VLM brain on navigation-domain data to predict geometric goals. However, such adaptation can substantially alter base VLM weights and degrade general visual capabilities. We introduce ZeroVLN, a slow-fast navigation framework that achieves effective navigation with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain. Rather than teaching the brain to predict geometric goals, we equip it with a semantic tool-calling interface for conveying movement decisions to an action expert in natural language. We first adapt the action expert to carry out these movement requests, then jointly improve the brain's movement decisions and the action expert's continuous execution through closed-loop reinforcement learning (RL). Trained on the same navigation episodes, ZeroVLN substantially outperforms representative SFT-based hierarchical VLN methods on standard VLN-CE (continuous environments) benchmarks, while inducing only minor changes to the brain's weights and largely preserving its general capabilities. To our knowledge, ZeroVLN is the first slow-fast VLN framework with zero navigation-domain SFT of the VLM brain, and the first to jointly optimize its slow and fast policies through closed-loop agentic RL in VLN-CE.
evidence_items.title: ZeroVLN: Learning to Navigate without Supervised Fine-Tuning of the VLM Brain

evidence_items.summary: Diffusion distillation accelerates image and video generation by compressing a pretrained teacher's iterative sampling process into a few network evaluations. Distribution-based methods achieve this by matching the student's output distribution to the teacher's. This matching is often driven by reverse-KL objectives, whose mode-seeking bias favors dominant teacher modes at the expense of diversity across samples. We introduce Posterior Matching Distillation (PMD), a new member of the distribution-based distillation family that combines mode-covering posterior sampling with any-step generation. At zero population loss, PMD recovers the teacher's full posterior of clean images at each trained noise level. Its stochastic student supports any-step sampling budgets within the trained timestep grid without further training. To learn these posteriors, PMD matches exponentially reweighted averages of student samples conditioned on a fixed noisy state to corresponding teacher posterior means. Under Gaussian corruption, exponentially tilted posterior mean is a single teacher evaluation at a shifted input. We prove that, matching tilted means over an open neighborhood uniquely identifies the full posterior. PMD thus supervises the entire conditional distribution through a family of mean constraints, without any auxiliary student-score network. Experiments on SDXL and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B demonstrate that PMD achieves the best FID among 4-step methods on both models, while maintaining competitive or leading performance across prompt-alignment and perceptual-quality metrics.
evidence_items.title: Posterior Matching Distillation

evidence_items.summary: Task success alone does not specify which behaviors post-training should reinforce. Even successful teacher trajectories can contain unsupported assumptions, unproductive repetition, or superficial verification. We propose Skill-FT (Skill-Guided Fine-Tuning), which uses natural-language skills to suppress undesirable habits and elicit underrepresented effective behaviors during teacher rollouts, then fine-tunes a target model on the resulting trajectories. We introduce AutoMaster, an autonomous post-training system in which an LLM agent develops these interventions through trajectory analysis, skill design, data selection, and feedback from rollouts and target-model evaluation. Across Terminal, Search, and software engineering tasks with 4B and 9B target models, AutoMaster improves mean performance over Vanilla SFT on successful unguided teacher trajectories by 1.42-8.99 percentage points, with the teacher, task pool, training set size, and SFT recipe held fixed. Together with the ablations and trajectory analyses, these results suggest that behavioral shaping can make a fixed model a more effective teacher. We further find that retaining skill instructions during SFT yields higher mean performance than removing them across all six settings, despite their absence at evaluation and identical supervised outputs. These findings suggest that preserving skill context as part of a training demonstration can support better behavioral internalization.
evidence_items.title: AutoMaster: Autonomous Post-Training by Making the Same Model a Better Teacher

evidence_items.summary: Humans act in the visual world by inferring the 3D layout behind a 2D view, predicting how an action changes it, and correcting themselves after seeing the result. Can multimodal large language models (MLLMs) do the same? CAPTCHAs offer a natural test, since humans solve them through this very loop, clicking and dragging on the screen and adjusting after each result. Yet existing CAPTCHA benchmarks are largely solved and rarely spatial, while spatial benchmarks rarely require action. We therefore present TuringSpace, a synthetic web environment of 125 interactive CAPTCHAs that span five spatial abilities and must be solved through clicks and drags on the screen. Every task is a program that generates new instances with a checker and an oracle, so the tasks also form a scalable training gym. Humans solve 94.1% of the tasks, whereas the best model, GPT-6 Astra, still fails 25.9% of them, and the best open-weight model, Kimi K3, fails 68.0%. Our further analysis shows that most failures come from misreading the screenshot, and that model reasoning rarely corrects a wrong belief but hallucinates evidence to defend it. To test whether such spatial abilities can be learned, we fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this gym. Its success rate rises from 1.6% to 33.1%, above Kimi K3, and it improves on all seven out-of-distribution benchmarks, including a 9.9-point gain on the real-world indoor videos of VSI-Bench. These results show that grounding spatial intelligence in screen actions exposes what MLLMs lack and offers a scalable way to teach it, with gains that transfer to real-world scenes. We will release TuringSpace to support further study.
evidence_items.title: TuringSpace: Grounding Spatial Intelligence in Action with Interactive CAPTCHAs

evidence_items.summary: Experimentation teams must decide which proposed website changes to test with live traffic. We evaluated whether forecasts from simulated shoppers could inform that choice. We screened 412 historical website A/B tests and evaluated four systems on the 318 that ran longer than 21 days. Each system predicted an original win, a variant win, or an inconclusive result. Page roles were masked and recorded outcomes were withheld during inference. Squoosh UX-1, a model fine-tuned on human browsing data, simulated 1,000 shoppers per arm and correctly classified 267 of 318 outcomes (84.0%, 95% Wilson interval 79.5-87.6%, treating experiments as independent). Qwen3 Next 80B, the strongest general-purpose configuration on outcome accuracy, correctly classified 196 of 318 (61.6%). UX-1 favored the variant in 126 experiments. In the live tests, 118 of those variants won (93.7%), four lost, and four had inconclusive results. The remaining 192 experiments included 19 additional variant wins.
evidence_items.title: Squoosh Bench: Evaluating UX-1 on 318 Historical Website A/B Tests

evidence_items.summary: Optical neural networks promise fast, energy-efficient computing, but every device departs from its design and must be trained with the hardware. In situ training relies on an expert-built calibrated digital model of each device or on gradient-free trial and error. Coding agents, large language models that write and run programs, have shown an emergent ability to understand and edit the weights of digital neural networks. Here we introduce optics as code, a method in which a coding agent trains an optical neural network from measurements alone, through a harness that returns camera images of its probes and requires a hypothesis per request. We discovered that the agent forms a physical understanding of the optics and reparametrizes the network with interpretable optical elements tuned on the hardware. It outperforms gradient-free methods in classification and image encoding, approaching backpropagation through a calibrated model at a fraction of the cost. Needing neither per-device calibration nor gradients through the hardware, and improving with more capable models, optics as code offers a practical route to large, scalable optical neural networks and a general tool for calibrating and optimizing optical experiments.
evidence_items.title: In Situ Training of Optical Neural Networks by Coding Agents

evidence_items.summary: Hybrid attention models combine full and linear attention to achieve a better quality--efficiency trade-off. Converting pretrained Transformers into such models requires identifying which layers should retain full attention under a prescribed budget. We identify two off-policy mismatches in FlashMorph's layer selection: (i) continuous branch interpolation and teacher-forced hidden states differ from discrete hybrid computation; and (ii) frozen model weights fail to account for parameter adaptation during subsequent recovery. We introduce FlashMorph2, an on-policy layer-selection method that (I) evaluates sampled discrete hybrid architectures end to end using their own hidden states, and (II) jointly optimizes layer-selection scores and model weights under the recovery objective to reflect post-adaptation performance. Experiments across Qwen3 model scales and linear-attention variants show that FlashMorph2 consistently outperforms existing layer-selection methods, improving average scores over FlashMorph by +2.42 points on RULER, +1.08 on LongBench, and +0.76 on recall-intensive tasks, while completing layer selection in only 0.72--3.57 GPU hours across 0.6B--8B models, demonstrating high efficiency and scalability.
evidence_items.title: On-Policy Morphing into Hybrid Attention Models

evidence_items.summary: Our aim is to accelerate autoregressive vision-language-action models (VLAs), which generate robot actions one token at a time. Speculative decoding makes this possible: a lightweight draft model proposes several tokens at once, and the VLA verifies them in a single pass, accepting only those that match its own predictions, so decoding remains lossless. The speedup, however, is limited in robot control, where many different tokens encode nearly the same motion and a draft close to the correct action is still rejected. To address this, our approach, VSpark, is built upon three design choices: (i) rollouts collected with calibrated action noise, which expose the draft to a wider range of robot states; (ii) feature alignment, which trains the draft to match the VLA's hidden features rather than its output tokens alone; and (iii) continuation reuse, which keeps the predictions the VLA has already computed along rejected drafts as candidates for the next verification step, instead of discarding them. On four VLAs with different action tokenizers and four manipulation benchmarks, VSpark achieves 1.28x to 2.10x speedup while keeping the VLA's decoding lossless.
evidence_items.title: VSpark: Speculative Decoding for Autoregressive Vision-Language-Action Models

evidence_items.summary: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training; we call this self-rewriting. Given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, a 27B model diagnoses its failure and edits the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in a test fixed in advance, and another session's edit also makes it significantly better. It keeps getting better: it submits an edit only when its own tests support it, each edit replacing the last, and over its first eight such sessions its accuracy only rises. Unlike test-time scaling, the gain persists in its weights and adds no cost per answer; unlike training, it needs no pre- or post-training infrastructure, only an open model and hours on one GPU. It repairs a damaged copy of itself: it locates the corrupted matrix and rewrites it with values of its own, never reading the undamaged weights; found on text math problems alone, the repair lifts the copy on six image benchmarks it never saw from 7% to 70% accuracy, 83% of the undamaged model's. And the ability emerges with scale: across four sizes of one family, the 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves; only the 27B model works on itself as a human would, comparing its hidden states on answers that finish and on answers that run out of tokens, weakening the direction that separates them. Like a human, a model need not separate training from inference; improving a language model may come to take a conversation rather than a training run.
evidence_items.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights

evidence_items.summary:
A direction in a language model's hidden state can be used to probe whether a concept is present or to steer the model toward it. Although probe directions are often reused for steering, the direction that best detects a concept need not be the one that best changes it. We study this distinction in three instruction-tuned models from different families. We construct a one-parameter family of directions ranging from a covariance-adjusted discriminant to the mean difference, and evaluate probing and additive steering, which adds the direction to the hidden state, along the family at a fixed side effect. For truthfulness and sentiment, in every model, the best probe is not the best steering direction: steering consistently favors directions closer to the mean difference. This separation holds across 59 of 60 layer-model-concept combinations in a layer sweep, with matched probe and steering texts in all six model-concept combinations, and under a rotation-based steering operator. The exact steering optimum is less stable: for sentiment, an intermediate direction produces a 27-56% stronger steering effect than the mean difference, but this gain shrinks or disappears with matched texts and depends on the layer and the operator.
  The two roles also transfer differently across models. A probe transferred by a linear map fitted on neutral text retains 81-91% of the target model's above-chance probing performance, while the transferred mean difference retains less of its steering effect in 11 of 12 model pairs. This is a consistent tendency, although our predefined criteria classify only three pairs, and nine remain inconclusive. Finally, as an application on PopQA, steering toward "unknown" increases abstention by 18-44 percentage points on uncertain errors, versus 2-5 on confident errors, while rarely correcting errors in cases where a correct answer is reachable.
evidence_items.title: Do Probing and Steering Favor the Same Directions Within and Across Language Models?

evidence_items.summary: Image vectorization reconstructs raster images as compact scalable vector graph- ics (SVG), providing a structured and editable code representation of images. However, most existing vectorization methods optimize for pixel-level render- ing fidelity, often producing SVGs that lack alignment with human-perceived object-part hierarchies, making them difficult to manipulate. To address this, we propose Lang-SVG, which introduces an explicit tree structure to organize SVG primitives with semantic labels and parent-child relationships. Lang-SVG incorporates granularity-controllable and open-vocabulary segmentation priors to initialize object-part hierarchies and leverages multimodal large language models (MLLMs) with SVG tree context to assign semantic labels to unlabeled nodes. To reduce redundancy, we introduce depth-adaptive simplification to reduce shape complexity and Tree-Guided Pruning and Merging to eliminate redundant SVG nodes. L1-SAM-Prompting further recovers missing regions to improve recon- struction fidelity and structural completeness. Beyond reconstruction fidelity, we introduce a new evaluation protocol that measures structural quality and semantic part alignment. Experiments demonstrate that Lang-SVG achieves state-of-the-art performance in both rendering fidelity and structural quality. Project website: https://xiliu8006.github.io/Lang-SVG/.
evidence_items.title: Lang-SVG: Hierarchical Image Vectorization with Language Priors

cards.blurb: QUANTA is a new English-to-Arabic machine-translation error dataset organized into a four-level taxonomy with 23 detailed error classes and severity-oriented analysis, rather than collapsing heterogeneous translation failures into one score.
cards.title: Quanta: A Fine-Grained Dataset and Benchmark for Arabic Machine-Translation Error Analysis
